en: Having entered the great Daṇḍaka forest,
the self-possessed and invincible Rāma beheld a circle of hermitages belonging to ascetics.
Enveloped in a garment of kusha grass and cloth, and surrounded by Brahmanic splendor,
he was as unassailable as the blazing orb of the sun in the sky.
It was a refuge for all beings, with its courtyards always well-swept,
and it was constantly honored and attended by throngs of Apsarases who danced before it.
It was adorned with spacious fire-sanctuaries, sacrificial ladles and vessels, deerskins, kusha grass, sacrificial fuel, water-jars, and fruits and roots.
It was surrounded by great forest trees that were holy and bore sweet fruit;
it was consecrated with offerings and oblations, auspicious, and resounded with the chanting of the Vedas.
It was surrounded by wild flowers and a lotus pond filled with lotuses,
and was inhabited by self-controlled men who subsisted on fruits and roots and were clothed in bark and black antelope skins.
It was surrounded by ancient sages who shone like the sun and Vaiśvānara,
and graced by holy supreme seers who were restrained in their diet.
That place was as radiant as the abode of Brahmā, resounded with the chanting of the Vedas,
and graced by highly fortunate Brahmins who were knowers of Brahman.
Having seen that circle of ascetics' hermitages, the glorious Rāghava,
possessed of great splendor, approached it after unstringing his mighty bow.
Endowed with divine knowledge, those great seers, upon seeing Rāma and the illustrious Vaidehī, then approached them with joy.
Seeing him rising like the moon, those practitioners of dharma,
firm in their vows, welcomed him while offering auspicious blessings.
Those dwelling in the forest gazed upon Rāma’s physical form, his majesty, his delicacy, and his elegant attire, their faces filled with wonder.
All those forest-dwellers gazed upon Vaidehī, Lakṣmaṇa, and Rāma with unblinking eyes, as if they were beings of wonder.
For those highly fortunate ones, devoted to the welfare of all beings,
settled Rāghava, their guest, within the leaf-hut.
Then those highly fortunate practitioners of dharma, resembling fire in their splendor, respectfully brought water for Rāma according to the prescribed rites.
Having offered roots, flowers, fruits, forest produce, and a hermitage to the high-souled one,
those knowers of dharma then spoke with palms joined in reverence.
The protector of this people, a refuge, and one of great renown;
the king is worthy of worship and honor, the wielder of the rod of punishment, and the preceptor.
O Raghava, a king protects his subjects as if they were a fourth part of Indra;
therefore, honored by the world, he enjoys excellent pleasures.
As inhabitants of your domain, we are to be protected by you;
whether you reside in the city or in the forest, you are our king and lord of men.
"O King, we have laid down our staffs; we have conquered anger and subdued our senses.
You must always protect us, whose wealth is asceticism, as if we were embryos."
Having spoken thus, they honored Rāghava, along with Lakṣmaṇa, with wild fruits, roots, flowers, and various other kinds of food.
Likewise, other perfected ascetics, who were like fire in their brilliance and lived according to the righteous way, gratified the Lord Rāma in the proper manner.
Then Rāma, having been hospitably entertained until sunrise,
took leave of all the sages and plunged once more into the forest.
It was crowded with various herds of wild animals and frequented by tigers and wolves;
its trees, creepers, and shrubs were devastated, and its reservoirs of water were difficult to discern.
Accompanied by Lakṣmaṇa, Rāma beheld the heart of the forest, which was silent of birds yet resounded with the chirping of swarms of crickets.
But in the midst of that forest, which was filled with fierce wild beasts, the descendant of Kakutstha beheld a man-eater of great roar, resembling a mountain peak.
With deep-set eyes and a large mouth, hideous and with a misshapen belly,
loathsome, uneven, tall, deformed, and terrible to behold.
He was wearing a tiger skin, wet with fat and smeared with blood;
he was a terror to all beings, like Death itself with its mouth wide open.
Three lions, four tigers, two wolves, ten spotted deer,
and the great head of an elephant with its tusks, smeared with fat.
Impaled upon an iron stake and crying out with a great sound,
he saw Rāma, Lakṣmaṇa, and Sītā, the princess of Mithilā.
Highly incensed, he rushed forward like Death the Destroyer at the end of an eon,
letting out a terrifying roar that seemed to shake the very earth.
Taking Vaidehī by the arm and stepping away from there, he said:
"Both of you, wearing matted hair and bark garments, shall live out your lives together with your wife."
Having entered the Daṇḍaka forest bearing arrows, bows, and swords,
how can you two ascetics dwell there together with a woman?
"Who are you two, wicked practitioners of unrighteousness and defilers of sages?
I am a Rākṣasa named Virādha, and this forest is my impenetrable domain."
"Armed and always wandering about, devouring the flesh of sages,
this woman of beautiful limbs shall become my wife;
and I shall drink the blood of you two wicked ones in battle."
Hearing these bold and arrogant words of that evil-minded Virādha as he spoke thus, Sītā, the daughter of Janaka, trembled with agitation like a plantain tree in a gale.
Seeing the auspicious Sītā held in Virādha’s embrace, Rāghava,
his face parched with grief, spoke these words to Lakṣmaṇa.
Behold, O gentle one, the daughter of King Janaka,
my wife of auspicious conduct, who was raised in extreme luxury— the illustrious princess now cast into the lap of Virādha.
O Lakṣmaṇa, that which was intended for us, that dear boon which was chosen, has now been fully realized for Kaikeyī— this very day, and swiftly.
That far-sighted middle mother of mine, who was not satisfied with sovereignty for the sake of her son,
and by whom I— intent on the welfare of all beings— was sent to the forest;
she has now had her desire fulfilled.
But from the touch of Vaidehī, O Saumitri, there is no sorrow for me greater than the death of my father and likewise the seizure of my own kingdom.
While the descendant of Kakutstha was speaking thus, overwhelmed by tears and grief,
Lakṣmaṇa, enraged and hissing like a confined serpent, spoke.
O descendant of Kakutstha, you are the protector of all beings like Indra himself; why do you grieve so, as if you were helpless, when I am here as your servant?
Today, when the Rākṣasa Virādha has been struck down by me with an arrow in my wrath,
the earth shall drink his lifeless blood.
The anger that I felt toward Bharata because of his desire for the kingdom—
that I shall now release upon Virādha, as the wielder of the thunderbolt hurls his bolt at a mountain.
Let my great arrow, impelled by the force and speed of my arm, fall upon his broad chest;
let it strip life from his body, and then let him fall to the earth, reeling.
Then Virādha, filling the forest with his voice, spoke these words again:
"Tell me who you are; you who question me, where are you going?"
Then Rāma, possessed of great splendor, spoke to that rakṣasa of flaming countenance as he was inquiring about his own Ikṣvāku lineage.
"Know us to be two Kṣatriyas, perfected in conduct, who dwell in the forest.
But we wish to know you: who are you that wanders through the Daṇḍaka woods?"
Virādha then spoke to Rāma, whose prowess is truth:
"Ah, O King, I shall tell you; listen to me, O descendant of Raghu."
"I am indeed the son of Jaya, and Śatahradā is my mother;
all the rākṣasas on earth call me Virādha."
Moreover, through my ascetic penance, I have obtained by the grace of Brahmā immunity from being slain by weapons in this world, as well as invulnerability to cutting and piercing.
"Abandoning this woman and disregarding her, go quickly as you came; protect yourselves, for I shall not take your lives."
With eyes bloodshot with anger, Rāma replied thus to that evil-minded Rākṣasa Virādha of deformed appearance.
"O wretched one, shame on you! You seek death for a trivial purpose;
you will certainly find it in battle. Stay! You shall not escape from me alive."
Then, having strung his bow and swiftly aimed well-sharpened arrows, Rāma struck down the rākṣasa.
With his bow strung with a bowstring, he released seven arrows—
gold-feathered, of great velocity, and moving like Garuda or the wind.
Having pierced the body of Virādha, those arrows adorned with peacock feathers fell upon the earth,
smeared with blood and resembling blazing fires.
Having let out a great roar and seizing a spear that resembled the banner of Indra,
he then appeared resplendent like Death himself with his mouth wide open.
Rāma, the best among wielders of weapons, severed that spear— which was like a thunderbolt and resembled a blazing fire in the sky— with two arrows.
The son of Sumitrā broke the left arm of that fierce one,
while Rāma swiftly broke the right arm of that Rākṣasa.
With his arm shattered, the Rākṣasa Virādha, who resembled a cloud, fell swiftly to the earth like a mountain split by a thunderbolt; distressed,
he spoke these words to Kākutstha, that bull among men.
O dear one, Kausalyā has borne noble offspring; I know you to be Rāma, as well as the highly blessed Vaidehī and the greatly illustrious Lakṣmaṇa.
"Due to a curse, I have entered this terrible rakshasa body;
for I am a gandharva named Tumburu, cursed by Vaiśravaṇa."
And being propitiated by me, that highly illustrious one said to me:
"When Rāma, the son of Daśaratha, shall slay you in battle..."
"Then, having returned to your true nature, you shall go to heaven," King Vaiśravaṇa said to him who was infatuated with Rambhā.
Not being attended to by me, he spoke to me in great anger:
"By your grace, I have been released from a most dreadful curse; I shall go to my own abode. May it be well with you, O scorcher of foes! (Rāmāyaṇa 3.3.21)
"O dear one, the righteous and powerful great seer Śarabhaṅga,
who resembles the sun, dwells here at a distance of one and a half yojanas."
Go to him quickly; he will provide for your welfare.
And having cast me into a pit, O Rāma, depart in safety.
This is the eternal law for Rākṣasas who have lost their lives:
those who are cast into a pit attain eternal worlds.
Having spoken thus to the descendant of Kakutstha, the mighty Virādha, afflicted by the arrows, cast off his body and attained heaven.
Lifting up Virādha by his throat, with his ears pricked and making a great noise, he threw him—
who was roaring with a terrifying sound— into a pit.
Then, having slain those two Rākṣasas who wielded variegated golden bows and having recovered the princess of Mithilā,
they roamed joyfully in the great forest like the sun and the moon stationed in the sky.
Having slain that Rākṣasa Virādha of terrible strength in the forest,
the valiant Rāma then embraced Sītā and comforted her,
and spoke to his brother Lakṣmaṇa, who was possessed of radiant splendor.
"This forest is difficult and perilous, and we are not natives of the woods;
let us go quickly to Śarabhaṅga, whose wealth is his asceticism."
Rāghava went to the hermitage of Śarabhaṅga.
In the presence of that Śarabhaṅga, whose soul was purified by austerity and who possessed divine power, he beheld a great marvel.
He beheld the Lord of the Gods, resplendent with a body like that of the sun or the fire Vaiśvānara, not touching the earth.
The god was adorned with beautiful radiance, wearing stainless garments,
and was being worshipped by many high-souled beings of his own kind.
Not far from him, he beheld a chariot moving through the atmosphere, yoked with bay horses and resembling the rising sun.
He beheld a spotless umbrella, resembling a mass of white clouds and like the orb of the moon, adorned with variegated garlands.
Two excellent chowries with golden handles, of great value,
were held by two forest women and fanned over his head.
Many Gandharvas, Amaras, Siddhas,
and supreme ṛṣis praised the god stationed in the sky with the most excellent words.
Having seen Śatakratu there, Rāma said to Lakṣmaṇa:
"Those divine horses of Puruhūta Śakra that we have heard of in the past, moving through the atmosphere— these must surely be those very ones."
And these tiger-like men, O tiger among men, who stand on both sides of the chariot—
hundreds upon hundreds of youths wearing earrings and holding swords in their hands.
O son of Sumitrā, upon the chests of them all hang necklaces resembling blazing fire,
and they bear the appearance of twenty-five-year-olds.
For this, it is said, is the eternal age of the gods,
such as that which these tigers among men are seen to possess, so pleasing to behold.
"Stay here for a moment with Vaidehī, Lakṣmaṇa,
while I ascertain clearly who this radiant being is on the chariot."
Having thus spoken to the son of Sumitrā, saying, "Stay right here," the descendant of Kakutstha proceeded toward the hermitage of Śarabhaṅga.
Then, seeing that Rāma was approaching, the Lord of Śacī,
having taken leave of Śarabhaṅga, spoke these words to the gods:
"Before that Rāma arrives here and addresses me, bring this matter to its conclusion;
only then will he deign to see me."
"Before long, I shall behold him victorious and having accomplished his purpose;
for he must perform a great task that is exceedingly difficult for others. (Rāmāyaṇa 3.4.19)
Having thus addressed and honored that ascetic, the Vajra-wielder,
the subduer of enemies, departed for heaven in a chariot yoked with bay horses.
When the thousand-eyed Indra had departed, Rāghava, accompanied by his retinue,
approached Śarabhaṅga, who was seated performing the Agnihotra sacrifice.
Having clasped his feet, Rāma, Sītā, and Lakṣmaṇa sat down with his permission,
having been invited and granted lodging.
Then Rāghava inquired about Śakra’s arrival,
and Śarabhaṅga reported all of that to Rāghava.
"O Rāma, this granter of boons wishes to lead me to the world of Brahmā,
which has been won by fierce asceticism and is difficult for those of undisciplined souls to attain."
"O tiger among men, knowing that you were nearby,
I did not go to the world of Brahmā without having seen you, my beloved guest."
Having met with you, O tiger among men, I shall go to the third heaven frequented by the gods; for I have won imperishable and auspicious worlds—
both those of Brahmā and those on the vault of the sky— so please accept these gifts from me.
Thus addressed by the seer Śarabhaṅga, Rāghava, that tiger among men and master of all scriptures, spoke these words.
"O great sage, I myself shall bring all the people;
however, I desire that a dwelling place be assigned for me here in this forest."
Thus addressed by Rāghava, who possesses strength equal to that of Śakra,
the highly wise Śarabhaṅga spoke these words once again.
Go to the very austere ascetic Sutīkṣṇa in a pure and delightful forest region; he will provide you with a dwelling.
This is the path, O tiger among men; look at me for a moment, my dear, while I cast off these limbs like a snake sheds its worn-out skin.
Then, having kindled the fire and offered oblations of clarified butter with mantras,
the highly effulgent Śarabhaṅga, who was learned in sacred formulas, entered the consuming flame.
The fire consumed the body hair and the head hair of that high-souled one,
as well as his aged skin, bones, flesh, and blood.
And that youth, resembling fire, was born;
rising from that heap of flames, Śarabhaṅga shone with splendor.
Passing beyond the worlds of those who maintain the sacred fires, of the high-souled sages,
and of the gods, he ascended to the world of Brahmā.
That bull among brahmins, a man of meritorious deeds, beheld the Grandfather (Brahmā) together with his attendants in that world;
and the Grandfather, seeing that twice-born one, rejoiced and said, "A most welcome greeting to you! (Rāmāyaṇa 3.4.36).
When Śarabhaṅga had attained heaven, the assembled hosts of sages approached Rāma, the descendant of Kakutstha, who blazed with radiant splendor.
There were Vaikhānasas, Vālakhilyas, Samprakṣālas, Marīcipas,
many Aśmakuṭṭas, and ascetics who subsisted on leaves.
Some were "tooth-mortarers," while others were "surface-swimmers"; some sages subsisted on water, and others still lived on air alone.
Some dwell in the open air, while others sleep on the bare ground; likewise, there are those who live in the upper stories, self-controlled, and those who wear only wet garments.
Accompanied by their prayers, constant in austerity, and likewise engaged in the fivefold penance,
all those ascetics— endowed with Brahmanic splendor and firmly established in yoga—
approached Rāma at the hermitage of Śarabhaṅga.
Having approached Rāma, the knower of dharma and the best among the upholders of dharma,
the assembled hosts of sages, being composed in mind, spoke to him who was supremely learned in dharma.
You are the great chariot-warrior of this Ikṣvāku lineage and of the entire earth;
you are the foremost and the protector, like Maghavan among the gods.
Renowned throughout the three worlds for both your glory and your prowess,
in you reside devotion to your father, truthfulness, and abundant righteousness.
"O Lord, having approached you, a high-souled one who knows the dharma and loves righteousness, we shall speak out of our need; you ought to forgive us for that."
But great unrighteousness, my dear, would accrue to that lord of the earth who takes a sixth part as tax yet does not protect [his subjects] like his own children.
Like one harnessing his own vital breaths with his very life-force, as if tending to beloved sons,
he remained ever-yoked and constantly protected all those dwelling within his realm.
O Rāma, he attains eternal fame lasting for many years;
having reached the station of Brahmā, he is honored there as well.
Whatever supreme dharma a sage who subsists on roots and fruits performs,
a fourth part of that belongs to the king who protects his subjects in accordance with dharma.

"O Rāma, this great community of forest-dwellers, consisting mostly of brahmins, has you as its protector; yet, being like those without a protector, it is being violently slaughtered by the rākṣasas."
"Come, behold the bodies of many sages of purified souls, slain in various ways by the terrible Rākṣasas in the forest."
A great slaughter is being carried out against those who dwell by the Pampā river, those along the Mandākinī as well, and those whose home is Citrakūṭa.
Thus, we cannot endure this terrible mistreatment being inflicted upon the ascetics in the forest by Rākṣasas of fearsome deeds.
Therefore, we have approached you, the worthy refuge, for the sake of protection;
O Rāma, protect us as we are being slaughtered by the night-stalkers.
Having heard this from the ascetics performing austerities, the righteous-souled descendant of Kakutstha spoke thus to all those ascetics:
"It does not behove you to speak to me in this manner; I am one who must be commanded by the ascetics."
"I have come here by chance for the sake of accomplishing your purpose;
thus, this dwelling of mine in the forest shall bear great fruit.
Desiring to slay my enemies, the Rākṣasas, I wish to fight alongside these ascetics. (Rāmāyaṇa 3.5.20)
Having granted a boon to those whose wealth is asceticism, the hero, his soul fixed on righteousness, departed with Lakṣmaṇa;
honored for his conduct by the ascetics, he proceeded toward Sutīkṣṇa.
But Rāma, the scorcher of his foes, together with his brother and Sītā,
went to the hermitage of Sutīkṣṇa along with those twice-born ones.
Having traveled a long distance and crossed rivers with abundant waters,
he beheld a vast mountain rising high like a great cloud.
Then those two descendants of Raghu, the best of the Ikṣvākus, entered that forest together with Sītā, which was constantly filled with various kinds of trees.
Having entered the formidable forest, which was filled with trees bearing many flowers and fruits,
he beheld a hermitage in a secluded spot, adorned with garlands of bark-cloth.
There, Rāma addressed Sutīkṣṇa, who was seated as an ascetic, covered in dirt and matted hair, and advanced in his penance, according to the prescribed custom.
"I am Rāma, O Blessed One; I have come to see you.
Therefore, address me, O knower of dharma, great seer of true valor."
Then, having gazed upon the hero Rāma, the best among the upholders of dharma,
and having embraced him with both arms, he spoke these words.
"Welcome indeed to you, O hero Rāma, best among the upholders of dharma! Now that this hermitage has been entered by you, it is as if it has found its protector."
O illustrious hero, awaiting you alone,
I shall not ascend from this earth to the world of the gods after casting off my body upon the ground.
"I have heard that you were deprived of your kingdom when you took up residence at Citrakūṭa.
Now that the descendant of Kakutstha has arrived here, the king of the gods, Śatakratu,
declares all the worlds conquered by my meritorious deeds."
In these regions frequented by celestial sages, which have been conquered by me through asceticism,
you may dwell and sport with your wife and Lakṣmaṇa by my grace.
To that great ṛṣi, who was resplendent with fierce asceticism and truthful in speech,
the self-controlled Rāma replied, as Vāsava might reply to Brahmā.
"O great sage, I myself shall bring the worlds;
however, I desire a dwelling place designated for me here in this forest."
"You are skilled in all things and devoted to the welfare of all beings; so it was told by the high-souled Gautama Śarabhaṅga. (Rāmāyaṇa 3.6.14)
Thus addressed by Rāma, the great seer, renowned throughout the world,
spoke these sweet words, overflowing with great joy.
This very hermitage, O Rāma, is full of virtues; let it be enjoyed here, for it is frequented by hosts of sages and always provided with roots and fruits.
O highly illustrious one, having come to this hermitage and wandered about, herds of deer,
fearless from any quarter, depart after having been enticed by you.
Having heard those words of the great seer, the steadfast elder brother of Lakṣmaṇa drew his bow with an arrow fixed and spoke these words.
O highly fortunate one, I would slay those assembled herds of deer with a sharp-edged arrow possessing the brilliance of a thunderbolt.
If you were to become attached to that, what could be more distressing than that?
However, I do not consider it appropriate to dwell in this hermitage for long.
Having thus addressed the granter of boons, Rāma approached the evening twilight;
having performed the evening prayers, he made his dwelling there for the night.

Then, at the conclusion of the twilight prayers and observing that night had fallen, the high-souled Sutīkṣṇa himself, having honored them with great respect, gave those two bulls among men auspicious food fit for ascetics.
But Rāma, together with the son of Sumitrā, having been honored by Sutīkṣṇa and having passed the night there,
woke up at dawn.
Having risen at the proper time, Rāghava, together with Sītā,
performed his ablutions with very cool water scented with the fragrance of lotuses.
Then, at dawn, in that forest which was a refuge for ascetics, Vaidehī duly worshipped the fire, the gods, Rāma, and Lakṣmaṇa according to the prescribed rites.
Seeing the sun rising, their impurities vanished;
they approached Sutīkṣṇa and spoke these gentle words.
"We have dwelt happily, O Blessed One, having been honored by you, who are yourself worthy of honor.
We take our leave and shall depart; the sages urge us to haste."
We hasten to see the entire circle of hermitages belonging to the sages of virtuous conduct who dwell in the Daṇḍaka forest.
We wish to be permitted to depart along with these bulls among sages,
who are ever-devoted to dharma, self-controlled through austerity, and like fires without smoke.
As long as the sun, with its unbearable heat, does not shine forth intensely,
it is like one born of a noble lineage who has obtained wealth through improper means.
Having said, "We wish to depart for now," Rāghava, together with Sītā and the son of Sumitrā, paid homage at the feet of the sage.
Raising them up as they touched his feet, that bull among sages embraced them firmly and spoke these words with affection: "Ram_3,7.10"
"Go safely on your path, O Rāma, together with the son of Sumitrā and with this Sītā, who follows you like a shadow."
Behold, O hero, the delightful hermitage of these ascetics dwelling in the Daṇḍaka forest, whose souls have been purified by austerity.
The forests were filled with excellent fruits and roots and were in full bloom;
the herds of deer were peaceful, and the flocks of birds were tranquil.
There were clusters of blooming lotuses and ponds with clear waters,
as well as lakes and reservoirs strewn with kāraṇḍava ducks.
You shall behold mountain cascades pleasing to the sight,
as well as delightful forests resounding with the cries of peacocks.
"Go, dear son Saumitri, and you too must depart;
yet you must come back again to see me at my hermitage."
Thus addressed, the descendant of Kakutstha, together with Lakṣmaṇa, replied, "So be it," and having circumambulated the sage, he prepared to depart.
Then the large-eyed Sītā gave to those two brothers two excellent quivers and two bows, and thereafter she gave them two stainless swords.
Having fastened their two auspicious quivers and taken up their sounding bows,
both Rāma and Lakṣmaṇa departed from the hermitage to go forth.
When the joy of the Raghus had been granted leave by Sutīkṣṇa and was about to depart,
Vaidehī addressed these words to her husband in an affectionate voice.
This great Dharma is attained by a most subtle method;
and it can be realized here by one who has desisted from the calamities born of desire.
In this world, there are indeed three vices born of desire;
false speech is the worst among them, while both approaching another's wife and cruelty without enmity are even more grievous than that.
O Raghava, a false word has never been uttered by you, nor will it ever be;
how much less could there be a desire for the wives of others, which destroys righteousness?
And all of that, O mighty-armed one, can be borne by those who have conquered their senses;
and I know your mastery over the senses, O you of auspicious appearance.
This third [evil], namely this fierce act of harming the lives of others,
which is committed out of delusion even toward those who bear no enmity— that has now come upon you.
O hero, you have indeed pledged for the sake of protecting the sages dwelling in the Daṇḍaka forest the slaughter of the rākṣasas in battle.
And for this reason, this forest is renowned as Daṇḍaka;
you have set out for it with your brother, bearing your bow and arrows.
Therefore, seeing you set out, my mind will be overwhelmed with anxiety;
for as I contemplate your conduct, it will surely lead to what is most beneficial and auspicious.
"O hero, I do not approve of your journey toward the Daṇḍaka forest.
I shall tell you the reason for this; listen to me as I speak."
For you, with bow and arrows in hand, having gone to the forest with your brother, might not see all the forest-dwellers and discharge your arrows? (Rāmāyaṇa 3.8.11)
In this world, for Kṣatriyas, the bow and the fuel of the sacrificial fire greatly increase their inherent power and strength when kept close at hand.
Long ago, O mighty-armed one, there was a certain ascetic, truthful in speech and pure,
who dwelt in a sacred forest filled with deer and birds that delighted in him.
Then Indra, the lord of Śacī, assuming the form of a soldier with a sword in hand, came to that hermitage in order to create an obstacle to his very asceticism.
At that time, an excellent sword was deposited in that hermitage;
it was given according to the ritual of a trust to him as he remained engaged in meritorious asceticism.
Having obtained that weapon, he remained intent on guarding the deposit;
he wandered through the forest indeed, protecting his own reputation.
Wherever he goes to gather roots and fruits,
intent on guarding his deposit, he does not go without that sword.
Constantly carrying his weapon, that ascetic gradually made his own mind fierce, abandoning his resolve for penance.
Then that sage, delighting in cruelty, intoxicated by passion, and corrupted by unrighteousness, went to hell because of his association with that weapon.
Out of affection and great respect, I am merely reminding you, not instructing you;
by no means whatsoever should that [bow] be drawn by you while holding your bow.
O hero, it is not my intention to slay the Rākṣasas dwelling in Daṇḍaka without enmity,
nor to slay people without offense.
For heroic Kṣatriyas who have restrained their selves in the forests, the purpose of the bow is only this: the protection of those who are distressed.
Where is the weapon, and where is the forest; where is the duty of a Kshatriya, and where is asceticism?
These things are mutually contradictory for us; rather, let the laws of the country be honored.

O best among the foremost of men, all the deer were the offspring of Mṛgī;
likewise, the bears, sṛmaras, and camaras were the offspring of Mṛgamandā.
From her, Bhadramadā gave birth to a daughter named Irāvatī;
her son was Airāvata, the great elephant and lord of the world.
And Śārdūlī gave birth to sons: Haryāśva bore the apes, the ascetic monkeys, and the golāṅgūlas; she also bore the tigers.
Furthermore, O bull among men, Mātaṅgī gave birth to elephants as her offspring;
and Śvetā bore a son named Diśāgaja, who had white eyes.
Then, O Rāma, the goddess Surabhi gave birth to two daughters—
Rohiṇī, may you be blessed, and the illustrious Gandharvī.
Rohiṇī gave birth to cows, Gandharvī to horses as her sons,
Surasā gave birth to the Nāgas, and Kadrū, O Rāma, to the Pannagas.
Manu begot human beings from the high-souled Kaśyapa—
namely Brāhmaṇas, Kṣatriyas, Vaiśyas, and Śūdras, O bull among men.
"From the mouth the Brāhmaṇas were born, likewise from the chest the Kṣatriyas;
from the thighs the Vaiśyas were born, and from the feet the Śūdras—so says the Śruti. (Rāmāyaṇa 3.13.30)
Anala also gave birth to all the trees that bear meritorious fruit;
Vinatā was the granddaughter of Śukī, while Kadrū’s sister was Surasā.
Kadru gave birth to a thousand earth-supporting serpents, while Vinata had two sons: Garuda and Aruna.
Therefore, O subduer of enemies, know me as Jaṭāyu, the son of Śyenī, born from Aruṇa; Sampāti is my elder brother.
Therefore, O dear one, if you wish, I shall become your companion in your dwelling;
and I will protect Sītā when you have departed along with Lakṣmaṇa.
Having honored Jaṭāyus and embraced him with joy, Rāghava bowed low;
for the self-possessed prince had heard from his father again and again of his friendship with Jaṭāyus as recounted by him.
Having entrusted Sītā, the princess of Mithilā, there to that exceedingly powerful bird,
he went with Lakṣmaṇa to Pañcavaṭī, desiring to consume his enemies like fire consuming moths.
Then, having gone to Pañcavaṭī, which was filled with various beasts of prey and wild animals,
Rāma spoke to his brother Lakṣmaṇa, who was radiant with splendor.
"We have come to this very place as directed by the great seer;
O gentle one, this is the region of Pañcavaṭī with its flowering groves."
"Cast your gaze everywhere in the forest, for you are indeed skilled;
in which region would a hermitage be most agreeable to us?"
"O Lakṣmaṇa, let such a place be found, near a body of water, where Vaidehī, you, and I may take our pleasure."
Where there is the beauty of forests as well as the beauty of waters,
and where sacrificial fuel, flowers, kusha grass, and water are all in close proximity.
Thus addressed by Rāma, Lakṣmaṇa, with palms joined in reverence,
spoke these words to the descendant of Kakutstha in the presence of Sītā.
"O descendant of Kakutstha, I am dependent upon you for a hundred years;
therefore, tell me yourself which region is pleasing to you. (Rāmāyaṇa 3.14.7)
Highly pleased by those words of Lakṣmaṇa, the immensely radiant Rāma reflected upon it and chose a location endowed with every excellence.
Having reached that delightful region suitable for the duties of a hermitage,
Rāma took Saumitri by the hand and spoke to him with his own hand.
"This region is level and glorious, surrounded by trees in full bloom;
O gentle one, you ought to establish a hermitage here in the proper manner."
Not far away, this lovely lotus pond, adorned with lotuses that shine like the sun and possess fragrant scents, is visible.
Just as it was described by the sage Agastya, whose soul was purified:
"This lovely Godāvarī is surrounded by trees in full bloom."
It was filled with swans and *kāraṇḍava* ducks and graced by *cakravāka* birds;
it was neither too far nor too near, and was frequented by herds of deer.
O gentle one, lofty mountains resounding with the cries of peacocks, delightful, possessing many caves,
and covered with trees in full bloom, are now visible.
With their golden, silver, and copper [ornaments], and with minerals in every region,
the elephants appear as if they were latticed windows through their supreme devotion.
They were adorned with *sāla*, *tāla*, and *tamāla* trees, as well as *kharjūra*, *panasa*, and *āmra* trees, along with *nīvāra*, *timiśa*, and *puṃnāga* trees.
They were covered by various trees, including mangoes, aśoka, tilaka, campaka, and ketaka, as well as by flowering shrubs, creepers, and other such plants.
With sandalwood, syandana, nīpa, panasa, and lakuca trees,
as well as dhava, aśvakarṇa, khadira, śamī, kiṃśuka, and pāṭala trees.
"This place is auspicious, this is pure, and it abounds with many deer and birds;
here we shall dwell, O son of Sumitrā, together with this bird."
Thus addressed by Rāma, the exceedingly powerful Lakṣmaṇa, slayer of enemy heroes,
soon constructed a hermitage for his brother.
There he built a very spacious leaf-hut with well-compacted clay, supported by sturdy pillars of long bamboo, and beautifully constructed.
Having gone to the river Godāvarī at that time, the illustrious Lakṣmaṇa bathed,
took lotuses, and returned once more with fruit.
Then, having performed an offering of flowers and a ritual for peace according to the prescribed rules,
he showed that hermitage which he had established to Rāma.
Having seen that pleasant hermitage prepared by him, Rāghava, together with Sītā, experienced supreme joy within the leaf-hut.
Then, greatly delighted, he embraced Lakṣmaṇa with both arms and spoke these words, both very affectionate and firm: (Rāmāyaṇa 3.14.25)
"I am pleased with you, O Lord, for this great deed has been performed by you;
it is for this reason that I have offered you my embrace."
O Lakṣmaṇa, because of you— a son who knows my feelings, who is grateful, and who knows the dharma— my righteous father has not been truly fulfilled.
Having thus spoken to Lakṣmaṇa, Rāghava, the increaser of prosperity and master of his senses,
dwelt happily in that region abounding in fruit.
For some time, that righteous-souled one dwelt there, attended by Sītā and Lakṣmaṇa,
like an immortal in the world of heaven.
While that great-souled Rāghava was thus without happiness,
the winter season, which is beloved, set in at the end of autumn.
Once, when the night had turned to dawn, that delight of the Raghus went to the beautiful Godāvarī river for the purpose of ritual ablution.
Bowing with the water-pot in his hand, the valiant brother, the son of Sumitrā, followed behind him together with Sītā and spoke these words: *Ram_3,15.3*
"O sweet-spoken one, that beloved season has now arrived which you hold dear,
by which this auspicious year appears as if adorned."
The world is harsh with frost, the earth is garlanded with crops,
the waters are unfit for enjoyment, and the sacrificial fire is auspicious.
Having worshipped the ancestral deities with offerings of the first-fruits of the harvest,
the virtuous, having performed the *āgrayaṇa* sacrifice at the proper time, were freed from all taint.
The provinces abound with desired objects and possess an abundance of cow's milk products;
the rulers of the earth wander there for the sake of expeditions, desiring victory.
While the sun firmly occupies the quarter frequented by Death,
the northern direction does not shine, like a woman deprived of her forehead mark.
By its very nature rich in masses of snow, and with the sun now far away, the mountain Himavat clearly bears its name as it truly signifies: "The Snowy One."
The days, with their fortunate suns, allow for the easy movement of those who seek extreme comfort; they are pleasant to the touch at midday, yet shadows and water have become difficult to find.
Nowadays the days appear with mild suns, accompanied by mist, sharp cold, and winds; they shine over empty forests laid waste by the frost.
Now the nights pass away, their cold intensified by the lengthening of the year; they are led by the month of Puṣya, reddened by frost, and the sky has ceased its sleeping.
Having transferred its good fortune to the sun, the moon— with its orb reddened by frost— does not shine, like a mirror obscured by breath.
The moonlight, soiled by frost on the full-moon night, does not shine;
like Sītā darkened by the sun's heat, it is merely visible but does not gleam.
By its very nature cool to the touch,
the western wind now blows, doubly cold at this time because it is pierced by the frost.
The forests, filled with barley and wheat and veiled in mist,
shine as the sun rises, resounding with the cries of cranes and saras cranes.
The golden-hued rice stalks, slightly bending, shine with their heads full of grain, shaped like dates.
With its approaching rays veiled by frost and mist,
the sun, though risen high, appears like the moon.
In the forenoon its vigor is ungraspable; at midday it is pleasant to the touch;
reddened and slightly pale, the sunlight shines beautifully upon the earth.
With its young grass slightly moistened by the falling of dew,
the forest floor, upon which the morning sunlight has just settled, shines with beauty.
Enveloped by the darkness of frost and shrouded in the gloom of mist,
the rows of forest trees, devoid of flowers, appear as if they are fast asleep.
With their waters shrouded by mist and their cranes recognizable only by their cries,
the rivers now shine with banks whose sands are moistened by frost.
Due to the falling of snow, the mildness of the sun,
and the cold, even the water situated on the mountain peaks generally possesses flavor.
With leaves withered by age, their filaments and pericarps decayed,
and reduced to mere stalks, the lotus ponds do not shine, destroyed by the frost.
But at this time, O tiger among men, the righteous-souled Bharata, filled with sorrow, practices austerities in the city out of devotion to you.
Having renounced his kingdom, his honor, and many various enjoyments, he,
an ascetic with restricted diet, lies upon the cold surface of the earth.
Surely he too, having prepared for his consecration at this very hour,
goes regularly to the Sarayū river surrounded by his ministers.
Reared in extreme luxury, delicate, and afflicted by the cold,
how is it that he plunges into the Sarayū during the latter watches of the night?
With eyes like lotus petals, dark-complexioned, glorious, slender-waisted, and great;
a knower of dharma, a speaker of truth, restrained by a sense of shame, and one who has conquered his senses.
Speaking kindly and sweetly, long-armed subduer of enemies,
he renounced various enjoyments and took refuge in the Noble One with his whole soul.
"Your high-souled brother Bharata has already conquered heaven,
for he follows you even as you dwell in the forest practicing asceticism."
"Bipeds do not follow the father's side, but the mother's"—
this worldly proverb was made otherwise by Bharata.
How indeed could that mother Kaikeyī be so cruel in her vision, whose husband was Daśaratha and whose son was the virtuous Bharata?
While the righteous Lakṣmaṇa was thus speaking these words out of affection, Rāghava, unable to endure that censure of his mother, replied.
"O father, you must not disparage our mother Madhyamā in any way;
speak only of that story concerning Bharata, the lord of the Ikṣvākus."
For although my mind is resolved and firm in its vow regarding residence in the forest,
it is again rendered childish, tormented by affection for Bharata.
Lamenting thus, the descendant of Kakutstha reached the river Godāvarī there and performed his ablutions along with his younger brother and Sītā.
Then, having gratified the ancestors and the deities with libations of water,
they, being composed in mind, praised the risen sun and the gods.
Having been consecrated, Rāma shone together with Sītā and Lakṣmaṇa,
like the blessed Lord Rudra, accompanied by Nandin, after being consecrated with the daughter of the mountain king.
Having performed their ablutions, Rāma, Sītā, and the son of Sumitrā then departed from the bank of the Godāvarī and went to their own hermitage.
Having reached that hermitage with Lakṣmaṇa, Rāghava performed his morning rites and entered the leaf-hut.
Seated in the leaf-hut together with Sītā,
the mighty-armed Rāma shone like the moon with the Citrā constellation;
he engaged in various conversations with his brother Lakṣmaṇa.
Then, while Rāma was seated with his mind absorbed in conversation,
a certain rākṣasī arrived at that place by chance.
That sister of the ten-necked Rākṣasa, named Śūrpaṇakhā, having approached Rāma, beheld him who resembled a god.
With the chest of a lion and mighty arms, his eyes resembling lotus petals;
delicate yet a great being, endowed with the marks of royalty.
Seeing Rāma, dark as a blue lotus and possessing a splendor like that of Kandarpa, the rākṣasī became infatuated with desire, appearing like Indrāṇī herself.

The foul-faced woman [stared] at the fair-faced Rāma; the pot-bellied woman at him of slender waist; the deformed-eyed woman at the large-eyed one; and she with copper-colored hair at him with beautiful locks.
She who was beautiful became ugly; she who had a sweet voice became harsh-voiced;
she who was young became cruel; and she who was old spoke with eloquence. She who was right-handed became left-handed.
A woman of evil conduct, who appeared unpleasant despite her beauty, possessed by the passion of the flesh— a true rakshasi— spoke to Rama, who was steadfast in righteous conduct.
Wearing matted hair and assuming the form of an ascetic, accompanied by your wife and carrying a bow and arrows,
how have you come to this region inhabited by Rākṣasas?
Thus addressed by the Rākṣasī Śūrpaṇakhā, the scorcher of foes,
out of his straightforward nature, began to relate everything.
There was a king named Daśaratha, whose prowess was equal to that of the gods;
I am his eldest son, known among people by the name Rāma.
"This is my younger brother named Lakṣmaṇa, who is devoted to me;
and this is my wife Vaidehī, renowned as Sītā. (Rāmāyaṇa 3.16.14)
But constrained by the command of my father, the lord of men, and of my mother,
and desiring righteousness for the sake of dharma, I have come here to dwell in the forest.
But I wish to know you; tell me, who are you and to whom do you belong?
For what purpose have you come here? Speak the truth.
Having heard those words, the Rākṣasī, afflicted by passion, spoke these words:
"Listen, O Rāma; I shall speak my words according to the truth."
"I am a Rākṣasī named Śūrpaṇakhā, able to assume any form at will; I wander this forest alone, terrifying all beings."
My brother is the Rākṣasa named Rāvaṇa, the lord of the Rākṣasas;
and Kumbhakarṇa, possessed of great strength, is always in a state of deep sleep.
But Vibhīṣaṇa was righteous in soul and did not act like a Rākṣasa;
nor did the two brothers, Khara and Dūṣaṇa, who were renowned for their prowess in battle.
O Rāma, having surpassed them all because of my prior vision of you, I have approached you with my whole being as my husband, the supreme among men.
For a long time now, be my husband; what will you do with Sītā?
Deformed and misshapen, she is not a match for you;
I alone am a suitable wife for you—behold me in my beauty.
"This hideous, unchaste, and terrifying woman with her sunken belly—
I shall devour her, this human being, along with this brother of yours."
Then, O beloved, wandering through the Daṇḍaka forest together with me, you shall behold mountain peaks and various woods.
Thus addressed, the descendant of Kakutstha, skilled in speech, smiled at the woman with intoxicating eyes and began to speak these words.
Then Rāma, with clear and gentle words and preceded by a smile, spoke to Śūrpaṇakhā, who was bound by the noose of passion.
"I am already married, O lady, and this wife is my beloved;
for women such as you, the state of having a rival is exceedingly painful."
But this younger brother of mine, named Lakṣmaṇa, is virtuous, pleasant to behold, illustrious, and heroic; he has not yet taken a wife.
He has never had a wife before, he is desirous of one, he is young and handsome; such a husband will be worthy of this beauty of yours.
"O large-eyed one, resort to this man as your husband, my brother;
O lady of beautiful hips, be without a rival, like the radiance of the sun upon Mount Meru."
Thus addressed by Rāma, that rākṣasī, deluded by passion,
suddenly released Rāma and then spoke to Lakṣmaṇa.
"O lady of excellent complexion, I am a fitting wife for you with such a form;
together with me, you shall wander happily throughout all the Daṇḍaka forest."
Thus addressed by the rākṣasī, Lakṣmaṇa, the son of Sumitrā who was skilled in speech, smiled at Śūrpaṇakhā and spoke these fitting words.
"How can you, a female slave, wish to become the wife of me, a slave?
O lady of lotus-like complexion, I am subject to my noble brother."
O large-eyed lady, you whose purpose is fulfilled and whose complexion is joyful and stainless, become the younger wife of this noble man whose aims are fully realized.
Having abandoned this aged wife— who is deformed, unchaste, hideous, and pot-bellied— he will surely devote himself only to you.
For what wise man, O woman of excellent complexion, having abandoned this most excellent form, would set his heart upon human beings, O lady of noble limbs?
Thus addressed by Lakṣmaṇa, that hideous woman with a sunken belly,
being unskilled in discerning jest, took those words to be true.
Deluded by passion, she spoke to Rāma— the scorcher of foes, invincible, and seated with Sītā in the leaf-hut.
"By clinging to this ugly, unfaithful, hideous wife— old and with a sunken belly— you do not hold me in high regard."
"Today, while you look on, I shall devour this human woman;
I will roam with you at my pleasure, free from all rivals."
Having spoken thus, she whose eyes were like glowing embers rushed furiously toward the fawn-eyed woman, like a great meteor toward Rohiṇī.
Seizing that weapon, which resembled the noose of Death as it came rushing toward him, the mighty Rāma, filled with rage, then spoke to Lakṣmaṇa.
O son of Sumitrā, one should never engage in jesting with cruel and ignoble people; look, O gentle one, how Vaidehī might somehow still be alive.
O tiger among men, you ought to disfigure this hideous, unchaste, and excessively intoxicated Rākṣasī with her massive belly.
Thus addressed, the mighty Lakṣmaṇa, filled with rage while Rāma looked on,
drew his sword and cut off her nose and ears.
But Śūrpaṇakhā, her ears and nose severed, let out a discordant cry and fled in terror back to the forest by the way she had come.
That hideous and most terrible Rākṣasī, drenched in blood,
let out various roars like a rain-cloud in the monsoon.
Flowing with blood in many ways, her appearance terrifying,
she entered the great forest with her arms outstretched, uttering loud roars.

Then she, having been disfigured, approached her brother Khara— who was possessed of fierce energy and surrounded by a host of Rākṣasas— while he was in Janasthāna, and fell from the sky to the earth like a thunderbolt.

Then, drenched in blood and overwhelmed by fear, delusion, and fainting, Khara’s sister related everything to Rāghava— who had arrived in the forest with his wife and Lakṣmaṇa— concerning her own disfigurement.
Seeing his sister fallen in that manner, disfigured and drenched in blood,
the Rākṣasa Khara, consumed with rage, questioned her.
Endowed with strength and prowess, able to go wherever you wish and assume any form at will,
by whom have you been brought to this state, as if you had encountered Death itself?
"Among the gods, gandharvas, spirits, and the high-souled sages,
who is this being of such great prowess that has thus disfigured you?"
Indeed, I see no one in this world who could do me any harm,
except for the thousand-eyed Mahendra, the subduer of Pāka.
Today, with life-ending arrows, I shall take my own life,
like a crane drinking up milk that has been mixed with water.
Whose foamy, red blood shall the earth drink, once he has been slain by me in battle, his vital organs mangled by my arrows?
Whose bodies will the birds, having torn away the flesh,
gather together and joyfully devour once he has been slain by me in battle?
Neither the gods, nor the gandharvas, nor the piśācas, nor the rākṣasas are able to protect that wretched man, dragged away by me in this great battle.
Having slowly regained consciousness, you ought to tell me who that ill-behaved man was by whom you were overcome through his prowess in the forest.
Having heard these words of her brother, who was especially enraged, Śūrpaṇakhā then spoke these words through her tears: *Ram_3,18.10*
Young, endowed with beauty, delicate yet possessed of great strength,
their eyes as broad as lotuses, they were clad in bark garments and black antelope skins.
"Resembling two kings of the Gandharvas and endowed with the marks of royalty,
I cannot determine whether those two are gods or men."
There I saw a young woman, endowed with beauty and adorned with every ornament, standing between those two with her slender waist.
Together with both of them, they have brought me—who am truly without a protector—to this state concerning that woman. (Rāmāyaṇa 3.18.14)
And of her, who has acted with crooked conduct, and of those two slain ones,
I desire to drink the frothy blood upon the front of the battlefield.
"O father, this would be my first wish fulfilled by you:
that I might drink the blood of her and those two in battle."
While she was speaking thus, the enraged Khara commanded fourteen immensely powerful Rākṣasas who resembled the God of Death.
Two men, armed with weapons and clad in bark and black antelope skins,
have entered the formidable Daṇḍaka forest together with a young woman.
Having slain those two and that woman of evil conduct, you ought to return;
and this sister of mine shall drink their blood.
"O Rākṣasas, go and quickly fulfill this cherished desire of my sister by crushing those two with your own prowess."
Thus commanded, those fourteen Rākṣasas went there together with her, like clouds driven by the wind.
Therefore, the terrible Śūrpaṇakhā came to the hermitage of the descendant of Raghu and informed the Rākṣasas that those two brothers were there with Sītā.
They beheld the mighty Rāma seated in the leaf-hut together with Sītā, the princess of Videha, and Lakṣmaṇa.
Seeing them and that rākṣasī who had arrived, the glorious Rāghava,
Rāma, spoke to his brother Lakṣmaṇa of radiant splendor.
Wait a moment, O son of Sumitrā, standing close behind Sītā;
I shall slay those who have come here along her path.
Having heard these words of Rāma, who was self-realized,
Lakṣmaṇa honored Rāma’s speech by saying, "So be it."
The righteous Rāghava also made his great bow, adorned with gold, ready with a string,
and spoke to those rākṣasas.
"We two are the sons of Daśaratha, brothers Rāma and Lakṣmaṇa;
we have entered the difficult Daṇḍaka forest together with Sītā."
Why do you harm these two ascetics who subsist on fruits and roots, who are self-controlled, practitioners of dharma, and dwell in the Daṇḍaka forest?
"By the command of the sages, I have arrived in this great forest with my bow and arrows to slay you, evil-souled wrongdoers."
"Stay right here and be content; you ought not to advance further.
O night-stalkers, if you have any regard for your lives here, turn back!"
Having heard those words of his, those fourteen Rākṣasas—
slayers of Brahmins who bore tridents in their hands— spoke these words in great fury.
With bloodshot eyes, the fierce woman, delighted, beheld Rāma— whose own eyes were red at the corners, who spoke with harsh and unpleasant words, and whose prowess was already well-known.
Having provoked the wrath of our high-souled lord Khara,
you yourself shall lose your life today, slain by us in battle.
For what power do you have, being alone, to stand before us many at the head of the battle, much less to fight in combat?
By these iron clubs, spears, and sharp-edged pikes wielded by our arms,
you shall lose your life, your prowess, and the bow held firmly in your hand.
Having spoken thus, those fourteen enraged Rākṣasas,
with weapons and swords raised, rushed toward Rāma alone;
they hurled those spears at the invincible descendant of Raghu.
Kākutstha severed all those fourteen spears with an equal number of arrows adorned with gold.
Thereafter, the immensely powerful one, filled with supreme rage, seized fourteen iron arrows, sharpened on stone and radiant as the sun.
Taking up his bow and drawing it back, Rāghava aimed at the rākṣasa targets and released arrows like Śatakratu hurls thunderbolts.
And arrows with golden shafts, blazing and adorned with gold,
became equal in luster to great meteors in the sky.
Having pierced the chests of the rākṣasas with force, those arrows, drenched in blood and sounding like thunderbolts, then flew out and sank into the earth.
With their hearts shattered, they fell to the ground like trees cut at the root—
limbs drenched in blood, mangled, and deprived of life.
Seeing them fallen upon the ground, the rākṣasī, frantic with rage and terrified, again let out a terrible cry there.
Uttering a great roar, Śūrpaṇakhā then returned with speed to Khara;
her blood somewhat dried, she fell down again in distress like a sapless creeper.
Seeing the Rākṣasas struck down in battle, Śūrpaṇakhā then rushed forward again;
that sister of Khara reported the entire slaughter of all those demons in its full detail.

Seeing Śūrpaṇakhā fallen, Khara, out of anger, spoke with clear words to her who had come for his own ruin: "Rāma is not a man; he is a god. And Sītā is not a human woman; she is the goddess Lakṣmī herself. As for that Laksmana, he is the great-souled Viṣṇu, the younger brother of Indra. You have come here seeking to destroy us all, like a moth rushing into a flame. (Rāmāyaṇa 3.20.1)
But now, those heroic Rākṣasas who feed on blood have been dispatched by me for your sake;
why then do you weep once more?
They are devoted to me, loyal, and always well-disposed toward me;
even if they were to strike me, they should not be killed, nor should they fail to carry out my word.
I wish to hear the reason for which you,
crying out "Alas, my lord!", are writhing upon the ground like a serpent.
"Why do you lament like one who is helpless while I, your protector, am present?
Arise, arise! Do not fear; let this despondency be cast aside here."
Having been addressed in this way and consoled by Khara,
the invincible one wiped her tearful eyes and spoke to her brother Khara.
And those fourteen fierce and heroic Rākṣasas were sent by you to slay Rāghava along with Lakṣmaṇa for the sake of my pleasure.
But they, filled with indignation and bearing spears and battle-axes in their hands, were all slain in battle by Rāma with arrows that pierce the vital organs.
Seeing those mighty warriors fallen upon the earth in an instant,
and witnessing the great feat of Rāma, a profound terror came over me.
O night-stalker, I am afraid, agitated, and despondent;
seeing danger on all sides, I have come to you once again for refuge.
Why do you not rescue me as I am submerged in this vast ocean of grief, inhabited by the crocodiles of despondency and garlanded with waves of terror?
And these flesh-eating rākṣasas who have followed my path have been struck down upon the ground by Rāma with his sharpened arrows.
O night-stalker, if you have compassion for me, or if you have any regard for those Rākṣasas, and if you possess the power or the fiery energy to oppose Rāma,
then destroy this thorn in the side of the Rākṣasas who dwells in the Daṇḍaka forest.
If you do not slay my enemy Rāma today, I shall,
devoid of shame, give up my life right before your very eyes.
By my own discernment, I perceive that you are not capable of standing before Rāma in the great battle, facing him with his bow drawn in combat.
"You are not a hero, though you fancy yourself one; your prowess is falsely attributed to you, since you are unable to slay those two humans, Rāma and Lakṣmaṇa."
Depart quickly from Janasthāna along with your kinsmen;
what kind of dwelling could there be for one who is spiritless and of little prowess?
Overwhelmed by Rāma’s splendor, you shall indeed perish quickly;
for that Rāma, the son of Daśaratha, is endowed with such majesty,
as is his brother of great heroism, by whom I have been disfigured.
Thus insulted by Śūrpaṇakhā,
Khara, the hero among the rākṣasas, then spoke these exceedingly harsh words in the midst of the demons.
"This incomparable anger of mine, born from your insult,
cannot be restrained, like the rising salt-water ocean."
I do not reckon Rāma as a man of prowess, for he is but a human whose life is spent;
he who has slain his own life through his evil deeds shall today be released from it.
Let these tears be restrained and this agitation be cast aside;
I shall lead Rāma, together with his brother, to the abode of Yama.
O Rākṣasī, today you shall drink the warm, red blood of Rāma, whose life-breath is failing as he lies upon the ground, struck down by my axe.
Delighted upon hearing those words fallen from the mouth of Khara,
she again praised her brother out of folly, he who was the foremost among the Rākṣasas.
Having been previously reviled by her and now being praised once again,
Khara then spoke to his commander-in-chief named Dūṣaṇa.
There were fourteen thousand Rākṣasas of terrifying speed, who followed my will and never retreated in battles.
Of those who were the color of dark blue clouds, terrible, performers of cruel deeds,
who took pleasure in harming the world, powerful, and possessed of fierce splendor.
O gentle one, command all the efforts of those Rākṣasas, who possess the pride of tigers, great mouths, and immense power, and who are exultant in every exertion.
"O gentle one, quickly bring my chariot, as well as my bows,
variegated arrows, swords, and various sharp spears."
Skilled in battle, I desire to go forth at the head of the high-souled descendants of Pulastya for the sake of slaying the ill-behaved Rāma.
While he was speaking thus, Dūṣaṇa then announced that great chariot, which was sun-colored and yoked with excellent, dappled horses.
That golden wheel, resembling the peak of Mount Meru,
adorned with refined gold, was unobstructed and possessed a pole made of lapis lazuli.
It was covered with fish, flowers, trees, and mountains, with golden suns and moons, auspicious flocks of birds, and stars.
Out of indignation, Khara mounted the chariot, which was equipped with banners and swords, adorned with tinkling bells, and yoked with excellent horses.
Seeing him mounted upon his chariot, the Rākṣasas of terrifying prowess stood surrounding him and the exceedingly powerful Dūṣaṇa.
But Khara, standing upon his chariot and seeing all those great archers with their terrible shields, weapons, and banners, said to all the Rākṣasas, "March forth! (Rāmāyaṇa 3.21.18).
Then that Rākṣasa army, with its terrible shields, weapons, and banners,
issued forth from Janasthāna with a great roar and immense speed.
With mallets, spears, spikes, and very sharp axes;
with swords, discuses held in their hands, and shining javelins.
With spears, terrible iron clubs, and oversized bows, and with maces, swords, bludgeons, and thunderbolts grasped in their hands— objects of fearsome appearance.
Fourteen thousand most terrible Rākṣasas, who followed the will of Khara, set out from Janasthāna.
Seeing those rākṣasas of terrifying prowess rushing toward him,
Khara’s chariot also moved forward a little after them.
Then, having understood Khara’s intention, the charioteer urged on those dappled horses adorned with refined gold.
Urged on, the chariot of Khara, the slayer of enemies,
swiftly filled the quarters and the intermediate directions with its sound.
But Khara, his fury intensified, with a harsh voice like the God of Death in haste for the sake of slaying his enemy,
urged his charioteer once more, roaring like a mighty cloud pouring down a rain of stones.
As that terrible and inauspicious army marched forth, a tumultuous great cloud, the color of a donkey and reddish-brown, rained down upon it with blood for its water.
The horses yoked to his chariot, possessing great speed,
stumbled by chance upon the royal road in a level place covered with flowers.
A dark halo with blood-red edges appeared,
resembling a whirling circle of fire as it received the sun.
Then, having approached the raised golden staff of the banner,
a massive and most dreadful vulture alighted upon it and stood there.
And having approached the vicinity of Janasthāna, the flesh-eating beasts and birds let out various discordant and harsh cries.
And in the direction that was ablaze, the jackals of the Yātudhānas, emitting terrible cries,
uttered an inauspicious and loud roar.
Resembling mountains split asunder and bearing the moisture of dried-up waters,
those formidable clouds made that sky appear as if it were no longer empty space.
A terrible, rising darkness arose that caused the hair to stand on end;
neither the cardinal nor the intermediate directions could be clearly discerned.
Resembling the color of fresh blood, it shone even though it was not the hour of twilight;
at that time, fierce beasts and birds cried out facing toward Khara.
Always bringing ill fortune in battle, the jackals of terrifying appearance howled toward the army with mouths vomiting flames.
A headless trunk, resembling a massive iron club, was seen near the sun;
the great planet Svarbhānu seized the sun out of season.
The wind blew swiftly, the sun became lusterless,
and stars, possessing the brilliance of fireflies, rose up even without night.
At that moment, the lotus ponds had their fish and birds huddled together, and the trees were stripped of both flowers and fruit.
And there, even without wind, dust rose as red as a rain-cloud;
the sarika birds there began to shriek with cries of "vīcī-kūcī."
Meteors, accompanied by thunderous sounds and terrifying to behold, fell from the sky;
and the earth, along with its mountains, forests, and groves, trembled violently.
As the wise Khara stood upon his chariot roaring,
his left arm trembled and his bow slipped from his grasp.
As he looked in every direction, his vision became blurred with tears;
a pain arose in his forehead, yet he did not turn back from his delusion.
Beholding those great and hair-raising portents that had arisen,
Khara then spoke to all the Rākṣasas with a laugh.
I do not take any account of all these great portents that have arisen, so terrible to behold; for through my vigor, I am as strong as one who regards the weak.
I could even cause Tārā to fall from the surface of the sky with my sharp arrows;
and being enraged, I shall unite Death himself with the nature of mortality.
I cannot return without having slain with my sharp arrows that Raghava, who is arrogant in his strength, and his brother Lakshmana as well.
"Let my sister have her desire fulfilled after she has drunk the blood of those two,
on whose account this calamity has befallen Rāma and Lakṣmaṇa."
"Never before have I suffered defeat in battles;
this is evident to you all, for I do not speak untruth."
Even the enraged King of the Gods, wielding the thunderbolt in his hand and mounted upon the rutting Airāvata, I could slay in battle; how much more so those two mere mortals?
Hearing that roar of the Rākṣasa, his great army,
already bound by the noose of death, experienced incomparable joy.
And the high-souled ṛṣis, gods, gandharvas, siddhas, along with the cāraṇas, assembled there, desiring to witness the battle.
Having come together, those performers of meritorious deeds spoke to one another:
"May it be well with cows and brahmins, and with those who are honored by the worlds."
May Rāghava be victorious in battle over the night-stalkers, the descendants of Pulastya,
just as the wielder of the discus was victorious in battle over all the foremost of the asuras.
Speaking these and many other words repeatedly, the supreme seers beheld that army of those Rākṣasas whose lives were spent.
Then Khara, in his chariot, rushed forth with speed from the front of the army;
seeing that Rākṣasa, other Rākṣasas likewise rushed out after him.
Śyenagāmī, Pṛthugrīva, Yajñaśatru, Vihaga, Durjaya, Karavīrākṣa, Paruṣa, and Kālakārmuka.
Meghamālī, Mahāmālī, Sarpāsya, and Rudhirāśana—
these twelve of great prowess set out toward Khara from all sides.
Mahākapāla, Sthūlākṣa, Pramāthin, and Triśiras—
these four leaders of the army followed behind Dūṣaṇa.
That extremely fierce army of heroic Rākṣasas, possessing terrible speed and eager for battle,
suddenly assailed those two princes like a garland of planets attacking the sun and the moon.
When Khara, of terrible prowess, had returned to his hermitage,
Rāma, together with his brother, beheld those very same portents.
Seeing those most terrible portents that had arisen, which caused the hair to stand on end and were harmful to all creatures, he spoke these words to Lakṣmaṇa.
Behold these great portents, O mighty-armed one, which have arisen to carry away all living beings and to destroy all the rākṣasas.
These harsh-sounding clouds, dark as donkeys and reddish-brown, are swirling in the sky, discharging streams of blood.
O Lakṣmaṇa, all my arrows, eager for battle, are emitting smoke,
and my gold-backed bows are twitching.
"From the way these forest-dwelling birds are warbling here,
it is clear that danger has come upon us and our very lives are in doubt."
"A very great battle will surely take place, there is no doubt;
this arm of mine, throbbing again and again, tells me so."
O hero, in our close proximity, victory for us and defeat for the enemy are certain;
for your face appears radiant and serene.
For those who have risen up for the sake of battle, O Lakṣmaṇa,
whose faces become lusterless, their life is at its end.
A wise man who desires his own welfare and anticipates misfortune must take measures in advance for the future.
Therefore, taking Vaidehī with you, bow in hand and arrows in grasp,
take refuge in a cave of the mountain that is difficult of access and thick with trees.
I do not wish for this speech of yours to be contradicted;
I adjure you by my feet, my child, depart without delay.
Thus addressed by Rāma, Lakṣmaṇa, taking up his bow and arrows along with Sītā, took refuge in a secure cave.
When Lakṣmaṇa had entered the cave together with Sītā,
Rāma, saying "Alas, he has gone forth," donned his armor.
Adorned with that armor which resembled fire,
Rāma appeared like a smokeless flame rising in the darkness.
Raising his great bow and taking up arrows, the valiant one stood there,
filling the quarters with the sounds of his bowstring.
Then the gods, along with the gandharvas, the siddhas, and the cāraṇas,
as well as the guhyakas, spoke to one another in great terror.
There are fourteen thousand Rākṣasas of fearsome deeds, and Rāma, the righteous-souled one, is alone; how will the battle proceed?
Then, an army of Yātudhānas, with a deep resonance and formidable armor, weapons, and banners, appeared on all sides.
They let out lion-like roars, bellowed at one another,
drew their bows, and yawned repeatedly.
The tumultuous sound of those who were shouting aloud and beating their drums filled that entire forest.
Terrified by that sound, the wild beasts roaming the forest fled silently to where they could not look back.
That army, possessing great speed and bearing various weapons, approached Rāma; it was deep and resembled the ocean.
Rāma, skilled in battle, casting his eyes in every direction,
beheld that army of Khara standing ready and intent upon combat.
Having drawn his formidable bow and extracted arrows from his quivers,
he summoned a fierce rage for the sake of slaying all the rākṣasas.
Enraged, he became difficult to behold, blazing like the fire at the end of an eon;
seeing him possessed by such splendor, the forest deities trembled with fear.
Then the appearance of the enraged Rāma was seen to be like that of the wielder of the Pināka bow (Śiva), who had risen up to destroy the sacrifice of Dakṣa.
Having arrived at the hermitage with his attendants, Khara beheld Rāma, the slayer of enemies, enraged and grasping his bow.
Seeing him, he raised his bow endowed with its string, which produced a harsh sound, and urged the charioteer toward Rāma, saying, "Drive forward! (Ram_3.24.2)
At Khara's command, the charioteer urged on the horses to where the mighty-armed Rāma stood alone, shaking his bow.
But seeing him having leapt forth, all those night-rangers,
his ministers, surrounded him while letting out a great roar.
Having entered into the midst of those Yātudhānas,
Khara took his place like the planet Mars risen in the center of the stars.
Then all those night-stalkers, filled with rage, showered that invincible Rāma, the wielder of the formidable bow, with various kinds of weapons.
In that battle, the Rākṣasas, intent on wrath, struck Rāma with iron mallets, spears, javelins, swords, and axes.
Resembling clouds, possessing great roars and immense strength,
they rushed toward Rāma, the descendant of Kakutstha, desiring to slay him in battle.
Those hosts of Rākṣasas discharged showers of arrows upon Rāma,
like rain-clouds pouring down torrents upon the king of mountains.
Surrounded by those terrible hosts of Rākṣasas, Rāghava appeared like Mahādeva surrounded by his throngs of attendants on sacred lunar days.
That descendant of Raghu received those weapons released by the Yātudhānas with his own arrows, just as the ocean receives the torrents of rivers.
With his limbs pierced by those terrible weapons, Rāma did not waver,
just as a great mountain remains unmoved by many blazing thunderbolts.
Pierced and smeared with blood on all his limbs, Rāghava,
that Rāma, appeared like the sun enveloped by the clouds of twilight.
The gods, Gandharvas, Siddhas, and supreme ṛṣis were distressed,
seeing that single being then surrounded by many thousands.
Then Rāma, greatly incensed, drew his bow into a circle and loosed sharpened arrows by the hundreds and thousands.
In the battle, Rāma effortlessly discharged straight-flying arrows fletched with heron feathers— arrows that were difficult to ward off, difficult to withstand, and like the noose of Death.
Those arrows, released effortlessly by Rāma upon the enemy armies,
took away the lives of the Rākṣasas like nooses fashioned by Time itself.
Having pierced those bodies of the Rākṣasas, those arrows, drenched in blood and possessing a brilliance equal to blazing fire, shone as they traveled through the sky.
But from the circle of Rāma’s bow, countless arrows—
exceedingly fierce and capable of snatching away the lives of the rākṣasas— shot forth.
By them were severed bows, the tops of banners, armor, and heads;
and many thighs, resembling the trunks of elephants, along with their hands and ornaments.
Then, being pierced by nalīkas, nārācas, and sharp-pointed vikarṇis,
the night-stalkers let out a terrible cry of distress.
Afflicted by Rāma with sharp arrows that pierced its vital organs, that army found no comfort, like a dry forest consumed by fire.
Some night-stalkers, heroic and possessed of terrible strength, being exceedingly enraged, hurled pikes, swords, and battle-axes at Rāma.
Having warded off those weapons with his arrows, the mighty-armed Rāghava took their lives in battle and severed their necks.
And those night-stalkers who remained there,
dejected and tormented by arrows, rushed toward Khara himself for protection.
Having taken them all back and comforted them, Dūṣaṇa,
enraged like Rudra at the end of time, rushed toward the descendant of Kakutstha.
But having turned back once more, all of them, fearless in their reliance on Dūṣaṇa, rushed toward Rāma alone, armed with *sāla* trees, *tāla* trees, and stones.
Then there occurred that wonderful, tumultuous, and hair-raising battle—
most terrible— between this Rāma and those rākṣasas once again.
The righteous Rāghava countered that great, life-destroying rain of trees and rocks with his sharp arrows.
Having accepted that boon, Rāma, like a bull with its eyes closed,
directed his supreme wrath toward the slaughter of all the Rākṣasas.
Then, overcome with rage and as if blazing with splendor,
he showered arrows from all sides upon the army along with Dūṣaṇa.
Then the enraged general Dūṣaṇa, the defiler of his enemies,
seized a hair-raising iron club that resembled a mountain peak.
Wound with golden bands, it crushed the armies of the gods;
it was strewn with sharp iron spikes and drenched in the blood of enemies.
Grasping that iron bar, which felt like a thunderbolt to the touch, which could shatter the gate-towers of an enemy city,
and which resembled a great serpent,
the night-stalker Dūṣaṇa, a doer of cruel deeds, rushed at Rāma in battle.
As Dūṣaṇa was charging toward him, that descendant of Raghu severed his two arms, along with their ornaments, using two arrows.
Slipping from his grasp, that massive iron club fell at the front of the battle like Indra’s banner when its staff has been severed from the hand.
With his two hands scattered, Dūṣaṇa fell to the earth like a spirited great elephant with its two tusks shattered.
Seeing Dūṣaṇa fallen on the ground, slain in battle, all beings honored the descendant of Kakutstha, crying out, "Excellent! Excellent!"
In the meantime, three enraged leaders of the army—
Mahākapāla, Sthūlākṣa, and the exceedingly powerful Pramāthin— bound themselves with the noose of death and together rushed toward Rāma.
The Rākṣasa Mahākapāla raised a massive spear;
Sthūlākṣa seized a sharp-edged lance (paṭṭiśa), and Pramāthin took up a battle-axe (paraśvadha).
But as soon as he saw them rushing toward him, Rāghava received them with sharp-pointed arrows, like a host receiving guests who have arrived.
The joy of the Raghus severed the head of Mahākapāla and crushed Pramāthin with countless floods of arrows.
He filled Sthulākṣa’s eyes with sharp arrows;
struck down, he fell to the earth like a great tree with spreading branches.
Then, with arrows resembling fire and adorned with gold and diamonds, the radiant hero struck the remainder of that army's rear.
Those gold-tufted arrows, like fires accompanied by smoke,
struck down those Rākṣasas as thunderbolts strike down great trees.
At the forefront of the battle, Rāma struck down a hundred rākṣasas with a single barbed arrow, and a thousand with a thousand.
With their armor and ornaments shattered and their bows cut to pieces,
those night-stalkers fell upon the earth, smeared with blood.
With those who had fallen in battle with disheveled hair and drenched in blood,
the entire earth was strewn as if with sacrificial grass upon a great altar.
In an instant, however, that most terrible forest, its rākṣasas slain,
became like a hellish pit, mired in mud of flesh and blood.
Fourteen thousand Rākṣasas of fearsome deeds were slain by Rāma alone, a mere human on foot.
Of that entire army, only Khara remained as a great chariot-warrior,
along with the Rākṣasa Triśiras and Rāma, the slayer of enemies.
Then, beholding that army of formidable strength slain in the great battle by the more powerful Rāma,
Khara approached Rāma on his great chariot, like Indra with his raised thunderbolt.
But as Khara was advancing toward Rāma, the commander of the army,
a Rākṣasa named Triśiras, approached him and spoke these words.
"O valiant one, employ me; desist from this rashness!
Behold the mighty-armed Rāma struck down in battle."
I swear this truth to you; I touch my weapon, swearing that I shall slay Rāma, who deserves to be killed by all the rākṣasas.
Either I shall be his death in battle, or he shall be mine in the fray;
setting aside your enthusiasm for combat for a moment, act as an umpire.
Either, with Rāma slain, you shall go to Janasthāna rejoicing;
or, with me killed, you shall approach Rāma for battle.
Khara was propitiated by Triśiras out of a desire for death;
permitted with the words, "Go and fight," he set out toward Rāghava.
And Triśiras, on a radiant chariot yoked with horses,
rushed toward Rāma in battle like a three-peaked mountain.
Releasing masses of arrow-showers like a great cloud,
he let out a roar resembling that of a drum moistened with water.
Seeing the three-headed Rākṣasa approaching, Rāghava received him with his bow,
brandishing sharp arrows.
That tumultuous and great battle between Rāma and Triśiras,
both exceedingly powerful, was like that between a lion and an elephant.
Then, struck on the forehead by Triśiras with three arrows, the indignant and enraged Rāma spoke these words in a state of agitation: *Ram_3,26.11*
"Aha! Such is the strength of this Rākṣasa, a hero in valor, by whose arrows I have been wounded on the forehead as if by flowers. Now, receive from me too these arrows released from the bowstring."
Having spoken thus, he, enraged and impetuous, struck fourteen arrows resembling venomous serpents into the chest of Triśiras.
With four straight-knotted arrows,
the radiant hero struck down his four horses.
With eight arrows, he struck down the charioteer from the seat of the chariot;
and with another shaft, Rāma cut down his lofty standard.
Then, as the night-stalker was leaping up from that destroyed chariot,
Rāma pierced him in the heart with arrows, and he became motionless.
Then that one of immeasurable soul, filled with indignation, struck off the three heads of that Rākṣasa with three hundred swift arrows.
Afflicted by Rāma’s arrow, that night-stalker fell to the ground vomiting blood,
after his own heads had already fallen.
Then the remaining Rākṣasas who had survived the slaughter, broken and taking refuge with Khara,
fled and did not stop, like deer terrified by a tiger.
Seeing them fleeing, the enraged Khara turned back himself and rushed toward Rāma alone, just as Rāhu rushes toward the moon.
Seeing Dūṣaṇa slain in battle along with Triśiras,
and witnessing the prowess of Rāma, even Khara was seized with terror.
Seeing that the Rākṣasa army, though possessed of great strength and unbearable,
had been slain by Rāma alone— along with both Dūṣaṇa and Triśiras— [he was struck with wonder].
Seeing that army mostly destroyed, the dejected Rākṣasa Khara approached Rāma,
just as Namuci once approached Vāsava.
Drawing his powerful bow, Khara discharged iron arrows that feed on blood,
like enraged venomous serpents, at Rāma.
Vibrating his bowstring repeatedly and displaying his mastery of weapons,
Khara, stationed upon his chariot, moved through various maneuvers in the battle with his arrows.
Seeing him, that great chariot-warrior filled all the directions and intermediate quarters with his arrows; and Rāma also took up a very great bow.
With his unbearable arrows, which were like sparks of fire,
