he left no space in the sky, just as a rain-cloud fills it with showers.
With those sharp arrows discharged by Khara and Rāma,
the sky became devoid of space, crowded on all sides with shafts.
Enveloped by a net of arrows, the sun did not shine then as the two fought together with a fury intent on killing one another.
Then, with hollow shafts, iron arrows, and sharp-pointed barbed bolts,
he struck Rāma in battle, as one strikes a great elephant with goads.
All living beings beheld that Rākṣasa standing upon his chariot, bow in hand, like Death himself with a noose in his grasp.
Seeing him, who was as valiant as a lion and possessed a gait like that of a lion, Rāma was not agitated, just as a lion is not disturbed by a small animal.
Then, in his great chariot which resembled the sun,
Khara encountered Rāma in battle, like a moth approaching a fire.
Then Khara, displaying his lightness of hand, severed the bow along with the arrow from the grip of the high-souled Rāma.
Then, filled with rage in that battle, he took seven other arrows, possessing a brilliance equal to Indra’s thunderbolt, and struck them into the armor.
Then that armor of Rāma, who possessed the splendor of the sun, fell to the ground, shattered by the well-jointed arrows discharged by Khara.
Pierced in all his limbs by those arrows, the enraged Rāghava shone in battle like a blazing fire without smoke.
Then Rāma, the destroyer of enemies, strung another great bow that emitted a deep resonance, for the final destruction of his foe.
Raising that excellent bow of Viṣṇu, which had indeed been bestowed by the great seer, he rushed toward Khara.
Then, filled with rage, Rāma severed Khara’s banner in battle with gold-feathered arrows of straight joints.
That beautiful golden banner, severed in many places,
fell to the earth like the sun by the command of the gods.
Then Khara, an expert in the vital points of the body, being enraged, pierced Rāma in his limbs and heart with four arrows, just as one strikes an elephant with iron pikes.
Pierced by many arrows discharged from Khara’s bow, Rāma,
his limbs drenched in blood, became exceedingly enraged.
Taking up his bow in that great battle, that best of archers, a supreme marksman,
released six well-aimed arrows.
He struck him on the head with one arrow, then on both arms with two,
and struck him in the chest with three crescent-headed shafts.
Thereafter, the immensely powerful one, enraged and desiring to slay the Rākṣasa, discharged thirteen iron arrows, whetted on stone and resembling the sun.
Then, with one arrow he cut his yoke, with four the four horses, and with the sixth he severed the head of Khara’s charioteer in the battle.
The powerful one [cut] the triple-bamboo pole with three arrows, and the exceedingly mighty one [cut] the axle with two;
then, with a twelfth arrow, he [severed] Khara’s bow along with its string.
Having severed [his bow] with an arrow resembling a thunderbolt, Rāghava, laughing as it were,
pierced Khara in battle with his thirteenth shaft, like Indra himself.
With his bow shattered, deprived of his chariot, his horses slain, and his charioteer killed,
Khara then leaped down and stood upon the ground with a mace in hand.

Then the gods and the great seers, having assembled together, stood upon the foremost of their celestial chariots; with palms joined in reverence and filled with joy, they praised that deed of the great car-warrior Rāma.
But Rāma, possessed of great splendor, spoke first mildly and then harsh words to Khara, who stood there deprived of his chariot with a mace in hand.
While standing amidst a vast army crowded with elephants, horses, and chariots,
you have committed a most cruel deed that is loathed by the whole world.
A cruel doer of evil deeds who causes terror among living beings does not remain in power, even if he were the lord of the three worlds.
O night-stalker, everyone slays one who performs actions contrary to the world, just as people kill a fierce, wicked snake that has appeared. (Rāmāyaṇa 3.28.4)
He who commits sins out of greed or desire and does not realize it,
having fallen, sees their end like a Brāhmaṇī woman [seeing] the inside of a water-pot.
O Rākṣasa, what fruit will you obtain by killing these highly fortunate ascetics who dwell in the Daṇḍaka forest practicing their dharma?
Those who perform evil deeds— cruel and despised by the world— do not remain long in power once they have attained it, like trees whose roots have rotted away.
The doer of an evil deed will inevitably reap its terrible fruit when the time arrives, just as a tree bears its seasonal blossoms.
O night-stalker, the fruit of evil deeds is obtained in this world before long,
like that of poisoned foods once they have been eaten.
O night-stalker, I have been encountered by those who commit terrible evil and desire the misfortune of the world, seeking to take my life.
For today, the gold-adorned arrows released by me shall pierce you and fall [to the earth] like serpents entering an anthill.
Those practitioners of dharma who were devoured by you in the Daṇḍaka forest—
you shall follow them today in battle, slain along with your army.
Today, let the supreme ṛṣis whom you previously harmed behold you slain by my arrows and situated in hell, while they themselves remain stationed in celestial chariots.
Strike as you please and exert your effort, O lowest of your lineage!
Today I shall strike down your head like the fruit of a palmyra tree.
Thus addressed by Rāma, he, enraged and with eyes bloodshot,
replied to Rāma, laughing while overwhelmed with fury.
"O son of Daśaratha, having slain the common rākṣasas in battle,
why do you praise yourself, who are not worthy of praise?"
Those bulls among men who are courageous and powerful do not say anything at all, being proud of their own splendor.
But those commoners of unrefined soul, the scum of the kṣatriya caste in this world,
boast in vain, just as you, Rāma, are boasting.
Proclaiming his lineage in battle, what hero would utter praise of himself at a time other than when death has arrived? (Rāmāyaṇa 3.28.19)
In every way, your worthlessness has been revealed by this boasting, like gold that appears to be real but is merely heated straw-fire.
Yet you do not see me standing here, bearing my mace,
like the immovable mountain Dharadhara, variegated with its minerals.
"With mace in hand, I am capable of taking your life in battle,
just as Death with noose in hand is capable of destroying even the three worlds."
Granted, there is much that ought to be said, yet I shall not speak it to you;
for the sun is about to set, and from that, an obstacle to battle would arise.
Fourteen thousand Rākṣasas have been slain by you;
today, because of your destruction, I shall wipe away their tears.
Having spoken thus, the exceedingly enraged Khara, adorned with magnificent armlets, hurled that mace at Rāma like a blazing thunderbolt.
That great, blazing mace, released by Kharabāhu,
reduced the trees and shrubs to ashes and approached his side.
As that flaming mace, resembling the noose of Death,
was falling through the air, Rāma shattered it into many pieces with his arrows.
Shattered and pierced by arrows, it fell upon the surface of the earth like a female serpent brought down by the power of spells, herbs, and clubs.
Having shattered that mace with his arrows, Rāghava, who is devoted to righteousness, smilingly addressed these words of intense fury to Khara: "Ram_3.29.1"
This is the entirety of your strength that has been displayed, O lowest of Rākṣasas;
you roar in vain, for you are far more devoid of power than I am.
This mace, shattered by Bāṇa's arrow, has fallen to the surface of the earth;
it is the destroyer of the confidence of you who are so bold in your boasts.
As for what you said— that you would wipe away these tears of the deceased Rākṣasas— that word of yours was also false.
I shall take away the life of this base, vile-natured, and deceitful Rākṣasa, just as Garuḍa seized the nectar of immortality.
Today, as your throat is severed and you are torn apart by my arrows, the earth shall drink your blood, adorned with froth and bubbles.
With all your limbs covered in dust and your two arms cast down and relaxed,
you shall sleep embracing the earth as if it were a woman difficult to attain.
When you, O vilest of Rākṣasas, have fallen asleep with deep slumber,
these Daṇḍaka forests shall become a refuge for those who are currently without refuge.
O Rākṣasa, in Janasthāna, which has now become a place of slaughter for you by my arrows,
the sages shall roam fearlessly throughout the forest in every direction.
Today the Rākṣasīs, whose kinsmen have been slain, will flee in all directions;
their faces wet with tears and wretched, they will be filled with fear, bringing terror to others.
O night-stalker, today those wives of yours, who are from noble families worthy of you, shall come to know the taste of grief, now that they have such a husband as you.
O you of cruel character and base soul, constant thorn in the side of the Brahmins:
because of you, the sages offer oblations into the fire with apprehension.
To Raghava, who was speaking thus with such vehemence in battle,
Khara, with a voice even harsher than his own, rebuked him out of rage.
Truly, you are stubbornly arrogant and remain fearless even in the face of dangers;
therefore, being under the sway of death, you do not perceive what should and should not be said.
For those men who are ensnared by the noose of Time do not distinguish between what ought to be done and what ought not to be done; their six senses have been cast away.
Having spoken thus to Rāma, the night-stalker knit his brows in a frown and then beheld a great sāl tree not far away.
Looking all around for a weapon for the sake of combat,
he tore it out upon seeing its fang-like edge.
Lifting him up with his two arms and roaring loudly, the one of great strength hurled him toward Rāma and said, "You are slain!"
Having cut down that [missile] as it came flying with a flood of arrows, the powerful Rāma summoned a fierce rage in order to slay Khara in battle.
Then Rāma, his eyes red at the corners from rage and perspiring,
pierced Khara with a thousand arrows in that battle.
From the wound caused by his arrow, much frothy blood flowed forth,
like the outpouring of waterfalls from a mountain stream.
Rendered frantic by those arrows in the combat, Khara,
intoxicated by the scent of blood, rushed swiftly toward Rāma himself.
As he charged forward, enraged and drenched in blood, Rāma, skilled in weaponry,
stepped back one pace at a time with swift strides.
Then, for the sake of slaying Khara in battle, Rāma seized an arrow resembling fire, like a second staff of Brahmā.
Having received that which was given by Maghavan, the wise king of the gods,
that righteous-souled one aimed it and released it toward Khara.
That great arrow, released by Rāma who had raised his bow, fell upon Khara’s chest with a sound like a thunderclap.
Scorched by the fire of his arrows, he fell to the ground like Andhaka in the Śveta forest, utterly consumed by Rudra.
Like Vṛtra struck by the thunderbolt, like Namuci by the foam, or like Bala slain by Indra’s lightning bolt, the slain Khara fell down.

Then all the royal sages and supreme seers, having gathered together and honored Rāma with joy, spoke these words: Ram_3,29.29: "Then all the royal sages and supreme seers, having gathered together and honored Rāma with joy, spoke these words."
For this purpose, the highly effulgent Mahendra, the subduer of Pāka and destroyer of cities,
came to the holy hermitage of Śarabhaṅga.
"You have been brought to this place by the great seers through a stratagem,
for the sake of slaying these cruel Rākṣasas of evil deeds."
Thus, O son of Daśaratha, this task has been accomplished by you for us;
the great seers shall now practice their dharma in comfort within the Daṇḍaka forests.
In the meantime, the heroic Lakṣmaṇa, together with Sītā,
emerged from the mountain fastness and entered the hermitage in comfort.
Then the victorious hero Rāma, being honored by the great seers,
entered the hermitage after being saluted by Lakṣmaṇa.
Seeing him, the slayer of enemies who brings happiness to the great seers,
Vaidehī was filled with joy and embraced her husband.
Then Śūrpaṇakhā saw that fourteen thousand Rākṣasas of terrible deeds had been slain by Rāma alone.
Seeing Dūṣaṇa, Khara, and Triśiras slain in battle,
she, who resembled a rain-cloud, let out a great roar once again.
Having seen the deed performed by Rāma, which was exceedingly difficult for others to accomplish,
she went, deeply agitated, to Laṅkā, which was ruled by Rāvaṇa.
At the front of the celestial chariot, she beheld Rāvaṇa, blazing with splendor,
seated there with his ministers like Vāsava among the Maruts.
He was seated upon a supreme golden throne, radiant as the sun,
like a blazing fire placed upon a sacrificial altar of gold.
Invincible in battle even by gods, gandharvas, spirits, and high-souled rishis, he was a hero with a mouth wide open like that of Death himself.
His chest bore scars inflicted by the thunderbolt during the battles between the gods and the asuras,
and it was marked by calluses from being gored by the tips of Airāvata’s tusks.
He had twenty arms and ten necks, was adorned with beautiful ornaments,
possessed a broad chest, and was a hero marked by the auspicious signs of royalty.
Resembling smooth lapis lazuli, with earrings of refined gold,
he possessed beautiful arms, white teeth, a large face, and was like a mountain.
In that battle with the gods, his body was struck hundreds of times by the falls of Viṣṇu’s discus as well as by all the weapons of the deities.
He who agitates the oceans that are as unshakeable as they are vast, who acts with swiftness,
who hurls away the mountain peaks, and who crushes the gods.
He was a destroyer of dharma, a violator of the wives of others, one who constantly invoked all divine weapons, and a perpetual obstructer of sacrifices.
Having gone to the city of Bhogavatī and defeated Vāsuki,
he conquered and carried off the beloved wife of Takṣaka.
Having gone to Mount Kailāsa and defeated Naravāhana,
he indeed seized his Puṣpaka chariot, which travels at will.
That powerful one, out of anger, destroys the divine Caitraratha forest, the Nalinī lake, the Nandana grove, and the celestial gardens of the gods.
He who, resembling a mountain peak, restrains with his two arms the illustrious sun and moon as they rise, those scorchers of the foe.
In former times, having performed austerities for ten thousand years in the great forest,
that wise one offered his own heads to the Self-Existent One (Brahmā).
He who possesses fearlessness in battle against gods, dānavas, gandharvas, piśācas, birds, and serpents— save for death at the hands of a human.
That one of great strength who destroys the sacred Soma, consecrated with mantras by the twice-born during the sacrifices, within the sacrificial sheds.
Rāvaṇa, who robbed the sacrifices of the worthy, was cruel, a slayer of Brahmins, and a practitioner of evil deeds;
he was harsh, merciless, and devoted to the harm of his subjects,
bringing fear to all beings and all the worlds.
She beheld her cruel and mighty brother,
that illustrious lord of the Rākṣasas, the delight of the lineage of Pulastya, adorned with celestial garments and ornaments and graced by divine garlands.

Having displayed that blazing and wide-eyed [form], Śūrpaṇakhā— terrified, deluded, and fainting— spoke these most cruel words to the great-souled one who moves fearlessly, she having been disfigured by him.
Then Śūrpaṇakhā, distressed and enraged, spoke these harsh words to Rāvaṇa, the one who makes the world cry out, in the midst of his ministers.
Addicted to sensual pleasures, acting according to your own whims and unrestrained,
you do not perceive the terrible danger that has arisen, even though it must be recognized.
Subjects do not hold in high regard a king who is attached to vulgar pleasures, who acts out of lust,
and who is greedy, just as they do not value the fire of a cremation ground.
That king who does not personally attend to his duties at the proper time indeed perishes, along with his kingdom and those very duties.
Men avoid from afar a king who acts improperly, who is difficult to behold, and who lacks self-control,
just as elephants avoid the mud of a river.
Those kings who do not protect their realm because they lack self-control do not shine with prosperity, just like mountains submerged in the ocean.
Having provoked hostilities with the self-possessed gods, Gandharvas, and Dānavas,
how will you, being fickle and lacking secret spies, become a king?
O best among victors, those kings whose spies, treasury, and policy are not under their own control are equal to common folk.
Because kings perceive all matters situated at a distance through their spies, they are therefore called "long-sighted."
I consider you to be acting imprudently, surrounded as you are by common ministers, since you do not perceive that your own kinsmen and Janasthāna have been destroyed.
Fourteen thousand Rākṣasas of fearsome deeds,
along with Khara and Dūṣaṇa, were slain by Rāma alone.
Fearlessness has been granted to the seers, and the Daṇḍaka forest has been made secure;
Janasthāna has been laid waste by Rāma, whose actions are effortless.
But you, O Rāvaṇa, are greedy, heedless, and dependent on others,
for you do not perceive the danger that has arisen within your own domain.
All living beings flee from a king who is harsh, stingy, negligent, arrogant, and deceitful when he falls into calamity.
Even his own kin will slay a king who is arrogant, ungraspable, self-conceited, and prone to anger when faced with misfortune.
He will not attend to his duties, nor will he fear dangers;
soon fallen from his kingdom and wretched, he will become like a blade of grass.
A task may be accomplished with dry wood, or even with clods of earth and dust;
but no purpose can be served by kings who have fallen from their rightful place.
Just as a garment that has been worn out, or as a garland that has been crushed,
even so one who has fallen from his kingdom is useless, even if he remains capable.
That king who is vigilant, all-knowing, has conquered his senses,
is grateful, and is virtuous in character, shall endure for a long time.
Though his physical eyes may be closed in sleep, he remains awake with the eye of policy;
that king, whose anger and favor are manifest, is honored by the people.
But you, O Rāvaṇa, are evil-minded and devoid of these virtues,
since this great slaughter of the Rākṣasas remained unknown to you through your spies.
One who disregards others, is attached to sensual objects, does not understand the true nature of the distinctions between place and time,
and lacks the wisdom to discern virtues from faults, will soon fall from his kingdom once it has already been ruined.
Having thus reflected with his intellect upon the faults proclaimed by her, Rāvaṇa, the lord of the night-rangers, endowed as he was with wealth, pride, and power, pondered for a long time.
Then Rāvaṇa, enraged, questioned Śūrpaṇakhā— who was herself furious and speaking harsh words— in the midst of his ministers.
And who is Rāma? Of what prowess is he, what is his form, and what is his valor?
And for what purpose has he entered the Daṇḍaka forest, so difficult to traverse?
And what was the weapon of Rāma by which the rākṣasas were slain,
and by which Khara was killed in battle, as well as Dūṣaṇa and Triśiras?
Thus addressed by the lord of the rākṣasas, the rākṣasī, overwhelmed with anger,
then began to relate the matter concerning Rāma according to the facts.
Long-armed and large-eyed, clad in bark and the skin of a black antelope,
Rāma, the son of Daśaratha, possesses a form equal to that of Kandarpa.
Drawing his bow, which resembled Indra’s rainbow and was adorned with golden armlets,
he discharged blazing iron arrows like highly venomous serpents.
I do not see Rāma in battle taking up his terrible arrows, nor releasing them, nor drawing his great bow, despite his immense strength.
I beheld that army being slaughtered by showers of arrows,
like a magnificent crop struck down by Indra with a rain of stones.
Fourteen thousand rākṣasas of terrible prowess were slain by his sharp arrows, all alone on foot.
In slightly more than half a muhūrta, Khara along with Dūṣaṇa were slain;
safety was granted to the sages, and the Daṇḍaka forest was rendered secure.
Somehow I was released by that great-souled one,
Rāma, who knows his own self and who, fearing the slaughter of a woman, showed me contempt.
And his brother, named Lakṣmaṇa, is possessed of great splendor, equal to him in virtue and prowess, valiant, devoted, and loyal.
Impatient, invincible, a conqueror, valiant, wise, and powerful—
he is Rāma’s right arm, his very life-breath moving outside his body.
Rāma’s illustrious and lawful wife, however, was the large-eyed Sītā,
the daughter of Videha, who possessed beautiful limbs and a slender waist.
Neither a goddess, nor a Gandharva woman, nor a Yakṣī, nor a Kiṃnarī—
never before have I seen a woman of such form upon this earth.
He whose wife Sītā might become, and whom she might joyfully embrace,
would surpass all others in the worlds, even Purandara himself.
She is virtuous, her form is praiseworthy, and she is peerless in beauty upon this earth;
she is a wife worthy of you, and you likewise are a husband for her.
I am indeed prepared to bring that fair-faced woman, with her broad hips and full, elevated breasts, to be your wife.
But upon seeing Vaidehī today, her face like the full moon,
you will fall under the power of the arrows of the god of love.
If the intention arises within you to take her as your wife,
let your right foot be swiftly raised here for the sake of victory.
O Lord of the Rākṣasas, do what is pleasing to those Rākṣasas by slaying that cruel Rāma who dwells in the hermitage.
Having slain him with sharpened arrows, as well as the great car-warrior Lakṣmaṇa,
you shall enjoy Sītā at your ease, now that her protector has been destroyed.
O Lord of the Rākṣasas, O Rāghava, if these words of mine please you, let my command be carried out without hesitation.
Having heard that the night-stalkers dwelling in Janasthāna have been slain by Rāma with his straight-flying arrows,
and knowing that Khara and Dūṣaṇa have also been killed, you ought today to determine what must be done.
Then, having heard those hair-raising words of Śūrpaṇakhā and having understood the task at hand, he took leave of his ministers and departed.
Then, having investigated that task and understood it correctly, he weighed the relative strength of the faults and the virtues.
Having thus made a firm resolve within himself that "this is what must be done," he,
steady in intellect, then went to the beautiful carriage shed.
Then, having gone to the carriage shed, the lord of the rākṣasas, remaining concealed,
urged the charioteer, saying, "Let the chariot be yoked."
Thus addressed, the charioteer, swift in his movements, in an instant harnessed that excellent chariot which was desired by him.
He mounted a golden chariot that moved at will, adorned with jewels,
and yoked to donkeys with faces like Piśācas and decorated with gold ornaments.
With a roar resembling the sound of clouds, that glorious lord of the Rākṣasas, the younger brother of Dhanada, proceeded toward the lord of rivers and streams.
He had ten faces, a white parasol, and a white chowrie;
he resembled smooth lapis lazuli and was adorned with ornaments of refined gold.
Ten-faced and twenty-armed, with magnificent retinues,
he was the enemy of the gods and the slayer of the Lord of Sages, appearing like the ten-peaked king of mountains.
Mounted upon his chariot that moved at will, the lord of the rākṣasas shone like a cloud in the sky accompanied by lightning and cranes.
The valiant one gazed upon the ocean shore together with its mountains,
strewn with thousands of trees laden with various flowers and fruits.
It was surrounded on all sides by lotus ponds with cool, auspicious waters,
and by spacious hermitage sites provided with sacrificial altars.
It was densely crowded with plantains and *āḍhaki* trees, adorned with coconut palms,
and filled with *sāla*, *tāla*, and *tamāla* trees in full bloom.
It was adorned by supreme ṛṣis who subsisted on strictly regulated diets,
as well as by thousands of nāgas, suparṇas, gandharvas, and kinnaras.
It was graced by those who had conquered their desires, by the Siddhas, and by the Cāraṇas;
as well as by the Ājas, Vaikhānasas, Māṣas, Vālakhilyas, and Marīcipas.
He was surrounded by thousands of Apsarases of divine form, adorned with celestial ornaments and garlands, who were skilled in the arts of play and pleasure.
It was frequented by the glorious wives of the gods and graced with splendor;
it was also traversed by hosts of gods and dānavas who subsist on nectar.
It was filled with swans, cranes, and water-fowl, and resounded with the cries of cranes;
it was delightful with floors of lapis lazuli, and glossy with the splendor of the ocean.
On all sides were vast, white celestial chariots, adorned with divine garlands and graced by the sounds of musical instruments and song.
As he traveled through the worlds won by their asceticism,
the younger brother of the Giver of Wealth beheld Gandharvas and Apsarases who move at will.
He beheld thousands of sandalwood forests, gentle and pleasing, filled with the sap and roots of exudations, which brought satisfaction to the sense of smell.
And there were forests and groves of the finest agaru trees,
as well as those of excellent takkola trees and fragrant fruits.
And there were blossoms of the tamāla tree and clusters of pepper plants,
as well as heaps of pearls drying upon the shore.
There were heaps of conch shells as well as clusters of coral,
and mountains made entirely of gold and silver on every side.
There are delightful streams and clear lakes,
abounding in wealth and grain, and surrounded by jewels among women.
Beholding cities densely packed with elephants, horses, and chariots,
he observed that [the land] was level on all sides and possessed a soft touch from the gentle breeze.
He beheld the marshy region of the King of Rivers, which resembled the third heaven;
there he saw a banyan tree, dark as a cloud, surrounded by sages.
On all sides, its branches extended for a hundred yojanas;
to one such branch, the mighty Garuḍa came, carrying a massive elephant and a tortoise, intending to eat them.
Then that best of birds, Suparṇa, endowed with great strength, suddenly broke that branch thick with leaves under his weight.
There, the great seers— the Vaikhānasas, Māṣas, Vālakhilyas, Marīcipas, Ajas, and Dhūmras— were gathered together.
Out of compassion for them, Garuḍa took that branch, which was a hundred yojanas long,
and departed with great speed, carrying both those two, the elephant and the tortoise.
Having devoured that meat with one foot,
and having destroyed the Niṣāda territory with his wing, that best of birds,
whose nature is dharma, attained incomparable joy after liberating the great sages.
With his prowess doubled by that very joy,
the wise one indeed set his mind upon the task of bringing back the nectar of immortality.
Having crushed the iron nets and broken through the excellent jewel-house,
he then brought forth the nectar from the secure abode of Mahendra.
The younger brother of the Giver of Wealth beheld that banyan tree named Subhadra, frequented by hosts of great seers and marked with the sign of Suparṇa.
Having reached the far shore of that ocean, the lord of rivers,
he beheld a hermitage in a secluded spot within a holy and beautiful forest.
There he beheld a Rākṣasa named Mārīca, wearing a black antelope skin, clad in matted hair and bark garments, and restricted in his diet.
Having met with that Rākṣasa according to the prescribed rites, Rāvaṇa,
who was skilled in speech, then spoke these words.
"O Mārīca, my dear father, listen to the words I speak;
I am distressed, and for me in my distress, you are indeed the supreme refuge."
"You know Janasthāna, where my brother Khara resides,
as well as the mighty-armed Dūṣaṇa and my sister Śūrpaṇakhā."
And the immensely powerful three-headed Rākṣasa, the flesh-eater,
as well as many other heroic night-stalkers who were skilled marksmen.
By my command, the Rākṣasas dwell there and harass the sages who practice dharma in the great forest.
There were fourteen thousand rākṣasas of terrifying deeds— heroes who had achieved their aims and followed the will of Khara.
But now, those mighty ones dwelling in Janasthāna have come together and are utterly intent on engaging in battle with Rāma.
Then Rāma, having become enraged at the head of the battle,
without uttering a single harsh word, destroyed the bow with his arrows.
Fourteen thousand rākṣasas of fearsome deeds were slain with sharp arrows by a human on foot.
Khara was slain in battle and Dūṣaṇa was struck down;
having also killed Triśiras, the Daṇḍaka forest has been rendered free from fear.
Banished by his angry father along with his wife, his life nearly spent,
that Rama, a disgrace to the Kshatriyas, is the slayer of that army.
Lacking virtue, harsh, sharp-tongued, foolish, greedy, and with senses unsubdued, he had abandoned righteousness; being unrighteous in soul, he delighted in the harm of living beings.
By him, who harbors enmity in the forest without cause, my sister has been disfigured by the severing of her ears and nose, relying solely on his own strength.
"I shall bring his wife Sītā, who resembles the daughter of a god, from Janasthāna by means of my prowess; be my ally in this matter."
O one of great strength, with you as my companion standing by my side and with my brothers, I do not fear all the gods together in battle.
Therefore, be my ally, O Rākṣasa, for you are indeed capable;
in heroism, in battle, and in pride, there is truly no one equal to you.
For this purpose, O night-stalker, I have come into your presence;
hear that task which must be performed with your assistance at my word.
Becoming a golden deer, variegated with silver spots,
roam about in the hermitage of that Rāma, right before Sītā.
But upon seeing you in the form of a deer, Sītā will undoubtedly say to her husband and to Lakṣmaṇa, "Seize him!"
Then, upon their departure, when they are gone and it is empty, I shall carry off Sītā at my pleasure, free from all hindrance, just as Rāhu seizes the light of the moon.
After that, when Rāma has been emaciated by the abduction of his wife,
I shall strike him confidently, with my inner soul having achieved its purpose.
Upon hearing that account of Rāma from the high-souled Mārīca,
his mouth became parched and he was seized with terror.
In that great forest, his mind terrified and dejected, knowing Rāma’s prowess, he addressed these words— truthful, beneficial, and for his own good— to Rāvaṇa with palms joined in reverence.
Having heard those words of the lord of the Rākṣasas, the highly wise Mārīca, who was skilled in speech, replied to the sovereign of the Rākṣasas.
O King, men who always speak pleasant words are easy to find; however, one who speaks what is unpleasant yet beneficial, as well as one who listens to such words, is rare indeed.
Surely you do not realize that Rāma is of great heroism and exalted in virtue, resembling Mahendra and Varuṇa; you are fickle and lack proper spies.
"O father, may it be well with all the Rākṣasas on earth;
might Rāma, even when enraged, not rid the world of its Rākṣasas?"
I hope that the daughter of Janaka has not been born for the end of your life; I hope that Sītā has not become the cause of some great calamity.
Moreover, even though you have obtained sovereignty and act according to your own will without restraint,
may the city of Laṅkā not perish along with you and the rākṣasas.
For a king like you, who acts according to his lusts, is ill-behaved, and follows evil counsel— that foolish ruler destroys himself, his kinsmen, and his kingdom.
He was never abandoned by his father, nor was he ever lacking in propriety;
he was neither greedy, nor ill-behaved, nor a disgrace to the kṣatriya caste.
Nor was he deficient in the virtues of dharma; he increased the joy of Kausalyā.
He was not harsh toward any living beings, for he was devoted to the welfare of all.
Seeing his father deceived by Kaikeyī,
the righteous-souled one, thinking "I shall fulfill [his word]," then departed for the forest.
For the sake of pleasing Kaikeyī and his father Daśaratha,
he has abandoned the kingdom and all enjoyments and entered the Daṇḍaka forest.

"O dear one, Rāma is neither harsh, nor unlearned, nor one who has failed to conquer his senses; he has never spoken an untruth, nor anything contrary to the sacred scriptures. You ought not to speak thus."
Rāma is righteousness incarnate, virtuous, and one whose prowess is truth;
he is the king of the entire world, just as Vāsava is among the gods.
How can you desire to seize by force Vaidehī, who is protected by his own splendor, like the radiance of the sun?
You ought not to rashly enter the fire of Rāma, which blazes fiercely in battle, with arrows for its flames, being unassailable, and with bows and swords for its fuel.
With his bow drawn into a blazing mouth and the rays of his arrows as its flames,
the indignant hero held his bow and arrow, the destroyer of enemy armies.
O dear one, having renounced your kingdom, your happiness, and even your own cherished life,
you ought not to seek to approach the end-maker Rāma here.
For that daughter of Janaka possesses immeasurable splendor;
you are not capable of abducting her while she is under the protection of Rāma’s bow in the forest.
Sītā of the slender waist, ever devoted to him, was dearer to him than his own life; she was like the cresting flame of a blazing fire.
O Lord of the Rākṣasas, why have you made this futile effort?
If you are seen by him in battle, that will be the end of your life,
as well as your happiness and your kingdom, which are so difficult to attain.
Having consulted with all his ministers, who were headed by Vibhīṣaṇa and were most righteous, he made his own decision.
Having carefully weighed the strengths and weaknesses of both faults and virtues,
and having truly understood your own strength as well as that of Raghava,
you ought to determine what is beneficial for you and do what is appropriate.
But I think it is not fitting for you to encounter the son of the King of Kosala in battle;
therefore, O Lord of the Night-rangers, listen once more to these supreme words, which are both appropriate and reasonable.
Once, while wandering this earth with vigor,
I possessed the strength of a thousand elephants and was like a mountain.
Resembling a dark blue cloud, wearing earrings of refined gold,
and armed with an iron club, he— wearing a diadem and striking terror into the world—
roamed the Daṇḍaka forest devouring the flesh of sages.
Then the righteous and great sage Viśvāmitra, terrified of me,
went in person to King Daśaratha and spoke these words.
"O Lord of Men, may this Rāma, composed in mind, protect me during the time of the festival; for a terrible fear of Mārīca has arisen within me."
Having been addressed in this manner, King Daśaratha, whose soul was devoted to righteousness,
then replied to the illustrious great sage Viśvāmitra.
"This Raghava is less than sixteen years of age and has not yet mastered weapons; however,
O best of sages, my army will go with me at my command, and I shall slay your enemy as you desire."
Thus addressed, that sage spoke again to the king:
"In this world, there is no force other than Rāma sufficient to overcome that Rākṣasa."
"Though he is but a child, he possesses great majesty and is capable of subduing him.
I shall go taking Rāma with me; may it be well with you, O scorcher of foes!"
Having spoken thus, the sage Viśvāmitra, taking the prince with him, departed for his own hermitage, filled with supreme joy.
At that time, Rāma remained stationed in the Daṇḍaka forest, having been initiated for the sake of the sacrifice,
stretching his wonderful bow.
The illustrious youth, whose characteristics were not yet fully developed, was dark-complexioned with beautiful eyes;
wearing a single garment, carrying a bow, and adorned with a topknot and a golden garland.
Adorning the Daṇḍaka forest with his own radiant splendor,
Rāma then appeared like the newly risen crescent moon.
Then, resembling a cloud and wearing earrings of refined gold, I— powerful and having received boons— approached that hermitage out of pride.
He saw me enter suddenly with my weapon raised;
but upon seeing me, he unhesitatingly strung his bow.
Out of delusion, disregarding Rāghava as a mere child,
I rushed in haste toward Viśvāmitra’s sacrificial altar.
Then he released a sharp arrow, the destroyer of enemies;
struck by it, I was cast into the ocean a hundred yojanas away.
Repelled by the force of Rāma’s arrow, my consciousness reeling,
I was then cast down by him into the deep waters of the ocean; having regained my senses after a long time, O dear one, I went back toward the city of Laṅkā.
Thus was I liberated at that time, while your companions were struck down by the youthful Rāma, whose deeds are effortless, even though he had not yet mastered the divine weapons.
If, despite being restrained by me, you engage in conflict with Rāma,
you will quickly meet with a terrible calamity and perish.
You shall bring about distress and misfortune for the Rākṣasas, who are skilled in the arts of play and pleasure and devoted to social festivals.
For the sake of Maithilī, you shall behold the city of Laṅkā destroyed— once crowded with palaces and mansions, and adorned with various jewels.
Even those who do not commit evil deeds may perish through association with the wicked due to their reliance on them,
just as fish in a dragon's lake are destroyed by the sins of others.
Because of your transgression, you shall see the Rākṣasas, their limbs smeared with divine sandalwood paste and adorned with celestial ornaments, struck down upon the ground.
You shall see the night-stalkers— the survivors of the slaughter, now without refuge— fleeing in the ten directions, some having lost their wives and others accompanied by them.
"You will undoubtedly see Laṅkā surrounded by a net of arrows, enveloped in flames of fire, and its palaces consumed."
O King, you have thousands of women as your wives;
be devoted to your own wife and protect your lineage, O Rākṣasa.
If you desire to enjoy for a long time your honor, prosperity, kingdom, and your own cherished life, do not act in opposition to Rāma.
If, despite being vehemently forbidden by me, your friend, you should by force violate Sītā,
you shall go to the abode of Yama with your strength exhausted and your kinsmen, your life taken away by Rāma’s arrow.
Thus was I somehow liberated by him in that battle at that time;
now hear what happened next.
Thus treated by those two Rākṣasas in the form of deer, I entered the Daṇḍaka forest without losing heart.
With a flaming tongue, a massive body, sharp horns, and great strength,
that great deer, a consumer of flesh, roamed the Daṇḍaka forest.
O Rāvaṇa, I wandered through the sacred fire-chapels, holy fords, and sacred trees,
acting most terribly by assailing those ascetics.
Having slain the ascetics who practice dharma in the Daṇḍaka forest,
he drank their blood and likewise devoured their flesh.
Cruel, devouring the flesh of sages and terrifying the forest-dwellers,
I then roamed the Daṇḍaka forest, intoxicated by blood.
Then, while wandering in the Daṇḍaka forest as a destroyer of dharma,
I encountered Rāma, an ascetic who was devoted to righteousness.
And the highly fortunate Vaidehī, and Lakṣmaṇa the great chariot-warrior,
and the ascetic who is restrained in diet and devoted to the welfare of all beings.
Thus, having gone to the forest, I disregarded the mighty Rāma,
perceiving him as a mere ascetic while recollecting our former enmity.
Greatly enraged, with sharp horns and the form of a deer, I rushed forward,
desiring to kill him and remembering that previous blow, for I was lacking in wisdom.
Drawing his powerful bow, he released three sharp arrows capable of destroying enemies, which flew with a speed equal to that of Garuda or the wind.
Those three arrows, resembling thunderbolts, most terrible, and feeding on blood, all arrived together with their joints perfectly straight.
Knowing Rāma’s prowess and having previously witnessed his power, that deceitful one fled;
thus he escaped, while both those Rākṣasas were slain.
Having somehow escaped being released by Rāma’s arrow and regained my life,
I have become an ascetic here, disciplined and composed in meditation.
Indeed, tree after tree I see Rāma, clad in bark and black antelope skin,
holding his bow like Death himself with a noose in hand.
"O Rāvaṇa, terrified, I see thousands of Rāmas;
this entire forest appears to me as being composed entirely of Rāmas."
"O Lord of the Rākṣasas, in my solitude I see only Rāma;
having seen Rāma appearing in my dream, I wander about, deprived of my senses."
O Rāvaṇa, names beginning with the letter 'Ra'— such as Rāma and Rāvaṇa—
as well as jewels and chariots, all strike terror into me.
I know his power; it is not fitting for you to engage in battle with him.
Fight with Rāma in combat, or else grant me your leave, O Rākṣasa.
You should have no further talk of Rāma, if you wish to see me.
If you do not accept these words spoken by me, who seeks the welfare of my kinsmen, then,
slain today in battle by Rāma with his straight-flying arrows, you shall lose your life along with all your followers.
But Rāvaṇa did not accept those words spoken by Mārīca— which were both appropriate and logical— just as one who desires to die refuses medicine.
Driven by time, the lord of the Rākṣasas spoke these harsh and improper words to Mārīca, who had spoken what was beneficial and wholesome.
O Mārīca, this speech which you address to me is indeed unreasonable;
it is utterly fruitless, like seed sown in barren soil.
It is not possible for me to be dissuaded from battle with Rāma by your words—
especially since he is a mere mortal, foolish and evil-natured.
He who, having abandoned his friends, kingdom, mother, and father,
departed for the forest all at once upon hearing the common words of a woman.
Nevertheless, in battle against that slayer of Khara, I must certainly seize Sītā— who is dearer to him than his own life— in your very presence.
"O Mārīca, such is the firm resolve that dwells within my heart;
it cannot be turned back even by the gods and asuras led by Indra."
When questioned regarding the fault or the merit, the misfortune or the remedy for the determination of this matter, you alone ought to speak thus.
A wise minister who desires his own prosperity should, when questioned by the king, speak with palms joined in reverence.
The lord of the earth should be addressed with speech that is non-opposing, gentle at the outset, auspicious, beneficial, and endowed with courtesy.
But when Mārīca speaks words that are beneficial yet full of censure, the king— who is worthy of honor— does not welcome them, for they are devoid of respect.
Kings of immeasurable power assume five forms:
those of Agni, Indra, Soma, Yama, and Varuṇa;
namely, heat, valor, gentleness, punishment, and serenity.
Therefore, kings are to be honored and worshipped in all circumstances;
you, however, having failed to understand dharma, have resorted solely to delusion.
Out of wickedness, you speak such harsh words to me, a guest.
O Rākṣasa, I do not inquire into merits or faults, nor what is appropriate for myself; rather, you ought to provide assistance to me in this matter.
Having become a golden deer, variegated with silver spots,
you should entice Vaidehī and then depart as you please.
But seeing you as a golden illusory deer, Maithilī will be filled with wonder and will quickly say to Rāma, "Bring him here!"
Once the descendant of Kakutstha and Lakṣmaṇa have departed at their ease,
I shall bring back Vaidehī, just as the thousand-eyed Indra brought Śacī.
"Having thus accomplished this task, go wherever you wish, O Rākṣasa.
O Mārīca of noble vows, I shall grant half of my kingdom to you."
"Go, gentle one, upon an auspicious path for the success of this undertaking.
Having found Sītā and having deceived Rāghava without a fight,
I shall go back to Laṅkā with you, my purpose accomplished."
"You must perform this task for me, even by force;
for one who stands in opposition to the king never prospers in happiness."
Having encountered him, your life is in peril; for by opposing me today, death is certain for you.
Having reflected upon this with your intellect exactly as it is, do whatever is beneficial in this situation.
Commanded like a king, the night-stalker Mārīca spoke these harsh words in opposition to the command of the lord of the Rākṣasas.
O night-stalker, by what evildoer was this destruction of you— along with your sons, your kingdom, and your ministers— prophesied?
O King, what evildoer would not rejoice in you who are thus happy?
By whom was this taught to you as a means to the very door of death?
O night-stalker, it is quite evident that your enemies, being weak in valor,
desire you to be destroyed while you are held in check by one more powerful than yourself.
"O night-stalker, by what mean and malicious speaker was this taught to you— you who desire your own destruction through your own deeds?"
O Rāvaṇa, your ministers truly deserve to be slain, yet they are not killed,
for they do not restrain you in every way as you have mounted upon a path of ruin.
For a king who acts according to his lusts and has taken to a wrong path must be restrained in every way by the virtuous; yet you, though worthy of restraint, are not being restrained by them.
O best among victors, O night-stalker, through the favor of their master, ministers obtain dharma, wealth, pleasure, and fame.
But in the opposite case, O Rāvaṇa, all that becomes useless;
other people suffer calamity due to the faults of their master.
For righteousness and victory have their root in the king, O best among victors;
therefore, in all circumstances, the lord of men must be protected.
O night-stalker, a kingdom cannot be protected by one who is harsh;
nor, O Rākṣasa, can it be protected by one who is antagonistic or undisciplined.
Those ministers who employ harsh counsel are surely broken along with him,
just as chariots with a slow driver are quickly destroyed on uneven terrain.
Many virtuous men in this world, who were devoted to the practice of dharma,
have perished along with their attendants because of the transgressions of others.
O Rāvaṇa, when subjects are ruled by a hostile and harsh master,
they do not prosper, just as sheep do not thrive when guarded by a jackal.
O Rāvaṇa, all these Rākṣasas will surely perish,
for you are their harsh king— evil-minded and one who has not conquered his senses.
Thus, you have encountered this terrible and accidental calamity;
what could be more wretched than that you, along with your army, shall perish here?
"Once that Rāma has slain me, he will slay you before long;
by being killed by an enemy, I shall have accomplished my purpose."
"Know that I am already slain by the mere sight of Rāma;
know yourself, along with your kinsmen, to be slain for having abducted Sītā."
If you bring Sītā from the hermitage accompanied by me,
then neither you shall exist, nor I, nor Laṅkā, nor the Rākṣasas.
But though being restrained by me, who desires your welfare, you do not accept these words, O night-stalker;
for men whose lives have reached their end and who are like the departed do not heed the beneficial advice offered by friends.
Having spoken these harsh words to Rāvaṇa, Mārīca,
dejected from fear of the lord of the night-stalkers, then said, "Let us go."
Furthermore, I was seen by him as he held his bow, arrows, and sword;
with a weapon raised against one such as me, my life has been destroyed.
But what can I possibly do against you, O evil-minded one?
Here I go, my dear; may it be well with you, O night-stalker!
Delighted by those words, that Rākṣasa embraced him very closely and spoke these words.
This speech of yours, though filled with such audacity, sounds as if it were uttered under the influence of my name;
now you are Mārīca, but previously you were another night-stalker.
"Ascend quickly this chariot, adorned with jewels and yoked to donkeys with the faces of Piśācas; it is ready for me."
Then Rāvaṇa and Mārīca, having mounted that chariot as if it were a celestial vehicle, departed swiftly from that circle of hermitages.
In that very manner, they beheld there towns and forests,
all the mountains and rivers, as well as kingdoms and cities.
Then, having arrived at Daṇḍaka forest, Rāvaṇa, the lord of the rākṣasas, together with Marīca, beheld the hermitage of Rāghava.
Then, descending from that chariot adorned with gold,
Rāvaṇa took Mārīca by the hand and spoke these words.
"There is seen this site of Rāma's hermitage, surrounded by plantain trees;
O friend, let that which we have come for be accomplished quickly."
Having heard Rāvaṇa’s words, the rākṣasa Mārīca then became a deer and wandered about at the entrance of Rāma’s hermitage.
His horns were tipped with the finest jewels, his face was white and black in appearance,
his mouth was like a red lotus and a blue water-lily, and his ears were like blue lotuses.
With his neck slightly uplifted, his belly resembling sapphire,
his sides like the madhūka flower, and his complexion like the filaments of a lotus.
His hooves resembled lapis lazuli, his shanks were slender and well-knit,
and he was adorned above with a tail the color of a rainbow.
With a captivating and lovely complexion, adorned with various kinds of jewels,
the Rākṣasa in an instant became a most beautiful deer.
Assuming a captivating and beautiful form, that Rākṣasa set fire to the lovely forest and to that delightful hermitage of Rāma.
To entice Vaidehī, he wandered about, moving gracefully across the meadows on all sides, his body variegated with various minerals.
Variegated with hundreds of silver droplets and beautiful to behold,
he wandered about, breaking off and eating the tender shoots of the trees.
Having entered the plantain grove, he moved slowly from place to place among the *karṇikāra* trees, seeking at that time a sight of Sītā.
With a back variegated like a peacock's tail, that great deer shone brightly as he roamed at his pleasure near the precincts of Rāma’s hermitage.
Having gone forth and returned again, that best of deer roamed about;
after proceeding for a moment with haste, he turned back once more.
Sporting again upon the ground, he would sit down once more;
having reached the gate of the hermitage, he would pass by the herds of deer.
Followed by herds of deer,
the Rākṣasa who had assumed the form of a deer returned once more, longing for the sight of Sītā.
Leaping forth, he whirled in various circles,
and all the other deer who roam the forest gazed up at him.
Having approached and sniffed them, they fled in the ten directions;
yet that rākṣasa, who delighted in hunting deer, continued to pursue those wild animals.
To conceal his true state of mind, he did not eat while touching the food;
at that very moment, Vaidehī, the lady of auspicious eyes, [spoke].
Intent on gathering flowers,
the intoxicating-eyed woman passed by the *karṇikāra*, *aśoka*, and *cūta* trees.
Gathering flowers, that woman of radiant countenance,
who was unworthy of dwelling in the forest, beheld that deer made of jewels,
its limbs variegated with pearls and gems.
With eyes wide open in wonder, she gazed affectionately upon him, whose teeth and lips were radiant and whose body hair was like silver ore.
And that illusory deer, beholding the beloved of Rāma,
roamed about there, as if illuminating that forest.
Having seen that deer, composed of various jewels, which she had never seen before,
Sītā, the daughter of Janaka, was filled with the utmost wonder.
As she was gathering flowers, that woman of beautiful hips beheld him,
adorned on both sides by flanks with the hue of gold and silver.
Exultant, with faultless limbs and the complexion of refined gold,
she called out to her husband and to Lakṣmaṇa, who was armed.
Summoned by her, those two tigers among men, Rāma and Lakṣmaṇa, while surveying that region, then beheld a deer.
But seeing him, Lakṣmaṇa, filled with apprehension, said to Rāma:
"I believe this very deer is that same Rākṣasa Mārīca."
"O Rāma, while wandering joyfully in the forest on a hunt, kings were slain by this one through a wicked stratagem, for he can assume any form at will."
"O tiger among men, this illusory form of a deer has been created by this master of illusion; it is like a city of the Gandharvas, shimmering with light."
"O Raghava, Lord of the World, there is no deer such as this, adorned with jewels, to be found in the world; this is surely an illusion, there is no doubt."—Rāmāyaṇa 3.41.7.
To the descendant of Kakutstha who was speaking thus, Sītā— her mind captivated by his artifice— restrained him with a pure smile and spoke with great joy.
"O noble son, this deer is so enchanting that it captivates my heart.
Bring him here, O mighty-armed one; he shall serve as our plaything."
"In this hermitage of ours, many deer of auspicious appearance roam together, as do yaks and sṛmara antelopes."
Bears, herds of spotted deer, monkeys, and likewise kinnaras—
possessing excellent forms and great strength— roam about, O mighty-armed one.
And never before, O King, has a deer like this been seen,
equal in splendor, patience, and radiance to this best of deer.
With limbs variegated by many colors and covered with jewel-like spots,
he shines like the moon, illuminating the forest with undistracted splendor.
"Oh, what beauty! Oh, what splendor! And how magnificent is the perfection of his voice! This wonderful and extraordinary deer captivates my very heart."
If your deer should come into the grasp of the snare while still alive,
it will become a marvel and will produce great astonishment.
"When we have completed our forest exile and are once again established in our kingdom,
this deer shall serve as an ornament for the inner apartments."
O Lord, this divine form of a deer will cause wonder to Bharata, to my noble husband, to my mothers-in-law, and to me.
O tiger among men, if that best of deer does not come into my grasp while alive, his hide will be a beautiful one for me.
"When this creature has been slain, I wish to sit upon its Jāmbūnada-golden skin, which has been prepared as a cushion of young grass."
"This fierce conduct of passion is considered unbecoming of women;
yet, because of the character of this being, it has produced wonder in me."
At that sight— of the bull with golden hair and horns tipped with excellent jewels,
possessing the hue of the rising sun and the splendor of the path of the stars—
even the mind of Rāghava was filled with wonder.
Having thus heard Sītā’s words and having seen the wonderful deer,
Rāghava, filled with joy, spoke these words to his brother Lakṣmaṇa.
"Behold, Lakṣmaṇa, this longing of Vaidehī for the deer;
because of its supreme beauty, this deer shall surely cease to exist today."
Neither in the Nandana grove nor in the Caitraratha forest,
O Saumitri, is there any deer on earth that is his equal— how could there be?
And beautiful, variegated lines of hair, both running upward and downward,
shine as they follow the deer, adorned with golden spots.
Behold his tongue, resembling a blazing crest of fire, as it issues forth from his mouth while he yawns, like lightning flashing from a cloud.
With a face like emerald and a belly like a conch shell or a pearl,
whose mind would this handsome deer not captivate?
Upon seeing whose form— divine, composed of various jewels, and possessing the luster of Jāmbūnada gold— would the mind not be struck with wonder?
O Lakṣmaṇa, for the sake of meat and for the purpose of sport, kings with their bows slay deer in the great forest during the hunt.
Wealth is gathered through industry even in the great forest,
as are various minerals, gems, jewels, and gold.
O Lakṣmaṇa, all that is the essence for men, their wealth which increases their store, and everything they have conceived in their minds, just as in the case of Śukra.

O Lakṣmaṇa, those who are learned in the treatises on statecraft and those who seek worldly ends declare that when one pursues a particular objective without hesitation, that is what constitutes "artha" (worldly purpose).
Upon the priceless golden skin of this jewel among deer,
the slender-waisted Vaidehī shall sit together with me.
It is my conviction that neither the kadali, nor the priyaki, nor the praveṇī, nor even woolen cloth could ever equal this in terms of its touch.
This glorious deer and that divine one who moves through the sky— both these deer are celestial, being the stellar deer and the earthly deer respectively.
Or if it should be as you tell me, O Lakṣmaṇa—
that this is the illusion of a Rākṣasa— then his slaughter must be carried out by me.
For by this cruel Mārīca, who has not disciplined his soul,
many bulls among sages were previously harmed while he was wandering in the forest.
"Many lords of men, who were supreme archers, have risen up and been slain by him during the hunt; therefore, this deer must be killed."
Previously, Vātāpi, having humiliated the ascetics here,
would kill the twice-born while staying within their bellies, like a fetus killing its mother, the mule.
Once, after a long time, he encountered the great sage Agastya,
who was endowed with spiritual power, and he indeed became his food.
And observing Vātāpi in such a state, desiring to perform that act, the Blessed One smiled and spoke these words to him.
O Vātāpi, because you disregarded and insulted the best of the twice-born in the world of the living by means of your power, you have therefore reached this state of old age.
In that case, O Lakṣmaṇa, he would not be a Rākṣasa like Vātāpi,
who would thus overstep one such as me— ever constant in dharma and with senses conquered.
"May this one be slain by me as Vātāpi was by Agastya;
you, however, remain here prepared and restrained, and protect Maithilī."
"O descendant of Raghu, whatever task is incumbent upon us depends on this:
I shall either kill this deer or capture it."
"O Saumitri, I am going now to quickly bring back the deer;
look, Lakṣmaṇa, at Vaidehī, who has set her heart upon the deer-skin."
"Indeed, because of his precious skin, this deer shall no longer exist today;
therefore, you must remain vigilant while staying at the hermitage with Sītā."
"O Lakṣmaṇa, I shall slay this spotted deer with a single arrow; having killed it and taken its hide, I will return quickly."

O Lakṣmaṇa, being vigilant and guarding Maithilī at every moment with constant apprehension, you must remain alert against the exceedingly powerful bird Jaṭāyu, who is endowed with great intelligence.
Having thus instructed his brother, the joy of the Raghus,
endowed with great splendor, fastened his sword which had a hilt made of gold.
Then, taking up his bow which was bent into three curves and fastening his two quivers as his own adornment, he of formidable prowess set forth.
Deceiving that lord of kings, he indeed vanished out of fear upon seeing him rushing toward him, and then appeared once more.
Having girded his sword and taken up his bow, he ran toward where the deer was;
he saw it before him, shining as if with its own radiance.
In the great forest, with bow in hand, he once pursued him as he ran, looking back again and again,
luring him away from the range of his arrow.
Terrified and utterly bewildered, as if leaping into the sky,
he was bitten by some unseen creatures in certain unfamiliar regions.
Like the autumnal orb of the moon veiled by scattered clouds,
it was seen for only a moment, yet it shone brightly from afar again and again.
By appearing and then disappearing, he drew Rāghava toward him;
yet Kakutstha became enraged, rendered helpless and deluded by him.
Then, having become very weary, he stood resting in the shade upon a grassy plot;
surrounded by wild deer, he was seen nearby.
Seeing him, the immensely powerful Rāma, having resolved to slay him,
fixed an arrow upon his very firm bow and drew it back with great force.
Aiming at that very deer, he released a blazing,
flaming weapon created by Brahmā, which was like a serpent on fire.
That supreme arrow, resembling a thunderbolt, having pierced through the deer-form, split right through the heart of Mārīca himself.
Then, leaping up to the height of a palm tree, he, afflicted by the arrow, fell down;
with his life nearly spent, he let out a terrible cry upon the earth.
As he was dying, Mārīca abandoned that artificial body.
Perceiving that the time had come, he then uttered a cry resembling that of Rāghava himself: "Alas, Sītā! O Lakṣmaṇa!"
Pierced in his vital organ by that incomparable arrow,
Mārīca, as he was giving up his life, cast off that deer-form and assumed his own form as a Rākṣasa of truly massive proportions.
Then, struck by the arrow, the Rākṣasa— adorned with variegated armlets, decorated with all ornaments, wearing a golden garland, and possessing great fangs— fell.
Seeing that Rākṣasa of terrible appearance fallen upon the ground,
he went in his mind to Sītā, remembering the words of Lakṣmaṇa.
Crying out "O Sītā! O Lakṣmaṇa! in a loud voice, that Rākṣasa died; having heard this, how will Sītā fare?
"And what state will the mighty-armed Lakṣmaṇa reach?"— thus reflecting, the righteous Rāma’s hair stood on end with joy.
Then, having killed that Rākṣasa in the form of a deer and having heard its cry, a sharp fear born of despair took possession of Rāma.
Having slain another spotted deer and taken its flesh,
Rāghava then hurried toward Janasthāna.
Recognizing that cry of distress in the forest as being like her husband's,
Sītā said to Lakṣmaṇa, "Go and find Rāghava."
Indeed, neither my life nor my heart remains steady in this place;
for I have heard the intense cry of one who is wailing in supreme distress.
You ought to rescue your brother who is crying out in the forest;
run quickly toward that brother of yours who seeks your protection.
Though addressed in such a manner, he did not go, for he recognized the command of his brother; he had fallen into the power of the Rākṣasas like a bull among lions.
Then, there, the daughter of Janaka spoke to him in anger:
"O son of Sumitrā, in the guise of a friend, you are like an enemy to your brother."
Since you do not come to your brother’s aid in this state,
O Lakṣmaṇa, you desire that Rāma perish for my sake.
I think this calamity is pleasing to you; you have no affection for your brother, for which reason you remain at ease, not seeing that one of great luster.
For what indeed should be done by me, standing here, regarding him who has fallen into uncertainty,
since you, the leader, have arrived?
To Vaidehī, who was speaking thus while overwhelmed by tears and grief,
and who was as terrified as a doe, Lakṣmaṇa spoke.
O Goddess, among gods and humans, among gandharvas and birds,
among rākṣasas, piśācas, kinnaras, and wild animals—
And among the terrible Dānavas, O beautiful lady, there would not be found anyone who could fight against Rāma, who is like Vāsava himself, in battle.
"Rāma is invincible in battle; you ought not to speak thus.
I cannot bear to leave you in this forest without Rāghava."
His power is irresistible even by the forces of the most powerful,
even if the three worlds were to rise up together with their lords and the gods.
"May your heart be at peace; let this distress be abandoned.
Your husband will return soon after having slain that best of deer."
That voice was clearly not his own, nor did it belong to any deity;
it was the illusory power of that Rākṣasa, resembling a city of the Gandharvas.
"O Vaidehī, you have become my trust; you were entrusted to me by the high-souled Rāma. O lady of beautiful limbs, I cannot bring myself to abandon you here."
"O auspicious lady, O Queen, we have incurred the enmity of these night-stalkers on account of the death of Khara and the slaughter at Janasthāna."
O Vaidehī, these rākṣasas, who delight in violence, utter such words in this great forest according to their nature; you ought not to worry about them.
Thus addressed by Lakṣmaṇa, she became enraged, her eyes bloodshot with anger,
and spoke these harsh words to the truth-speaking Lakṣmaṇa.
O ignoble one, you who lack compassion, cruel defiler of your lineage!
Because I hold you dear, you speak these words.
"O Lakṣmaṇa, it is no wonder that such evil should exist among enemies—
especially among cruel men like you who always move about in disguise."
"You are most wicked that you follow Rāma alone into the forest alone;
you have gone there in disguise, either for my sake or instigated by Bharata."
How could I, having taken as my husband Rāma— who is dark as a blue lotus and has eyes like lotuses— desire an ordinary man?
In your presence, O son of Sumitrā, I shall give up my life without a doubt;
for without Rāma, I cannot live upon this earth even for a moment.
Having been addressed with these harsh words by Sītā, which caused his hair to stand on end,
Lakṣmaṇa, who had conquered his senses, spoke to Sītā with palms joined in reverence.
"I do not venture to speak further, for you are a divinity to me;
yet, O Maithilī, it is no wonder that women should utter such improper words."
Indeed, this is the inherent nature of women seen throughout these worlds:
women are fickle by their very character, sharp-tongued, divisive, and devoid of steadfast virtue.
"Let all these forest-dwellers, who have become my witnesses, hear me:
I have been addressed with harsh words by you, though I spoke according to justice."
Fie on you! Having perished today, you thus suspect me—who am established in the word of my elder—because of your womanhood and your wicked nature.
I shall go where the descendant of Kakutstha is; may it be well with you, O fair-faced one.
May all the forest deities protect you, O large-eyed lady.
"For although these terrible omens appear before me,
I hope that upon my return I may see you once again together with Rāma."
Thus addressed by Lakṣmaṇa, Janaka’s daughter, weeping and overwhelmed with tears,
then replied with these piercing words.
"O Lakṣmaṇa, without Rāma I shall enter the Godāvarī,
or else I shall hang myself or cast my own body from a precipice."
I would drink fierce poison or enter the blazing fire;
but I shall not touch even with my foot any man other than Rāghava.
Having thus reviled Lakṣmaṇa, Sītā, overcome with grief and weeping,
struck her belly with both hands out of sorrow.
Seeing her in such a state of distress, despondent and weeping, the large-eyed Sītā, the son of Sumitrā, comforted her; yet she said nothing at all to her husband’s brother.
Then Lakṣmaṇa, having saluted Sītā with joined palms and bowing slightly,
looked back at Maithilī many times and, self-possessed, went into the presence of Rāma.
But having been addressed harshly by her, the younger brother of Rāghava became enraged;
longing intensely for Rāma, he set out as if not long at all.
Then, having quickly found an opportunity, the ten-necked Rāvaṇa approached Vaidehī,
assuming the form of a wandering mendicant.

Clad in smooth saffron robes, with his topknot tied and carrying an umbrella and sandals, he then hung a beautiful staff and water-pot over his left shoulder and approached Vaidehī in the guise of a wandering mendicant.
The exceedingly powerful one approached her in the forest, deprived of her two brothers,
as great darkness approaches the twilight when it is bereft of both the sun and the moon.
Then, like a most cruel planet, he beheld that illustrious princess, the young girl, who was like Rohiṇī separated from the Moon.
Beholding that fierce evildoer, the trees growing in Janasthāna did not tremble, nor did the wind blow.
And seeing him looking about with blood-red eyes,
the river Godāvarī, her current swift, began to flow sluggishly out of fear.
Seeking an opportunity against Rāma, the ten-necked Rāvaṇa approached Vaidehī in the guise of a mendicant during that interval.
Unworthy though he was, he approached Vaidehī— who was mourning her husband while appearing in the form of a worthy woman— just as Saturn approaches the star Citrā.
That wicked one, disguised in a pleasing form like a well concealed by grass,
remained there watching the illustrious Vaidehī, the wife of Rāma.
She was beautiful, with lovely teeth and lips, and a face like the full moon;
she sat within the leaf-hut, overwhelmed by tears and grief.
That evil-minded night-stalker approached Vaidehī, whose eyes were like lotus petals and who was dressed in yellow silk.
Pierced by the arrows of the god of love and uttering the sound of Vedic recitation,
the lord of the Rākṣasas spoke these humble words in private.
Rāvaṇa praised her, who was the most excellent in the three worlds, shining with a body like the goddess Śrī bereft of her lotus.
Who are you, O lady with the luster of gold, dressed in yellow silk,
bearing a beautiful garland of lotuses like a goddess of the lotus-pond?
O lady of auspicious countenance, are you Hrī, Śrī, Kīrti, or the auspicious Lakṣmī; or perhaps an Apsaras, O fair-hipped one? Or are you Bhūti, or Rati wandering at will?
Your teeth are even, pointed, smooth, and white;
your eyes are large and clear, with red corners and black pupils.
Her hips are broad and her thighs are full, resembling the trunks of elephants; these two are well-fleshed, rounded, joined together, and firm.
Your lovely breasts are full and elevated, resembling smooth palm fruits;
adorned with exquisite jewels, they are truly beautiful.
O Rāma, with your lovely smile, lovely teeth, and lovely eyes, you captivate my mind, O playful one, just as a riverbank is swept away by the water.
With a waist as slender as a lotus stalk, beautiful hair, and firm breasts,
she is neither a goddess, nor a Gandharva woman, nor a Yakṣī, nor a Kiṃnarī.
Never before have I seen a woman of such form upon this earth;
dwelling here in this wilderness maddens my heart.
"Go back, may you be blessed; you ought not to dwell here.
This is the abode of terrible Rākṣasas who can assume any form at will."
The most excellent and delightful palaces, as well as the city gardens, are abundant,
fragrant, and fit for you to enjoy.
"O beautiful one, O dark-eyed lady, I consider excellent garlands, excellent drink, excellent clothing, and an excellent husband to be worthy of you."
"Who are you among the Rudras, or the Maruts, O lady of radiant smiles, or among the Vasus, O beautiful one? You appear to me to be a goddess."
Neither Gandharvas, nor gods, nor Kinnaras come here;
this is the dwelling place of Rākṣasas. How indeed have you come here?
Here there are monkeys, lions, leopards, tigers, and deer, as well as bears, hyenas, and herons; how is it that you do not fear them?
O lady of beautiful countenance, how is it that you alone do not fear in this great forest those fierce and swift elephants filled with rut?
Who are you, to whom do you belong, and from where have you come? For what purpose, O auspicious lady, do you wander alone through these terrible Daṇḍaka forests inhabited by rākṣasas?
Thus was Vaidehī praised by the evil-minded Rāvaṇa;
for, seeing that Rāvaṇa had arrived disguised as a twice-born brahmin,
Maithilī honored him with every hospitable rite due to a guest.
Having first brought forth a seat and invited him with water for his feet, he then said to that one of gentle appearance, "It is ready."
Seeing that he had arrived in the guise of a twice-born, carrying a vessel and saffron robes, Maithilī—
perceiving him as impossible to unmask through any stratagem— invited him as one would a Brāhmaṇa who had come to her.
"O Brahmin, here is a seat; please sit as you wish. Accept this water for washing your feet.
And let this excellent forest-grown food, prepared for your sake, be enjoyed here without distraction."
Being thus invited, Rāvaṇa beheld Maithilī, the consort of the king, speaking with such full assurance; laughing, he set his mind upon her abduction for the sake of her own destruction.
Then, waiting for her well-attired husband who had gone hunting along with Lakṣmaṇa,
she gazed about and beheld that vast green forest, but neither Rāma nor Lakṣmaṇa.
Then Vaidehī, when questioned by Rāvaṇa— who was desirous of abducting her while disguised as a wandering mendicant— revealed her own identity to him.
"He is both a Brahmin and a guest; if unaddressed, he might indeed curse me.
Having reflected thus for a moment, Sītā spoke these words.
"I am the daughter of the high-souled Janaka of Mithilā;
my name is Sītā, O best of the twice-born, and may you be blessed; I am the wife of Rāma."
And for a year she dwelt in the residence of Raghava,
enjoying human pleasures, with every desire fully satisfied.
Then, after a year had passed, he, having assembled with the royal ministers, resolved to consecrate my husband Rāma.
While the preparations for Raghava’s consecration were being made,
my noble mother named Kaikeyi requested a boon from her husband.

Having won over my father-in-law by my virtuous conduct, Kaikeyī made two requests of her husband, that best of kings who was true to his word: my own exile and the consecration of my husband's brother, Bharata.
"I shall not eat today, nor shall I sleep, nor shall I ever drink;
this is the end of my life if Rāma is consecrated."
While Kaikeyī was speaking thus, my father-in-law, who bestows honor,
entreated her with meaningful requests, yet she did not grant his plea.
My husband is of great splendor, twenty-five years of age,
renowned in the world as Rāma; he is virtuous, truthful in speech, pure,
large-eyed, mighty-armed, and devoted to the welfare of all beings.
But when Rāma had come into the presence of his father for the consecration, Kaikeyī quickly spoke these words to my husband: "It is me [whom you must honor]. (Rāmāyaṇa 3.45.11)
"Listen to this, O Raghava, which has been commanded by your father:
'This kingdom, free from all obstacles, must be given to Bharata.'"
"You must indeed dwell for fourteen years in the forest;
go forth into exile, O descendant of Kakutstha, and deliver your father from falsehood."
"So be it," Rāma replied to Kaikeyī, free from fear;
my husband, firm in his vows, carried out her word.
One should give and not accept [gifts], one should speak the truth and not falsehood;
O Brāhmaṇa, this is the firm and unsurpassed vow of Rāma.
His half-brother, however, was the valiant Lakṣmaṇa,
a tiger among men and a slayer of enemies, who was Rāma’s companion in battle.
His brother, named Lakṣmaṇa, who practices righteousness and is firm in his vows,
followed me as I went forth into exile, bow in hand.
"O best of the twice-born, we three, having been deprived of our kingdom on account of Kaikeyī, are wandering through this deep forest by our own prowess."
"Take heart for a moment; you may stay here for a while.
My husband will arrive, bringing abundant forest produce."
Therefore, O twice-born one, tell me truly your name, your lineage, and your family; and for what purpose do you wander alone in the Daṇḍaka forest?
While Sītā, the wife of Rāma, was speaking thus, the mighty Rāvaṇa,
lord of the rākṣasas, gave this harsh reply.
"O Sītā, I am that Rāvaṇa by name, the lord of the hosts of Rākṣasas, by whom the worlds— including the gods, asuras, and pannagas— have been terrified."
But seeing you, O blameless one, with your golden complexion and clad in silk,
I find no pleasure in my own wives.
Of all the many excellent women brought here from various places— blessings be upon you— become my chief queen.
My great city named Laṅkā is situated in the midst of the ocean;
surrounded by the sea, it is established upon the summit of a mountain.
There, O Sītā, you shall wander with me through the forests;
and you, O beautiful lady, will no longer long for this dwelling in the wilderness.
Five thousand female slaves, adorned with every ornament,
shall serve you, O Sītā, if you become my wife.
Thus addressed by Rāvaṇa, the daughter of Janaka, her limbs faultless, became enraged and replied to that Rākṣasa with utter contempt.
I am devoted to Rāma, who is as immovable as a great mountain, like Mahendra,
and as unshakeable as the vast ocean.
I am devoted to Rāma, the great-armed and broad-chested one, who moves with the prowess of a lion; he is a lion among men, resembling a lion himself.
I am devoted to Rāma, the hero with a face like the full moon, who is like a prince, has conquered his senses, possesses vast fame, and has mighty arms.
But you, a jackal, desire me here, a lioness who is difficult to attain;
I cannot be touched by you, just as the radiance of the sun cannot be grasped.
O Rāvaṇa, you who desire the beloved wife of Rāghava are surely a man of meager fortune, for you see only many golden trees.
You wish to take a fang from the mouth of a hungry lion, a swift enemy of deer, or from that of a venomous serpent.
You wish to carry away Mandara, the best of mountains, with your hand;
you wish to depart in safety after having drunk the Kālakūṭa poison.
"You wipe with an eye-salve needle and lick with your tongue as if it were a razor;
yet you desire to obtain the beloved wife of Rāghava."
Having tied a stone around your neck, you wish to cross the ocean;
you wish to seize both the sun and the moon with your bare hands—
you who desire to violate the beloved wife of Rāma.
Having seen a blazing fire, you wish to seize it with your garment;
you who wish to abduct Rāma’s wife, who is of virtuous conduct.
You wish to walk upon the tips of iron-tipped spears,
you who desire to obtain Rāma’s wife, who is his equal.
The difference between a lion and a jackal in the forest, the difference between a mountain stream and the ocean,
and the difference between the finest wine and sour gruel— that same difference exists between you and the son of Daśaratha.
As great is the difference between gold and lead, as great as that between sandalwood paste and mud,
and as great as that between an elephant and a cat in the forest, so great is the difference between you and the son of Daśaratha.
As is the difference between a crow and Garuda, or between a water-fowl and a peacock,
as is the difference between a crane and a vulture in the forest, such is the difference between you and the son of Daśaratha.
While that Rāma, whose prowess is equal to the thousand-eyed Indra, stands with bow and arrow in hand,
even though I have been abducted by you, I shall not undergo decay, just as a thunderbolt swallowed by a fly remains unaltered.
Having thus spoken these well-considered words to that night-stalker with a pure disposition,
she— slender as a plantain tree shaken by the wind— became distressed by the trembling of her limbs.
Observing Sītā trembling, Rāvaṇa, whose power was equal to Death itself,
announced his lineage, strength, name, and deeds for the purpose of inspiring fear.
While Sītā was speaking thus, Rāvaṇa, provoked and knitting his brows upon his forehead, replied with harsh words.
"I am the half-brother of Vaiśravaṇa, O lady of excellent complexion;
my name is Rāvaṇa, the ten-necked and powerful one—may prosperity be yours."
Before whom the gods, along with the gandharvas, piśācas, birds, and serpents,
always flee in terror, just as living beings flee from death.
