By him, on another occasion, his half-brother Vaiśravaṇa was encountered in a duel and, displaying his prowess in battle, was utterly defeated out of anger.
Afflicted by fear of me, he has abandoned his own prosperous capital and now dwells on Kailāsa, the best of mountains, O rider of men.
O blessed lady, that auspicious aerial chariot named Puṣpaka, which travels at will, was won by me through my prowess; by means of it, I travel through the sky.
O Maithilī, as soon as they see my face when I am filled with rage,
the gods, led by Śakra, flee in utter terror.
Wherever I stand, the wind blows with apprehension;
and out of fear, the sun, though possessing fierce rays, becomes cool-rayed.
Wherever I stay and wherever I move, the trees have their leaves motionless and the rivers have still waters.
On the far shore of the ocean is my auspicious city named Laṅkā,
filled with terrible Rākṣasas like Indra’s Amarāvatī.
Encircled by a pale white wall,
the beautiful city shone with golden courtyards and gateways made of lapis lazuli.
Crowded with elephants, horses, and chariots, resounding with the music of trumpets,
and adorned with gardens filled with trees that bear the fruits of all desires.
Dwelling there with me, O Sītā, princess,
you will no longer remember human women, O high-minded lady.
Enjoying human pleasures and divine ones as well, O woman of excellent complexion,
you will not remember Rāma, that mortal whose life has come to an end.
Except for his beloved son, the king Daśaratha sent that eldest son, who was weak in valor, away to the forest.
O large-eyed lady, what will you do with that Rama, who has lost his kingdom, whose mind is gone, and who is now but a wretched ascetic?
You ought not to reject him who has come here of his own accord out of desire, the lord of all rākṣasas, for he is pierced by the arrows of Love.
For by rejecting me, O timid one, you will come to deep remorse,
just as Urvaśī did after striking Purūravas with her foot.
Thus addressed, Vaidehī, enraged and with bloodshot eyes,
spoke these harsh words to the lord of the Rākṣasas in that secluded place.
How is it that you wish to commit such an evil act by claiming Vaiśravaṇa— the god honored by all beings— as your brother?
O Rāvaṇa, all these Rākṣasas will surely perish,
for you are their harsh king— evil-minded and one who has not conquered his senses.
It might be possible to live after abducting Śacī, the wife of Indra;
but there is no life for me after having taken away my husband Rāma’s wife.
May you live long after violating Śacī, who possesses incomparable beauty, from the hand of the wielder of the thunderbolt!
But having violated one such as me, O Rākṣasa, there is no escape for you, even if you have drunk the nectar of immortality.
Having heard Sītā’s words, the powerful Ten-necked one struck his hands together and assumed a truly massive form.
Then he spoke these words again to Maithilī with great intensity:
"I think that my heroism and prowess have not been heard by you, O madwoman."
Standing in the sky, I could lift up the earth with my two arms;
I could drink up the ocean, and standing in battle, I could slay Death itself.
I could stop the sun with my sharp arrows and indeed split the surface of the earth;
O madwoman, behold me, your husband, who can assume any form at will and grant all desires.
When Rāvaṇa had spoken thus, his eyes, which were red with rage and bordered by tawny hair, became as radiant as fire.
Immediately casting off his gentle mendicant form, Rāvaṇa,
the younger brother of Vaiśravaṇa, assumed his own appearance, which resembled the very form of Death.
With bloodshot eyes, glorious, wearing earrings of refined gold,
ten-faced, and armed with a bow and arrows, he became a night-stalker.
Casting off that disguise of a wandering mendicant, the great-bodied Rāvaṇa, lord of the Rākṣasas, resumed his own form.
With eyes bloodshot from rage and possessing the luster of a mass of clouds,
he stood there wearing red garments, gazing at Maithilī, that jewel among women.
Rāvaṇa spoke to that Maithilī, who had dark hair-ends and was adorned with garments and ornaments, resembling the radiance of the sun.
"If you desire a husband renowned throughout the three worlds, take refuge in me, O lady of beautiful hips; I am a husband worthy of you."
Devote yourself to me for all time; I am a praiseworthy and dear lover to you. Never, O blessed lady, shall I do anything displeasing to you.
Let your human nature be cast aside, and let your heart be fixed upon me.
O foolish woman who fancies herself wise, for what virtues are you so devoted to Rāma— he who has been cast out from his kingdom, whose purpose is unfulfilled, and whose life is limited?
"He who, out of a woman's words, has abandoned his kingdom along with his friends and now dwells in this forest haunted by beasts of prey— that man is indeed of wicked mind."
Having spoken these words to Maithilī, who was worthy of affection and spoke so sweetly,
Rāvaṇa seized Sītā, as Budha seizes Rohiṇī in the sky.
With his left hand he grasped Sītā by her hair— she whose eyes were like lotuses—
and with his right hand he took hold of her by her thighs.
Seeing him, who resembled a mountain peak, with sharp fangs and mighty arms,
and who appeared like Death itself, the forest deities fled, afflicted by fear.
And that great chariot of Rāvaṇa, made of illusion, divine, yoked with donkeys, possessing the braying sound of donkeys, and adorned with golden parts, came into view.
Then, having threatened her with harsh words in a loud voice,
he took Vaidehī onto his lap and placed her upon the chariot.
Seized by Rāvaṇa, the illustrious Sītā, afflicted with grief, cried out "O Rāma! to Rāma, who was far away in the forest.
Then Rāvaṇa, afflicted by lust, seized her as she writhed against her will like the wife of a lord of serpents, and flew up into the air.
Then, as she was being carried through the air by the lord of the Rākṣasas,
she cried out loudly like one intoxicated, her mind bewildered as if she were afflicted.
"Alas, Lakṣmaṇa, O mighty-armed one, you who gladden the heart of your elder!
You do not know that I am being carried away by a Rākṣasa who can assume any form at will."
O Raghava, you do not see me being carried away by unrighteousness, even as you renounce life, happiness, and wealth for the sake of dharma.
Surely you are the disciplinarian of the undisciplined, O scorcher of foes;
why then do you not punish Rāvaṇa for such a sin?
Surely the fruit of an ill-disciplined action is seen immediately;
yet time also plays a part here, as it does for the ripening of crops.
Having performed this deed with his mind corrupted by time, he has brought about his own end; now, suffer this terrible calamity at the hands of Rāma.
"Now Kaikeyī, along with her kinsmen, has attained her desire;
yet I, the lawful wife of this illustrious man who loves righteousness, am being carried away."
I bid farewell to Janasthāna and the blossoming Karṇikāra trees;
quickly report to Rāma that Rāvaṇa is carrying away Sītā.
I pay homage to Mount Mālyavat, the peaked mountain, and to Mount Prasravaṇa;
quickly announce to Rāma that Rāvaṇa is carrying away Sītā!
I bow to the river Godāvarī, resounded by flocks of swans and cranes;
quickly announce to Rāma that Rāvaṇa is carrying away Sītā.
And the deities who dwell in this forest of various trees—I pay homage to them; tell my husband that I have been carried away.
Whatever beings dwell here, even including the multitudes of beasts and birds, I take refuge in them all.
"Proclaim that Sītā, who is dearer to her husband than his own life, has been carried away by Rāvaṇa while she was helpless and being abducted."
"Once he has learned of my whereabouts, that mighty-armed and exceedingly powerful one will use his prowess to bring me back, even if I have been carried off by Vaivasvata."
O Jaṭāyu, you must relate to Rāma and Lakṣmaṇa exactly as it happened— my abduction— in its entirety and without omission.
Then Jaṭāyu, while still asleep, heard that sound;
he quickly looked around and beheld Rāvaṇa and Vaidehī.
Then that glorious and best of birds, resembling a mountain peak with its sharp beak,
perched upon a great tree and uttered auspicious words.
O Ten-necked one, established in the ancient dharma and taking refuge in truth,
I am the mighty king of vultures known by the name Jaṭāyu.
Rāma, the son of Daśaratha, is the king of the entire world, equal to Mahendra and Varuṇa, and is ever intent upon the welfare of the worlds.
She is the illustrious lawful wife of that Lord of the World,
the noble-limbed lady named Sītā, whom you desire to abduct from here.
How could a king established in righteousness touch another's wife?
O mighty one, the wives of kings must be protected with special care;
turn your mind away from this base intent to violate another's wife.
A wise man should not practice that which another might censure;
just as one's own wife must be protected from improper scrutiny, so too must the wives of others.

O descendant of Pulastya, whether it concerns material gain or sensual pleasure, the learned determine what is right for kings by following the principles found in the scriptures, even regarding matters not explicitly mentioned therein.
The king is both righteousness and pleasure, and the supreme treasury of all things;
for virtue or vice, whether auspicious or sinful, proceeds with the king as its root.
O best of Rākṣasas, how have you, who are of a sinful nature and fickle,
attained such sovereignty, like a wicked man obtaining a celestial chariot?
The inherent nature of desire belonging to anyone cannot be wiped away;
for the noble state does not dwell long in the abode of those with corrupt souls.
Whether in the kingdom or in the city, since that mighty and righteous Rāma does not commit any offense against you, how can you commit an offense against him?

Tell me here truly, what transgression has Rāma committed,
that you, having abducted the wife of that lord of the world, shall depart?
