He who could cause the moon to fall from the sky to the earth, or destroy it,
or even dry up the ocean— he alone might release Sītā here.
"Your life is gone, your fortune is gone, your strength is gone, and your senses are gone;
because of you, Laṅkā shall be joined with widowhood."
This evil deed of yours will not result in happiness,
since I have been led by you from the forest away from my husband, without his presence.
For that husband of mine, endowed with divine power and great luster,
dwells fearlessly in the empty Daṇḍaka forest, relying upon his own heroism.
In battle, he will strip from your limbs that pride, strength, heroism, and such arrogance with a shower of arrows.
When the destruction of beings is seen, impelled by time,
then men, having fallen under the power of time, become negligent in their duties.
"O lowest of Rākṣasas, this time has come for you to attack me—
for your own destruction, for the destruction of the Rākṣasas, and for that of the inner apartments."
The sacrificial altar, situated in the midst of the sacrifice, adorned with ladles and vessels,
and purified by the mantras of the twice-born, cannot be desecrated by a Cāṇḍāla.
"This body is insentient; bind it or cause it to be slain.
O Rākṣasa, this body nor even my life is to be protected by me, for I shall not allow myself to bring reproach upon the earth."
Having spoken these very harsh words out of anger, Vaidehī,
the princess of Mithilā, said nothing more to Rāvaṇa there.
Having heard Sītā’s harsh and hair-raising words,
he then replied to her with speech that displayed his fear.
"Listen to my words, O Maithilī, O beautiful lady: for twelve months,
O woman of lovely smiles, if you do not yield to me by this time,
then the cooks shall cut you into pieces for their morning meal."
Having spoken these harsh words, Rāvaṇa, the terrifier of his enemies,
then, filled with rage, addressed these words to the rākṣasīs.
"O Rākṣasīs, you who feed on flesh and blood, quickly subdue her pride in this manner, for she is deformed and terrible to behold."
At his mere word, those hideous and terrifying creatures formed their palms in salutation and surrounded the princess of Mithilā.
Then King Rāvaṇa, of terrible appearance, spoke to them,
shaking the earth as it were with the forceful stamping of his feet.
"Let Maithilī be led into the midst of the Aśoka grove;
there she must be guarded by you, surrounded by you in secret."
"Therefore, all of you, bring this Maithilī under your control by means of both terrible threats and gentle conciliations, like a wild female elephant."
Thus commanded by Rāvaṇa, those rākṣasīs took Maithilī and went to the Aśoka grove.
It was filled with trees that bore the fruits of all desires and various flowers and fruits,
and it was frequented by birds that were intoxicated at all times.
But Maithilī, the daughter of Janaka, her limbs overwhelmed by grief and fallen under the power of the Rākṣasīs, was like a doe among tigresses.

But Maithilī, being excessively threatened by those women with disfigured eyes, found no comfort there; remembering her beloved husband and her brother-in-law, she became senseless, oppressed by fear and grief.
Having slain the Rākṣasa Mārīca, who was wandering in the form of a deer and capable of assuming any shape at will, Rāma quickly turned back on his path.
Then, as he was hurrying along, eager to see the princess of Mithilā,
a jackal howled behind him with a cruel voice.
Having recognized that jackal’s harsh and hair-raising cry,
he became apprehensive by the sound and began to reflect.
"Alas, I consider this to be an evil omen, for the jackal howls like this;
may it be well with Vaidehī, and may she not fall as food for the rākṣasas."
Having heard that voice and then leaving Maithilī, that son of Sumitrā,
dispatched by her, will quickly come here into my presence.
Surely Sītā’s death was desired by the Rākṣasas acting in concert;
for having become a golden deer, you lured me away from the hermitage.
But when Mārīca had been carried far away, struck by the arrow, he became a rākṣasa once more and uttered these words: "Alas, Lakṣmaṇa! I am slain!"
"May it be well with both of them even if they are separated from me in the forest;
for I have incurred the enmity of the Rākṣasas on account of Janasthāna,
and many terrible omens are seen today."
Reflecting thus upon hearing the cry of the jackal and his own abduction by the Rākṣasa in the form of a deer,
Rāghava, filled with apprehension, returned to Janasthāna.
As he was dejected in mind and distressed, the beasts and birds gathered around that high-souled one; keeping him to their left, they uttered terrible cries.
Having seen those most terrible omens, Rāghava then beheld Lakṣmaṇa approaching, shorn of his luster.
Then, not far from there, Lakṣmaṇa met with Rāma; the despondent met the despondent, the sorrowful met the sharer of his sorrow.
Then his elder brother reproached Lakṣmaṇa for having come there,
having left Sītā behind in the lonely forest frequented by rākṣasas.
And taking Lakṣmaṇa by his left hand, the joy of the Raghus spoke these words, which were harsh yet sweet in their ultimate effect, like one who is afflicted.
"O Lakṣmaṇa, alas! You have done something blameworthy, in that you have come here, O gentle one, leaving Sītā behind, wondering whether she might be well."
"O Hero, I have no doubt at all: Janaka’s daughter has either perished or been devoured by the forest-dwelling Rākṣasas."
"O Lakṣmaṇa, may we yet attain the reunion with Sītā, even though such inauspicious omens as these appear so frequently before me."
For this demon, appearing in the form of a deer, lured me far away;
though slain with great effort, that Rākṣasa became a demon even as he was dying.
My mind is dejected and lacks joy here, and my left eye throbs;
without a doubt, Lakṣmaṇa, Sītā is no longer present—either she has been abducted, or she is dead, or she lies somewhere along the path.
Seeing Lakṣmaṇa dejected in the empty place, the righteous son of Daśaratha questioned him, for he had arrived without Vaidehī.
"O Lakṣmaṇa, where is that Vaidehī who followed me when I set out for the Daṇḍaka forest— she whom you have left behind to come here?"
Where is that slender-waisted Vaidehī, my companion in sorrow, now that I have been deprived of my kingdom, am wretched, and am wandering through the Daṇḍaka forest?
O Hero, without whom I cannot bear to live for even a moment—
where is that Sītā, my companion in life, who resembles the daughter of a god?
O Lakṣmaṇa, neither the sovereignty over the immortals nor even the lordship of the earth would I desire without that daughter of Janaka, who possesses the luster of refined gold.
I hope Vaidehī, who is dearer to me than my own life, still lives;
I hope, O gentle one, that my exile will not have been in vain.
O son of Sumitrā, when I have died on account of Sītā and you have departed,
will that Kaikeyī finally have her desire fulfilled and be happy?
"O gentle one, will Kausalyā— who has achieved her purpose through her son and kingdom— serve Kaikeyī, that wretched woman whose sons have perished?"
If Vaidehī lives, I shall return to the hermitage;
but if she has perished, O Lakṣmaṇa, I shall give up my life, for she was one of such virtuous conduct.
"O Lakṣmaṇa, if Sītā does not speak to me with a smile when I have reached the hermitage, I shall perish."
"Tell me, Lakṣmaṇa, whether Vaidehī lives or not; while you were negligent, has that poor woman been devoured by the rākṣasas?"
Delicate, young, and never before having seen suffering,
Vaidehī will surely grieve with a heavy heart at her separation from me.
In every way, by that crooked and evil-minded Rākṣasa, who cried out "Lakṣmaṇa! loudly, fear was produced even in you.
I suspect that Vaidehī, being terrified, heard that voice which resembled my own and sent you; thus you have come quickly to see me.
In every respect, a grievous wrong has been committed by abandoning Sītā in the forest;
you have given the cruel Rākṣasas the opportunity to take their revenge.
Afflicted by the harsh blows of those flesh-eating Rākṣasas,
Sītā will undoubtedly have been slain by those terrible beings.
"Alas! I am utterly submerged in calamity, O destroyer of enemies;
yet what shall I do now? I fear that such a fate was destined to befall me."
Thus reflecting on Sītā, the lady of beautiful hips, Rāghava,
together with Lakṣmaṇa, returned to Janasthāna with great haste.
Reproaching his younger brother, who appeared distressed by hunger, fatigue, and thirst, he sighed with a parched mouth and dejected countenance; having reached the shelter, he beheld it empty.

Having entered his own hermitage and followed along some of the pleasure grounds, the hero, with his hair standing on end, became distressed as he thought, "This is that very place," while dwelling upon the site of his former residence.
Then, as they were returning from the hermitage, Rāma, the joy of the Raghus,
afflicted by grief, questioned the son of Sumitrā once again.
He said to him: "For what purpose have you come, having left Maithilī behind, when she was separated from me in the forest because of her trust in you?"
O Lakṣmaṇa, as soon as I saw you arrive having abandoned Maithilī,
my mind was truly distressed, suspecting some great calamity.
O Lakṣmaṇa, having seen you from afar on the path, separated from Sītā, my left eye, my arm, and my heart are throbbing.
Thus addressed, Lakṣmaṇa, the son of Sumitrā who bears auspicious marks,
being once again overwhelmed by sorrow, spoke to the grieving Rāma.
I did not come here of my own free will, having abandoned her;
urged on by her with harsh words, I have come here into your presence.
The cry "O Sītā! O Lakṣmaṇa! and the words "Save me! uttered by the noble one—those very words of Maithilī reached his ears.
Hearing that cry of distress, Maithilī, overwhelmed by fear and out of affection for you, spoke to me while weeping: "Go, go! (Rāmāyaṇa 3.57.8)
Being repeatedly urged by her with the words "Go," Maithilī replied with these words, which were imbued with confidence in you: ||| Ram_3,57.9 |||
"I do not see any demon who could bring him fear;
be at ease, for this has been spoken by someone who knows it is not so."
How could a noble one utter such a reproachable and base word as "Save me," O Sītā, he who would save even the thirty gods?
"For what reason, and by whom, was my brother's voice seized so that he uttered these discordant words, 'Lakṣmaṇa, save me'!
You must not give way to distress, which is the resort of base women."
Enough of resorting to despondency; be composed and free from anxiety.
There is no man in the three worlds—whether already born or yet to be born—who could defeat Rāghava in battle or in combat.
Thus addressed, Vaidehī, her mind utterly bewildered, shedding tears, spoke these harsh words to me: Ram_3.57.14.
An exceedingly wicked disposition has been placed by you toward me;
yet when your brother is destroyed and I have arrived, you shall not obtain me.
It is only by convention that you follow Rāma at Bharata’s command;
for you do not actually go to his side as he cries out so piteously.
"You are an enemy moving in disguise who follows me for my sake; seeking an opportunity against Rāghava, you do not even approach him."
Thus addressed by Vaidehī, he, enraged and with blood-red eyes,
his lips quivering with fury, emerged from the hermitage.
To Saumitri, who was speaking thus, Rāma, bewildered by grief, said:
"O gentle one, it was a misdeed that you have come here without her."
Although you knew me to be capable of warding off the rākṣasas,
you departed from Maithilī with these words of anger.
I am not at all pleased that you have come here after abandoning Maithilī,
having heard harsh words from an angry woman.
In every way, however, you have been deprived of Sītā because,
having fallen under the sway of anger when urged by her, you did not carry out my command.
For that Rākṣasa lies there, struck down by my arrow—
he who, in the form of a deer, carried me away from the hermitage.
Drawing his bow and fixing an arrow, he was struck by me with that playful shaft;
then, casting off his deer-like body, that Rākṣasa wearing armlets assumed a distressed voice.
Stricken by arrows and speaking with a pained voice that reached my ears from afar,
she uttered those most cruel words because of which you have come here, abandoning Maithilī.
As he was walking back and forth intensely, Rāma’s lower left eye throbbed, he stumbled, and a trembling came over him.
Having repeatedly observed those inauspicious omens, he nevertheless declared, "Is all well with Sītā? indeed.
Then, longing for a sight of Sītā, he went forth in haste;
seeing the dwelling empty, his mind became filled with anxiety.
As if reeling with speed, the joy of the Raghus cast his gaze about,
looking all around at the locations of the leaf-huts here and there.
Then he beheld the leaf-hut, deserted by Sītā,
stripped of its splendor and ruined like a lotus pond in the winter season.
With its trees appearing as if weeping, its flowers withered and its birds and beasts despondent,
the forest was bereft of splendor, devastated, and abandoned by its presiding deities.
Seeing the site of the empty hut with its deerskins and *kuśa* grass scattered about and its cushions and mats tossed aside, he lamented again and again.
"She must have been carried off, or killed, or lost, or devoured;
or perhaps the timid one is hidden, or has fled into the forest."
She has gone to gather flowers or perhaps fruits;
or else she has gone to the lotus pond, or has gone to the river for water.
Searching diligently through the forest, however, he did not find his beloved;
with eyes reddened by grief, he appeared as if driven mad by sorrow.
Running from tree to tree, from mountain to mountain, and from river to river,
Rāma wandered about lamenting, submerged in an ocean of the mire of grief.
"O Kadamba tree, have you seen my beloved, who is so fond of the kadamba? If you know, tell me of Sītā, she of the auspicious countenance."
O Bilva tree, tell me if you have seen her who resembles a tender sprout, who is clothed in yellow silk, and whose breasts are like bilva fruits.
Or rather, O Arjuna, tell me of that beloved who is dear to Arjuna—
that timid daughter of Janaka, whether she still lives or not.
The *kakubha* tree knows that Maithilī, whose thighs are like the *kakubha*;
for this lord of the forest shines forth, rich with creepers, shoots, and flowers.
And since this excellent tree is being celebrated by the bees,
it is evident that this Tilaka tree knows its beloved Tilaka creeper.
O Aśoka, dispeller of grief, quickly make me— who am struck down by sorrow— free from grief by the sight of my beloved, and let me truly bear your name.
O Tāla tree, if you have seen that woman of beautiful limbs, whose breasts are like ripe tāla fruits, tell me of her if you have compassion for me.
O Jambu tree, if you have seen Sita, who possesses the luster of refined gold,
and if you know my beloved, tell me without hesitation.
Or perhaps, O deer, you know Maithilī, whose eyes are like those of a young fawn;
that lovely woman with the gaze of a deer might be together with the does.
O elephant, if she whose thighs are like an elephant’s trunk has been seen by you, I believe she must be known to you; tell me, O noble elephant.
"O tiger, if that beloved Maithilī, whose face resembles the moon, has been seen by you, tell me with confidence; you shall have no fear."
"Why do you run away, my beloved? Surely you have been seen, O lotus-eyed one!
Why do you not answer me when you have hidden yourself behind a tree?"
"Stay, stay, O lady of excellent hips! You have no compassion for me;
you are not naturally prone to excessive laughter—why do you disregard me?"
O woman of excellent complexion, you were betrayed by your yellow silk garment;
though you are running away, you have been seen by me—stay, if there is any affection remaining!
Surely she is not there, or perhaps that sweet-smiling lady has been harmed;
for how could she possibly have neglected me when I am in such distress?
"Clearly that young girl has been devoured by flesh-eating Rākṣasas; having been separated from me, her dear one must have had all her limbs divided up."
Surely that face with its beautiful teeth and lips has lost its luster;
for that neck, which had the hue of a campaka flower and was adorned with a necklace, is now devoid of splendor.
Surely those two beautiful arms, tender as young shoots, were devoured while my beloved was lamenting in her distress as she was being torn apart.
With their trembling fingertips and their bracelets and armlets still upon them,
those two young women were indeed devoured by me for the consumption of the Rākṣasas when they were separated from me.
Abandoned like a caravan leader by his followers, and devoured by many beasts of prey—
alas, O mighty-armed Lakṣmaṇa, do you see my beloved anywhere?
"Alas, my beloved! Where have you gone, O blessed lady? Alas, Sītā!"—thus lamenting again and again, Rāma ran from forest to forest.
In one place he wanders with speed, in another he stumbles by force;
in some places, intent on searching for his beloved, he appears as if intoxicated.
He wanders with great speed through forests, rivers, mountains, mountain cascades, and groves, never remaining still.
Having thus gone to that vast and great forest and searched everywhere for Maithilī, he,
his hope still unfulfilled, again exerted the utmost effort in the search for his beloved.
Seeing the hermitage empty, Rāma, the son of Daśaratha,
saw that the leaf-hut was deserted and the seats were scattered about.
Not seeing Vaidehī there, and having searched everywhere,
Rāma cried out and, raising his beautiful arms, spoke:
"O Lakṣmaṇa, where indeed is Vaidehī? To what region has she gone from here?
By whom has she been carried off, O son of Sumitrā, or by whom has my beloved been devoured?"
"O Sītā, if you wish to mock me by hiding behind a tree, enough of this mockery today; come to me, for I am deeply distressed."
O gentle Sītā, those trusting young deer with whom you used to play— now deprived of you, O lovely one, they sit brooding with eyes clouded by tears.
In the other world, my father, the great king, will surely see me dead from the great grief born of Sītā’s abduction.
"How is it that, having promised me a pledge,
you have come here into my presence without having fulfilled that period of time?"
"In the next world, my father will clearly say to me, 'Fie on you!'"— referring to me as one who acts out of lust, who is ignoble, and a speaker of falsehoods.
Having abandoned me here— helpless, tormented by grief, wretched, and with my hopes shattered— O compassionate one, you have left me like fame deserts a man who is not upright.
"Where are you going, O lady of beautiful hips and slender waist, leaving me behind?
Bereft of you, I shall give up my own life."
Lamenting thus, Rāma, longing for the sight of Sītā and afflicted by great sorrow, did not see the daughter of Janaka, O Rāghava.
To that son of Daśaratha, who was unable to find Sītā and was sinking like an elephant that has reached a vast expanse of mud,
Lakṣmaṇa spoke at length to Rāma out of a desire for his welfare.
Do not despair, O mighty-armed one; exert yourself together with me.
For this forest, O hero, is adorned with many caves.
Accustomed to wandering in the Priyaka groves and intoxicated by the forest, Maithilī must have entered the woods or perhaps a lotus pond in full bloom.
Or perhaps she has reached a river frequented by fish and reeds;
or, wishing to frighten us away, she may be hidden somewhere in the forest;
or, O bull among men, Vaidehī may be lurking there, desiring to test you and me.
O glorious one, let us indeed strive swiftly to search for her;
we shall scour the entire forest where that daughter of Janaka may be,
if you so intend, O descendant of Kakutstha— do not set your mind on grief.
Thus addressed with affection by Lakṣmaṇa, Rāma, composed in mind,
set out together with the son of Sumitrā to search through the forests,
mountains, rivers, and lakes.
Searching everywhere for Sītā, the two sons of Daśaratha explored the plateaus,
caves, and peaks of that mountain.
Searching everywhere, they did not find her at all;
having searched the mountain on all sides, Rāma spoke to Lakṣmaṇa.
"O Saumitri, I do not see Vaidehī here on this auspicious mountain.
Then, tormented by grief, Lakṣmaṇa spoke these words.
Wandering through the Daṇḍaka forest, O one of great wisdom, you shall find your brother of radiant splendor and the princess of Mithilā, the daughter of Janaka.
"Just as the mighty-armed Viṣṇu bound Bali and [conquered] this earth,"—
having been addressed thus by the heroic Lakṣmaṇa, that descendant of Raghu...
With his mind struck by grief, he spoke in a piteous voice:
"The entire forest has been thoroughly searched, as have the lotus ponds with their blossoming lotuses."
And this mountain, O highly wise one, with its many caves and waterfalls,
does not reveal Vaidehī, who is dearer to me than my own life.
Thus lamenting, Rāma, emaciated by the abduction of Sītā,
wretched and overwhelmed by grief, became distraught for a moment.
With all his limbs trembling, his intellect gone, and deprived of consciousness, he was overcome by despondency and,
being wretched, he sighed long and hot breaths.
Sighing repeatedly, the lotus-eyed Rāma cried out many times, "O my beloved! his voice choked with tears.
Then Lakṣmaṇa, the knower of dharma, who was dear to his kinsmen, consoled him in many ways, being humble with palms joined in reverence.
But disregarding those words falling from the lips of Lakṣmaṇa,
not seeing his beloved Sītā, he cried out again and again.
Distressed, he spoke these words to Lakṣmaṇa in a piteous voice:
"Go quickly, Lakṣmaṇa, to the Godāvarī river and find out whether Sītā has gone there to fetch lotuses."
Thus addressed by Rāma, Lakṣmaṇa,
possessing swift prowess, went once again to the beautiful river Godāvarī.
Having searched through that Tīrthavatī, Lakṣmaṇa said to Rāma:
"I do not see her among the sacred fords; though I call out, she does not hear me."
"To what region has Vaidehī, the destroyer of suffering, gone?
For I truly do not know, O Rāma, where that slender-waisted woman is."
Having heard Lakṣmaṇa’s words, Rāma, dejected and bewildered by grief,
went himself to the river Godāvarī.
Approaching her, Rāma asked, "Where is Sītā? thus he spoke.
Even though she had been abducted by the lord of the Rākṣasas, who deserved to be slain,
the creatures and the river Godāvarī did not report her whereabouts to Rāma.
Then, urged by the spirits, they said to him, "Tell us of that beloved one," but Sītā, though questioned and grieving by Rāma, did not speak of her.
Reflecting upon that form and the deeds of the evil-minded Rāvaṇa, that river, out of fear, did not reveal Vaidehī to her.
Despairing of seeing Sītā by that river, Rāma, emaciated by the failure to find her, spoke to the son of Sumitrā.
"O Lakṣmaṇa, what painful words shall I speak when I meet Janaka and Vaidehī’s mother, being myself deprived of her?"
Where indeed has that Vaidehī gone, who used to dispel all the grief of me when I was deprived of my kingdom and living on forest fare in the woods?
Deprived of my kinsmen and no longer beholding the princess, I think that the nights will be long for me as I lie awake.
I shall search the Godāvarī, Janasthāna, and this Prasravaṇa mountain;
indeed, I will traverse all these places if Sītā is to be found.
While the two brothers were thus conversing with one another,
they both beheld a trail of flowers fallen upon the earth.
Seeing that shower of flowers fallen upon the earth, the heroic Rāma, filled with sorrow, spoke these sorrowful words to Lakṣmaṇa.
"I remember these very flowers here, Lakṣmaṇa;
they were gathered by me and given to Vaidehī in the forest."
Having spoken thus to Lakṣmaṇa, that bull among men, the mighty-armed one,
being enraged, addressed the mountain like a lion to a small deer.
O Mountain, show me that Sītā, who is golden-hued and radiant as gold,
before I destroy all your peaks.
Consumed by the fire of my arrows, you shall be reduced to ashes;
forever unfit for habitation, it shall be stripped of grass, trees, and shoots.
Or else, O Lakṣmaṇa, I shall dry up this river today if she does not tell me of Sītā, whose face resembles the moon.
Thus, enraged as if wishing to consume everything with his very eyes,
Rāma beheld upon the ground the great footprint of the Rākṣasa that had emerged there.
Having observed Sītā’s departure and that of the Rākṣasa,
Rāma, his heart filled with agitation, spoke to his beloved brother.
"Behold, Lakṣmaṇa, these scattered golden beads of Vaidehī’s ornaments,
O son of Sumitrā, and her various garlands."
Behold, O Saumitri, the surface of the earth covered on all sides with variegated drops of blood resembling glowing sparks.
I think, Lakṣmaṇa, that Vaidehī must have been torn apart again and again by the Rākṣasas who can change their form at will, or perhaps she has already been devoured.
O son of Sumitrā, on account of Vaidehī, a terrible battle took place here between those two Rākṣasas as they disputed with one another.
O gentle one, whose great bow— studded with pearls and gems and adorned with refined gold— has fallen broken upon the earth?
To whom does this golden armor belong, resembling the rising sun, studded with beads of lapis lazuli, now shattered and fallen upon the ground?
"O gentle one, whose is this divine parasol with its hundred ribs, adorned with celestial garlands, now fallen upon the ground with its staff broken?"
To whom did these asses belong, with faces like Piśācas, wearing golden breastplates, possessing terrifying forms and massive bodies, who were slain in battle?
To whom does this war-chariot belong— resplendent like a blazing fire, radiant, and bearing a banner in battle— which now lies cast aside and broken?
Whose arrows are these— each as long as a chariot axle, adorned with gold— that have been scattered about after being discharged by one of terrible deeds?
O gentle one, behold this hundredfold enmity of mine, which brings an end to life,
wrought by the Rākṣasas who are of most terrible heart and capable of assuming any form at will.
Sītā has indeed been carried off, or killed, or the poor woman has been devoured;
for dharma does not protect Sītā as she is being abducted in the great forest.
For even if Vaidehī has been devoured or carried away, O Lakṣmaṇa, who indeed in this world, O gentle one, could possibly do what is pleasing to me? Even if they were lords.
O Lakṣmaṇa, all beings might out of ignorance despise even the creator of the worlds, though he be a hero and one who feels compassion.
"Surely the lords of the thirty gods think of me as lacking in vigor, though I am gentle, devoted to the welfare of the world, self-controlled, and compassionate."
"Behold, Lakṣmaṇa, how even a virtue has turned into a fault upon reaching me!
Having withdrawn the moonlight for the destruction of all beings and the Rākṣasas this very day, I have risen like the great sun."
Neither Yakṣas, nor Gandharvas, nor Piśācas, nor Rākṣasas,
nor Kinnaras, nor humans, O Lakṣmaṇa, shall obtain happiness.
"Behold the sky, O Lakṣmaṇa, filled with my missiles and arrows;
today I shall indeed leave it impassable for those who roam the three worlds."
The multitude of planets was completely restrained, the moon was obscured,
and the brilliance of fire, wind, and the sun was shrouded in total darkness.
With the mountain peaks pulverized, the reservoirs of water drying up,
the trees, creepers, and shrubs destroyed, and the ocean utterly devastated.
The lords will not give up that unharmed Sītā to me;
at this very moment, O son of Sumitrā, they shall witness my prowess.
O Lakṣmaṇa, no living beings shall be able to fly into the sky while it is made continuous by the nets of arrows released from my bowstring.
"O Lakṣmaṇa, behold today this world afflicted by my iron arrows— its deer and birds destroyed and bewildered, thrown into total confusion, and stripped of all order."
With arrows drawn back to my ear, irresistible in this world of living beings, I shall rid the realm of Piśācas and Rākṣasas for the sake of Maithilī.
Today the gods shall behold the power of my arrows, released from my wrath and driven by indignation, as they fly far away.
Neither gods, nor Daityas, nor Piśācas,
nor Rākṣasas shall remain when the three worlds have been utterly destroyed by my wrath.
The worlds of the gods, dānavas, yakṣas, and even those of the rākṣasas shall fall in many ways, cut to pieces by floods of arrows;
today, with my shafts, I shall render these worlds devoid of all bounds.
Just as old age, death, time,
and destiny are never obstructed among all living beings, O Lakṣmaṇa,
so too am I, joined with wrath, undoubtedly not to be turned back.
If they do not point out to me today the blameless Sītā, the daughter of Mithilā, who possesses beautiful teeth,
then I shall overturn this entire world— including its gods, gandharvas, humans, and serpents, along with its mountains.
Thus Rāma was performing austerities, emaciated by the abduction of Sītā,
intent on the destruction of the worlds like the fire of universal dissolution.
He was looking at his strung bow and sighing again and again,
like the enraged Rudra desiring to slay the sacrificial animal at Dakṣa’s sacrifice.

Seeing Rāma enraged in a manner never seen before, Lakṣmaṇa, with palms joined in reverence and a parched mouth, spoke these words: Ram_3,61.3: "Having seen Rāma thus incensed, whom he had never seen so before, Lakṣmaṇa addressed him with his hands folded in salutation and his face withered."
Having formerly been gentle, self-controlled, and devoted to the welfare of all beings,
you ought not to abandon your true nature by falling under the sway of anger.
Fortune resides in the moon, radiance in the sun, movement in the wind, and forbearance in the earth;
all these qualities are constant, and in you, moreover, is unsurpassed glory.
But I do not know whose war-chariot, equipped with weapons and full of equipment, has been broken, by whom, or for what reason.
O Prince, this region, though its battles have ceased, is most terrible; it is scarred by hoof-marks and drenched with drops of blood.
"But this is the crushing defeat of one alone, O best of speakers, not of two;
for I do not see the tracks of a great army here."
You ought not to destroy the worlds for the sake of a single individual;
for rulers of the earth who are mild and tranquil employ punishment only when it is just.
"You are always the refuge and the supreme goal for all living beings;
O Raghava, who indeed would consider the loss of your wife to be a good thing?"
The rivers, the oceans, the mountains, the gods, the gandharvas,
and the dānavas are not capable of doing you any harm, just as virtuous men cannot offend one who is consecrated for a sacrifice.
O King, you ought to search for him by whom Sītā was abducted,
accompanied by me, bow in hand, and with the great seers as your companions.
And we shall search the ocean, as well as the mountains and forests,
the various formidable caves, and the lotus-lakes and mountain valleys.
With concentrated minds, we shall search through the worlds of the gods and the gandharvas until we find the one who has carried away your wife.
"O Lord of Kosala, if the lords of the thirty gods do not give you your wife through conciliation, then you shall do what is appropriate for the occasion thereafter."
O lord of men, if you do not obtain Sītā through virtue, conciliation, discipline, and prudent policy,
then destroy her with floods of gold-tufted arrows resembling the thunderbolt of great Indra.
To him, thus tormented by grief, lamenting like one who is helpless,
overcome by great delusion, utterly dejected, and senseless—
Then, after a moment as it were, Lakṣmaṇa, the son of Sumitrā, having comforted him,
addressed Rāma while pressing his feet.
O Rāma, through great austerity and through great deeds,
King Daśaratha obtained you, just as the immortals obtained the nectar of immortality.
Bound by your very virtues, the lord of the earth, the king, has attained divinity through separation from you, just as was heard regarding Bharata.
O descendant of Kakutstha, if you cannot endure this suffering that has come upon you,
then who else could endure it— anyone else being merely common, of little strength, and inferior?
For if you, being yourself afflicted, were to consume the worlds with your splendor,
O tiger among men, where indeed would the distressed subjects find relief?
This is indeed the very nature of the world: Yayāti, the son of Nahuṣa, attained the same world as Śakra, yet calamity touched him as well.
The great seer Vasiṣṭha, who was our father’s domestic priest, produced a hundred sons in a single day; likewise, they were slain again.
And this Goddess, the mother of the world, who is honored by all people—
O you whose word is true, even the trembling of her earth is now visible.
And these two eyes of the worlds, upon whom everything is established—
the mighty Sun and Moon— have both come under the grasp of Rāhu.
O bull among men, even the greatest of beings and the gods themselves cannot escape the power of destiny; so it is for all embodied beings.
O tiger among men, it is heard that both right conduct and misconduct exist even among the gods, beginning with Śakra; therefore, you ought not to be distressed.
"O sinless hero, even though Vaidehī has been lost or even abducted,
you ought not to grieve like some other ordinary man."
For those like you, who constantly perceive the truth, do not grieve even in the midst of great hardships; O Rāma, your vision remains undaunted.
Reflect upon this thoroughly with your intellect, O best of men;
for those endowed with wisdom and great insight discern the auspicious and the inauspicious through their intellect.
For actions whose merits and defects are unseen and which remain unperformed,
their desired fruit does not come to pass without the execution of those acts.
"For indeed, O hero, you yourself have instructed me many times in the past;
for who else could instruct you, even Bṛhaspati himself?"
And your intellect, O one of great wisdom, is difficult even for the gods to follow;
I shall awaken your knowledge, which has been overcome by grief.
Having observed your own divine and human prowess,
as well as that of the bull among the Ikṣvākus, strive for the destruction of your enemies.
O bull among men, what is the use of destroying everyone?
Rather, you ought to identify that very same wicked enemy and uproot him.
As soon as these well-spoken words were uttered by Lakṣmaṇa,
Rāghava, who grasps the essence, accepted that great essence even though he was his elder brother.
Restraining his own surging anger, the mighty-armed Rāma steadied his variegated bow and spoke to Lakṣmaṇa.
"What shall we do, dear child, or where shall we go, Lakṣmaṇa?
Consider by what means I might see Sītā."
To Rāma, who was thus afflicted by distress, Lakṣmaṇa said:
"You ought to search right here in Janasthāna."
It is strewn with many rākṣasas and filled with various trees and creepers;
here there are mountain fastnesses, as well as waterfalls and caves.
There were various formidable caves teeming with diverse herds of wild beasts,
as well as the dwellings of kinnaras and the abodes of gandharvas.
O bull among men, you, being endowed with such intelligence, ought to search for them together with me, for you are a great-souled one like me.
"They do not tremble in calamities, like mountains before the force of the wind.
Having been told this, he wandered through that entire forest together with Lakṣmaṇa.
Then the enraged Rāma, having fixed a terrible razor-headed arrow upon his bow,
[aimed it] at that most fortunate and best of the twice-born, who resembled the peak of a mountain.
He saw Jaṭāyu lying fallen on the ground, drenched in blood.
Seeing him, who resembled a mountain peak, Rāma said to Lakṣmaṇa:
"Sītā, the princess of Videha, has been devoured by this one; there is no doubt about it."
"This is clearly a Rākṣasa in the form of a vulture, wandering the forest;
having devoured the large-eyed Sītā, he sits at his ease.
I shall slay him with terrible, straight-flying arrows with blazing tips."
Having spoken thus, the enraged Rāma, as if shaking the earth bounded by the oceans, fixed a razor-sharp arrow to his bow and rushed toward the vulture.
Vomiting frothy blood,
the bird addressed Rāma, the son of Daśaratha, with a most piteous voice.
O long-lived one, that goddess whom you seek in the great forest like a medicinal herb— she is my very life, and both have been carried away by Rāvaṇa.
O Raghava, separated from you and Lakshmana,
the Queen was seen by me being carried away by the powerful Ravana.
I have rescued Sītā, and Rāvaṇa has been struck down upon the surface of the earth by me in battle, his chariot and parasol shattered.
This is his broken bow; this is his quiver;
and here, O Rāma, is his battle-chariot shattered in the fray.
"While I was exhausted, Rāvaṇa cut off my wings with his sword, seized Sītā, the princess of Videha, and leapt into the sky.
You ought not to kill me, who have already been struck down by the Rākṣasa. (Rāmāyaṇa 3.63.18)
But Rāma, having learned from him that story concerning his beloved Sītā,
embraced the king of vultures and wept along with Lakṣmaṇa.

Seeing him sighing with great difficulty on that narrow and difficult path, Rāma, himself distressed, spoke these words to the son of Sumitrā: "Ekam ekāyane durge niḥśvasantaṃ kathaṃcana / samīkṣya duḥkhito rāmaḥ saumitrim idam abravīt //" (Rāmāyaṇa 3.63.20) Having observed him sighing somehow or other on that single-track, treacherous path, the sorrowful Rāma addressed the son of Sumitrā as follows.
"Falling from my kingdom, dwelling in the forest, Sītā lost, and a brahmin slain—
such is this misfortune of mine that it could consume even fire itself."
Even if I were to cross the great ocean today in its entirety,
that lord of rivers would surely dry up through my misfortune.
"There is no one more unfortunate in this world of moving and unmoving beings than I, by whom this great snare of calamity has been encountered."
"This king of vultures, a friend of my father's, overcome by old age,
lies slain upon the ground due to the reversal of my own fortune."
Having spoken thus many times, Rāghava, together with Lakṣmaṇa,
touched Jaṭāyu, demonstrating his paternal affection.
Embracing that king of vultures, whose wings were severed and who was drenched in blood, Rāma cried out, "Where is Maithilī, my life’s equal? and, uttering these words, he fell to the ground.
But Rāma, seeing that vulture struck down upon the earth by the fierce one, spoke these words to Saumitri, who is endowed with friendship: Rām 3.64.1.
"Surely this bird, striving for my sake,
has been slain by a Rākṣasa in battle and is now giving up his life, which is so difficult to abandon."
"O Lakṣmaṇa, this vital breath remains within his body;
yet, deprived of his natural voice, he gazes about in distress."
O Jaṭāyu, if you are able to speak again,
tell me of Sītā— blessings be upon you— and tell me of your own death.
For what reason did Rāvaṇa carry off Sītā? What offense have I committed against him, that my beloved was seen and carried away by Rāvaṇa?
O best of the twice-born, how was that heart-stealing face, which resembled the moon, at that time? And what words were spoken by Sītā then?
Of what prowess is that Rākṣasa, what is his appearance, and what is his occupation?
And where is his dwelling, my dear father? Tell me as I ask you.
Then, looking up at Rāma as he was lamenting immediately thereafter, Jaṭāyu, his soul dejected, spoke these words to him with a very feeble voice.
She was carried away through the air by Rāvaṇa, the lord of the rākṣasas,
who employed a vast illusion filled with wind and stormy weather.
"O father, while I was exhausted, that night-stalker cut off my wings,
took Sītā, the princess of Videha, and departed toward the south."
My vital breaths are failing, O Raghava, and my vision is spinning;
I see golden trees with hair made of uśīra grass.
In the very moment that Rāvaṇa departs taking Sītā,
the owner of lost wealth quickly recovers it.
That moment indeed arrived, O descendant of Kakutstha, yet he did not perceive it;
like a fish seizing the hook, he will quickly perish.
And you should not feel any distress regarding Janaka’s daughter;
having slain that Rākṣasa in battle, you will soon take your pleasure with Vaidehī.
As the vulture, undeluded, addressed Rāma,
blood flowed from his mouth as he was dying over the meat.
"The son of Viśravas, the very brother of Vaiśravaṇa"—
having said this, the lord of birds gave up his life, which is so difficult to relinquish.
As Rāma, with palms joined in reverence, cried out, "Speak!
Speak!", the vital breaths of the vulture abandoned his body and ascended into the sky.
Then, having cast his head upon the ground, stretched out his feet,
and tossed his body about, he fell prostrate upon the surface of the earth.
Beholding that vulture with copper-hued eyes, lifeless and resembling a mountain,
Rāma, dejected by his many sorrows, spoke to the son of Sumitrā.
Having lived happily for many years in the dwelling of the rākṣasas,
this bird has wandered here through the Daṇḍaka forest.
He who has endured for many years and has persisted for a long time—here he lies today, slain; for time is indeed difficult to overcome.
"Behold, Lakṣmaṇa, this vulture who was my benefactor has been slain;
he indeed rescued Sītā from the powerful Rāvaṇa."
Having renounced his great ancestral kingdom of the vultures,
this lord of birds has given up his life for my sake.
"Indeed, O Saumitri, virtuous practitioners of the Dharma are seen everywhere— even among those born as animals— who are heroic and worthy of providing refuge."
O gentle one, O scorcher of enemies, the sorrow born from the abduction of Sītā does not affect me as much as the destruction of the vulture on my account.
"Just as the illustrious King Daśaratha, who is of great renown, is worthy of worship and honor by me, so too is this lord of birds."
"O Saumitri, bring wood; I shall kindle a fire.
I wish to cremate the king of vultures, who has met his death on my account."
"O Saumitri, I shall place this lord of the world of birds upon the funeral pyre; I will cremate him who was slain by the fierce Rākṣasa."

Whatever destination belongs to those devoted to sacrifice, whatever destination belongs to those who maintain the sacred fires, whatever belongs to those who never retreat in battle, and whatever belongs to those who bestow land as gifts— [may I attain that].
"Permitted by me, go to the unsurpassed worlds;
O Great Being, King of Vultures, you have been consecrated by me, so depart."
Having spoken thus, the righteous Rāma, filled with grief like one mourning for his own kinsman, placed the lord of birds upon the blazing pyre and cremated him.
Then the heroic Rāma, having gone to the forest with the son of Sumitrā,
killed large deer and spread them out for that twice-born man.
Having extracted the flesh of the rohita fish and formed it into patties, the highly illustrious Rāma gave them to Śakuni on a beautiful, verdant grassy meadow.
Rāma quickly recited that prayer for the deceased mortal which the twice-born recite, so that he might swiftly attain heaven.
Then, having gone to the river Godāvarī, both those sons of the best of men offered water for the funeral libation to that king of vultures.
That king of vultures, having performed a glorious and most difficult deed, was struck down in battle;
then, having been consecrated by one who was like a great seer, he went to his own auspicious and meritorious destination.
Having thus offered water to him, the two descendants of Raghu then set forth,
searching for Sītā in the forest as they traveled toward the western direction.
Having gone toward that southern direction, the two descendants of Ikṣvāku, bearing arrows, bows, and swords, set out upon a path that had never been trodden before.
Enveloped by many shrubs, trees, and creepers,
it was a fortress-like thicket, hidden on all sides, dense, and terrible to behold.
Having proceeded with speed toward the southern direction,
those two of great strength passed through that most formidable great forest.
Thereafter, having traveled three krośas from Janasthāna, those two Raghava princes of great prowess entered the dense Krauñca forest.
Resembling various dense clouds, it appeared joyful on all sides,
filled with auspicious flowers of many colors and throngs of beasts and birds.
Desiring to see Vaidehī, the two of them searched that forest,
lingering here and there, emaciated by the abduction of Sītā.
But Lakṣmaṇa, possessed of great splendor, courage, virtue, and purity,
spoke these words with joined palms to his brother of blazing majesty.
"My arm throbs violently, and my mind is as if agitated;
moreover, I perceive for the most part that the omens are unfavorable."
Therefore, noble one, prepare yourself and carry out this beneficial advice;
for indeed, my very omens portend immediate peril.
"This bird named Vañculaka is most dreadful;
it shrieks as if foretelling our victory in battle."
As they were thus searching through that entire forest with such vigor,
a vast sound arose, as if shattering the forest itself.
As if intensely enveloped by the wind,
the roar of that forest arose, as though filling the very heavens.
Seeking that sound, Rāma, together with his younger brother in the thicket,
beheld a Rākṣasa of immense body and broad chest.
Then he sat down there, facing those two who stood before him—
a headless and neckless trunk with its mouth in its belly, grown to a massive size.
Covered with sharp bristles, as lofty as a great mountain,
resembling a dark blue cloud, fierce, and sounding like the thundering of clouds.
With a single, formidable eye upon his chest— tawny, with great lashes, wide, and long— he who sees with rapid vision.
He was endowed with great tusks and was licking his massive mouth,
devouring most terrible bears, lions, deer, and elephants.
Displaying his two formidable arms, each a yojana in length,
he seized with his hands various bears, flocks of birds, and deer.
Dragging away and tearing apart many leaders of deer herds,
he stood blocking the path of those two brothers who had sought refuge with him.
Then, having passed beyond that distance, at the measure of a *krośa*, they beheld a massive,
cruel, and terrifying headless trunk (*kabandha*), enveloped by its own arms.
That mighty-armed one, stretching out his two vast arms to their full extent,
seized both Raghavas together, pressing them with force.
The two brothers, armed with swords and firm bows, possessing fierce energy and mighty arms, were being dragged along, rendered helpless despite their great strength.
The mighty-armed Kabandha, the best of the Dānavas, said to them:
"Who are you two, with shoulders like those of bulls, bearing great swords and bows?"
"Having reached this terrible region, you have arrived as my prey. Tell me, what is your business here, and for what purpose have you two come?"
Having reached this place, we two stand here afflicted by hunger,
equipped with arrows, bows, and swords like two bulls with sharp horns;
having come within the reach of my mouth, our life is now difficult to regain.
Having heard those words of the evil-minded Kabandha,
Rāma, with a parched face, spoke to Lakṣmaṇa.
O you of true prowess, having encountered a calamity more grievous than any hardship—
a terrible misfortune leading to the end of life— yet failing to find that beloved one, [I am consumed by grief].
The power of Time, O Lakṣmaṇa, is exceedingly great among all beings.
See how both you and I, O tiger among men, have been deluded by calamities.
There is no burden too heavy for Destiny to impose upon all creatures, O Lakṣmaṇa.
Even those who are brave, powerful, and skilled in weapons perish on the field of battle when overtaken by Time, like bridges made of sand.
Having spoken thus, the son of Daśaratha— possessing firm truth and prowess, great fame, and majesty—
looked upon the son of Sumitrā, who was likewise of exalted valor, and then confirmed his own resolve with a steady mind.
Seeing the two brothers, Rāma and Lakṣmaṇa,
standing there with their arms encircled like nooses, Kabandha spoke these words.
"Why do these two bulls among Kṣatriyas stand here, having seen me afflicted by hunger?
They must have been sent for the sake of food by fate, their minds having lost their senses."
Having heard those words, which were appropriate for the occasion and beneficial, Lakṣmaṇa— overcome with distress yet resolved upon valor— then spoke.
"Before that lowest of Rākṣasas can quickly seize both you and me,
let us therefore swiftly cut off his two heavy arms with our swords."
Then those two descendants of Raghu, skilled in the knowledge of place and time,
being greatly delighted, severed his arms at the shoulders with their very swords.
Then Rāma swiftly severed his right arm with his sword without hesitation, while the hero Lakṣmaṇa cut off his left.
With his arms severed, that mighty-armed one fell with a great roar,
making the sky, the earth, and all the directions resound like a thundercloud.
Seeing his two arms severed and drenched in a flood of blood, the wretched Dānava asked those two heroes, "Who are you? (Rāmāyaṇa 3.66.8).
While he was speaking thus, the mighty Lakṣmaṇa, endowed with auspicious marks, described the descendant of Kakutstha to Kabandha.
"This is the heir of Ikṣvāku, known to people by the name Rāma;
know me to be his younger brother, Lakṣmaṇa."
While this man of divine power was dwelling in the lonely forest, his wife was carried off by a rākṣasa; desiring her, we have come here.
But who are you, and for what purpose are you here in the forest, resembling a headless trunk,
writhing with your shanks broken and your mouth blazing upon your chest?
Thus addressed by Lakṣmaṇa, Kabandha,
remembering those words of Indra, spoke this reply with supreme joy.
"Welcome to you both, O tigers among men! By good fortune I behold you;
and by good fortune these two arms of mine have been severed by you."
O tiger among men, listen as I relate to you in truth how I came by this hideous form due to my lack of discipline. Ram_3,66.15.
"O Rāma, O mighty-armed one of great strength and prowess, in former times my form was inconceivable and renowned throughout the three worlds,
like the bodies of Soma, Śakra, and the Sun."
Having assumed this great form that terrifies the world,
O Rāma, I then and there terrified the sages dwelling in the forest here and there.
Then, the great seer named Sthūlaśiras, who was gathering various forest produce, was provoked to anger by me when he was insulted by this form of mine.
Having looked at me, he who uttered that terrible curse said this to me:
"Let this very same loathsome form of yours remain as it is, O cruel one!"

When I asked him for an end to the curse, he became enraged and spoke these words regarding the curse I had pronounced upon him: "Ram_3,67.5" [Note: The provided text fragment includes the verse number].
When Rāma, having severed your arms, shall burn you in the lonely forest,
then you will regain your own vast and auspicious form.
"Know, O Lakṣmaṇa, that this son of Danu, resplendent with beauty,
has attained this form upon the field of battle due to the wrath of Indra."
"For I gratified the Grandfather with fierce asceticism;
he granted me long life, and then delusion took hold of me."
"I have attained a long life; what can Śakra do to me?"—resolving thus, I defied Śakra in battle.
By the hundred-jointed thunderbolt released from his arm,
both his thighs and his head were driven back into his body.
Though entreated by me, he sent him to the abode of Yama;
he said to me, "Let the word of the Grandfather be true."
How is it possible that one whose thighs, head, and face are shattered, and who has been struck by a thunderbolt, could live for even a very long time without food?
Thus addressed by me, Śakra gave me two arms a yojana in length,
and he fashioned a mouth within my belly with sharp fangs.
Thus, drawing the forest-dwellers— lions, elephants, deer, and tigers— toward me with my two long arms, I devour them on all sides.
But Indra said to me: "When Rāma, together with Lakṣmaṇa, shall cut off your arms in battle, then you will go to heaven."
"You are that very Rāma; may prosperity be yours, O Rāghava! It was told by the great seer according to the truth that I cannot be slain by anyone else."
"For I shall provide counsel to you, O bull among men,
and I shall point out a friend to you both once you have been consecrated by the fire."
Thus addressed by that Danu, the righteous-souled Raghava spoke these words while Lakshmana listened.
My illustrious wife Sītā was carried off by Rāvaṇa while I had gone out from Janasthāna with my brother at our ease.
I know only the name of that Rākṣasa, but not his form;
neither do we know his dwelling place nor his power.
It is fitting for those who act with compassion and toward whom you have rendered assistance to show mercy to these helpless ones who are thus wandering about, afflicted by grief.
"O hero, having brought dry logs broken by elephants at the proper time, we shall devour you in a great pit that has been prepared."
Therefore, tell me of Sītā—by whom she was taken or where;
perform this great service for me if you know the truth of the matter.
Thus addressed by Rāma with these unsurpassed words, Danu,
skilled in speech, replied to the eloquent Raghava.
I possess no divine knowledge, nor do I know Maithilī;
once I have been consumed by fire and have resumed my own form, I shall tell you who it is that will know her.
"O Lord, as long as I am unburnt, I have no power to discern that immensely powerful Rākṣasa by whom your Sītā was carried away."
"O Raghava, my great consciousness has indeed fallen away due to the fault of a curse;
by my own doing, I have obtained this form, which is despised by the world."
"But as long as the sun, whose horses are weary, has not yet set,
O Rāma, throw me into a pit and cremate me according to the prescribed rites."
"O delight of the Raghus, I have been burnt by you in the pit according to justice;
O hero, I shall tell you of him who will recognize that Rākṣasa."
Therefore, O Raghava, you should form a friendship with him by acting with justice;
being pleased, he of swift prowess will provide you with assistance.
For there is nothing unknown to him in the three worlds, O Raghava;
he has indeed traversed all the worlds in the past for various reasons.
When those two heroes had been addressed thus by Kabandha, O lord of men,
they reached a mountain cleft and set fire to it.
Lakṣmaṇa, however, set the funeral pyre ablaze on all sides with great flaming torches; it blazed up fiercely in every direction.
That great body of Kabandha, resembling a mass of clarified butter as it was being cooked by its own fat,
was consumed only slowly by the fire.
Having quickly shaken off the funeral pyre, that one of great strength rose up like a smokeless fire,
wearing two stainless garments and a celestial garland.
Then, with great speed from the funeral pyre, he rose up instantly, radiant, clad in spotless garments, joyful, and adorned with ornaments on every limb.
Standing in a radiant, glory-bestowing celestial chariot drawn by swans,
that one of great splendor illuminated the ten directions with his brilliance.
Having ascended into the air, Kabandha spoke these words to Rāma:
"Listen, O Rāghava, to the truth of how you shall reach the boundary."

O Rāma, there are six methods in this world by which everything is deliberated; that which has been thoroughly examined by the end of its ten stages is what is pursued through the portion of those ten stages.
O Rāma, you and Lakṣmaṇa have fallen to a low state,
since for your sake you have encountered this calamity— the assault upon your wife.
Therefore, O best among friends, you must certainly act as that friend;
for even upon reflection, I do not see how you can achieve success without doing so.
Listen, O Rāma, I shall tell you: there is a monkey named Sugrīva who has been driven out by his enraged brother Vālin, the son of Śakra.
On Ṛṣyamūka, the best of mountains, adorned by the vicinity of Lake Pampā,
dwells that self-controlled hero together with four monkeys.
O Raghava, go from here this very day and quickly make him your friend;
having approached him while the fire is blazing, do so without malice.
And you must not disregard Sugrīva, the lord of the monkeys; for he is grateful, able to assume any form at will, seeks a companion, and is full of valor.
For you two are capable today of performing the task he desires to accomplish;
whether his purpose is achieved or not, he will carry out your business.
The son of Ṛkṣarajas,
the legitimate son of Bhāskara who had committed an offense against Vālin, wanders apprehensively around Lake Pampā.
Having quickly laid aside your weapons, O Raghava, by means of your truthfulness, make that monkey who dwells on Mount Rishyamuka your forest-dwelling companion.
For that elephant among monkeys, through his skill, thoroughly understands all the haunts in this world of those who eat human flesh.
O Raghava, subduer of enemies, there is indeed nothing in this world that is unknown to him,
as long as the thousand-rayed sun shines forth.
Having searched the vast rivers, mountains, mountain fastnesses,
and caves together with the monkeys, he will find your wife.
And Raghava will dispatch monkeys of massive body to search the quarters for that Sita, who is grieving due to separation from you.
That foremost of monkeys, having slain the demons, will restore your blameless beloved to you, whether she has gone to the peak of Mount Meru or is dwelling even in the depths of Pātāla.
Having thus pointed out the means for the recovery of Sītā to Rāma,
Kabandha, who was skilled in understanding the meaning of things, spoke these words full of significance once more.
O Rāma, this is the auspicious path where these blossoming trees,
situated in the western direction, shine forth, enchanting to the mind.
Jambū, priyāla, and panasa trees; plakṣa, nyagrodha, and tinduka; aśvattha and karṇikāra; mangoes and other such trees.
Either by climbing them or by forcibly felling them to the ground,
you two shall go along eating their fruits, which are like nectar.
Wandering through excellent regions from mountain to mountain and forest to forest,
you two heroes will then reach the lotus pond named Pampā.
O Rāma, it was free from gravel, devoid of treacherous spots, with level landing-stairs and no moss; it was covered with newly formed sands and adorned with lotuses and water-lilies.
There, O Raghava, swans, ducks, cranes,
and ospreys, dwelling in the waters of Pampā, warble with melodious voices.
"Those auspicious ones, unskilled in slaughter, do not tremble upon seeing men;
you shall devour those large twice-born ones who resemble lumps of clarified butter."
O Rāghava, O Rāma, there at Pampā you killed with your arrows those excellent fish— rohitas, vakratuṇḍas, and nalas.
Endowed with devotion to you, Lakṣmaṇa will offer you these iron spikes— unpeeled, heated, thick, and each possessing a single barb.
As you were eating many fish upon a bed of flowers by the Pampā,
its auspicious waters were fragrant with lotuses, pleasantly cool, and free from impurity.
Then, having drawn up that untroubled water which resembles silver and crystal,
Lakṣmaṇa will cause him to drink it from a lotus leaf.

O best of men, you will see in Pampā forest-dwelling wild boars, large and resting in mountain caves, who have returned out of a longing for water and are bellowing like bulls, endowed with beautiful forms.
Wandering in the evening, O Rāma, you will cast off your grief upon seeing the trees laden with blossoms and the cool waters of the Pampā.
There, O Raghava, were Tilaka and Naktamāla trees covered with *sumana* flowers, as well as blooming blue lotuses and red lotuses.
No man there was who would offer those garlands;
for there were the disciples of Mataṅga, sages who were deeply concentrated in meditation.
As they, tormented by the weight of their burden, were gathering forest produce for their preceptor,
drops of sweat fell rapidly from their bodies onto the earth.
O Rāghava, those garlands produced by the ascetic power of the sages at that time, arising from drops of perspiration, do not perish.
O descendant of Kakutstha, even today their female attendant, a long-lived female ascetic named Śabarī, is seen in that very place.
But seeing you, O Rāma— who are ever established in righteousness, honored by all beings, and like unto a god— she shall go to the heavenly world.
Then, O Rāma, descendant of Kakutstha, having reached the western shore of the Pampā, you will behold that incomparable and secret hermitage site.
The nāgas are unable to attack that hermitage,
for by the power of the sage Mataṅga’s ordinance, that forest is protected.
In that forest, which resembles the Nandana grove and is like a celestial park, filled with various kinds of birds, you shall take delight, O Rāma, in perfect peace.
But to the east of Pampā stands Ṛṣyamūka, with its trees in full bloom;
it is named Suduḥkhārohaṇa, protected by young elephants,
and was fashioned long ago by Brahmā as a noble place.
O Rāma, whatever wealth a man lying on the summit of that mountain obtains in a dream, he acquires upon waking.
But one of wicked conduct and evil deeds does not escape him;
right there, the Rākṣasas seize him while he sleeps and strike him down.
Furthermore, O Rāma, the great cry of young elephants dwelling in Mataṅga’s forest is heard as they play upon the Pampā lake.
Drenched by streams of blood, those supreme elephants, swift as clouds and dark in hue, move about scattered in various directions after having been struck together.
Having drunk there that pure, cool, and inexhaustible water,
those forest-dwellers, filled with agitation, turned back and plunged into the forests.
O Rāma, descendant of Kakutstha, that mountain possesses a great cave covered by a stone slab; however, entry into it is difficult.
At the eastern gate of that cave was a great lake of cool water,
delightful with its many roots and fruits, and surrounded by various trees.
Sugrīva dwells there with four monkeys;
sometimes he remains upon the summit of that mountain.
Having thus instructed both Rāma and Lakṣmaṇa,
the valiant Kabandha, wearing a garland and radiant as the sun, shone brightly in the sky.
Then Rāma and Lakṣmaṇa, as they were setting out, spoke these words from nearby to that illustrious Kabandha who was stationed in the air: "Go on your way."
"You must go for the sake of accomplishing your task," he said to them;
then, having taken leave of those two who were well-pleased, Kabandha set forth.
Having assumed that form, the Kabandha, surrounded by splendor and with a body like the sun, stood in the sky; beholding Rāma, he pointed him out and then spoke, saying, "Form a friendship."
Having been shown that path in the forest by Kabandha,
those two sons of the best of men set out toward the western direction from Lake Pampā.
Beholding upon the mountains many trees laden with fruits as sweet as honey, Rāma and Lakṣmaṇa proceeded to see Sugrīva.
Having made their dwelling upon the mountain ridge, those two descendants of Raghu,
the scions of the Raghus, arrived at the western shore of Pampā.
Having reached the western shore of the Puṣkariṇī Pampā,
they then beheld there the delightful hermitage of Śabarī.
Having reached that hermitage, which was surrounded by many trees and exceedingly beautiful, the two of them beheld it and approached Śabarī.
Seeing them then, the perfected one rose up with palms joined in reverence and grasped the feet of Rāma and the wise Lakṣmaṇa.
Then Rāma spoke to that female ascetic of rigid vows:
"Have your obstacles been overcome? Does your asceticism flourish?"
O lady rich in asceticism, is your anger restrained and is your food regulated?
Have you attained your religious observances, and is your mind at ease? O sweet-spoken one, has your service to your elders borne fruit?
Questioned by Rāma, that aged Śabarī— a perfected woman esteemed by the Siddhas— spoke as she stood before him.
When you reached Citrakūṭa, those celestial chariots of incomparable splendor by which I used to attend upon you ascended from here to heaven.
And I was told by those illustrious great seers, who were knowers of the Dharma:
"Rāma will come to this most holy hermitage of yours."
"You must accept him as a guest together with the son of Sumitrā;
upon seeing him, you shall go to the most excellent and imperishable worlds."
O bull among men, O tiger among men, I have gathered various forest fruits produced on the banks of the Pampā for your sake.
Thus addressed by Śabarī, the righteous Rāghava said this to Śabarī: "I know that you have always remained free from exclusion."
I have heard the true account of the power of that high-souled one from Danda; now, if you agree, I wish to see it for myself with my own eyes.
Having heard these words issuing from the mouth of Rāma,
Śabarī showed both of them that great forest.
Behold, O delight of the Raghus, the forest renowned as Mataṅgavana, which resembles a dense mass of clouds and is teeming with beasts and birds.
O one of great luster, here my gurus, whose souls were cultivated,
performed oblations at this sacred ford, which was consecrated by mantras and honored with sacred formulas.
This is the sacrificial altar in this very place where they, having been well-honored by me,
offer oblations of flowers with hands trembling from exhaustion.
O best of the Raghus, behold even today how, by the power of their asceticism,
those altars of incomparable splendor illuminate all directions with their radiance.
When they were unable to proceed, exhausted by the fatigue of fasting,
behold the seven oceans assembled together as soon as they were thought of.
The bark garments cast by them here upon the trees after their consecration have not dried even today, O descendant of Raghu, in this place.
This entire forest has been seen by you, and what was to be heard has been heard;
therefore, I wish to be permitted by you to cast off this body.
I desire to go into the presence of those sages of purified souls, whose hermitage I shall serve as an attendant.
Having heard those most righteous words, Rāghava, together with Lakṣmaṇa, spoke with a joyful countenance: "I grant you leave; go."
But having been permitted by Rāma, she offered herself as an oblation into the fire;
resembling a blazing flame, she departed for heaven itself.
By means of her own meditative concentration, Śabarī went to that holy place where those great seers of virtuous soul dwell.
When Śabarī had departed for heaven by virtue of her own deeds,
Rāghava, together with his brother Lakṣmaṇa, began to reflect.
Having reflected upon that power of the high-souled ones,
the righteous Rāghava spoke to Lakṣmaṇa, who was intent on his welfare and single-minded in devotion.
"O gentle one, this hermitage of those who have perfected themselves has been seen; it is full of many wonders, where deer and tigers dwell in confidence and which is frequented by various birds."
And at these bathing places, O Lakṣmaṇa, we have duly performed ablutions in the seven oceans and offered libations to our ancestors.
That which was inauspicious has perished, and this auspiciousness has arrived;
therefore, O Lakṣmaṇa, my mind is now filled with joy.
"For in your heart, O tiger among men, auspiciousness shall manifest.
Therefore come, let us go to that lovely Pampā."
There stands Mount Ṛśyamūka, visible not far away,
where dwells the righteous Sugrīva, the son of Aṃśumat,
who, ever terrified by the fear of Vālin, lives together with four other monkeys.
I am hastening to see Sugrīva, that bull among monkeys;
for, O gentle one, the search for Sītā depends entirely upon him.
To Rāma, who was speaking thus, the son of Sumitrā replied:
"Let us go there quickly; my mind also hastens."
Then, having departed from that hermitage, the lord of the people, the sovereign,
went to Lake Pampā together with Lakṣmaṇa.
Beholding that great forest on all sides,
abounding in flowers and vast trees, resounding with the cries of koyaṣṭis, arjunakas, śatapatras, and kīcakas, as well as various other birds, he gazed upon it.
Beholding various trees and diverse lakes, Rāma,
tormented by desire, proceeded toward a great lake.
Having reached that lake which flows with water from afar, Rāma entered the pool known by the name Mataṅgasaras.
Overcome with grief, Rāma, the son of Daśaratha,
entered the Pampā lotus pond, which was covered with lotuses.
It was filled with *tilaka*, *aśoka*, *puṃnāga*, *bakula*,
and *uddālaka* trees, crowded with delightful groves, and its waters were thick with lotuses.
Abounding in water as clear as crystal, covered with smooth sands,
crowded with fish and tortoises, and adorned by trees standing upon its banks.
It was entwined by creepers as if by devoted female friends;
it was frequented by kinnaras, uragas, gandharvas, yakṣas, and rākṣasas;
filled with various trees and vines, it was an auspicious reservoir of cool water.

With its copper-colored lotuses, it was like a crimson rug; with its circles of white water-lilies, it was white; with its clusters of blue lilies, it was blue; and with its many varieties of flowers, it was as if covered by a multicolored carpet.
It was filled with *aravinda* and *utpala* lotuses, abounding in fragrant *padma* lilies,
endowed with groves of blossoming mango trees, and resounded with the cries of peacocks.
Having seen that Pampā, the radiant Rāma, son of Daśaratha, together with the son of Sumitrā, lamented out of longing.
With *tilaka* trees, *bījapūra*, and *vaṭa* trees, as well as white trees in bloom, with *karavīra* and well-flowered *puṃnāga* trees; ||| Ram_3,71.21 |||
It was graced like a young woman by clusters of *mālatī* and *kundapuṣpa*, as well as by *bhaṇḍīra*, *nicula*,
*aśoka*, *saptaparṇa*, *ketaka*, and *atimuktaka* trees,
along with various other kinds of trees.
On its bank stands the previously mentioned mountain adorned with minerals,
renowned as Ṛśyamūka, its forests filled with variegated blossoms.
The son of that great-souled one named Ṛkṣarajas is Hari;
possessed of great heroism, he dwells there, renowned by the name Sugrīva.
"Go to Sugrīva, the lord of monkeys, O bull among men," he spoke these words again to Lakṣmaṇa, whose valor is truth.
Then, having gradually traversed that great path which extended for a long distance while surveying the forest,
he beheld Lake Pampā, whose woodland was beautiful to behold and crowded with many kinds of various birds.
